docs.text:
What does the record look like?

Why: before fitting any curve, look at the data. What you see decides which curves are worth trying.

  2. highest and lowest: the largest and the smallest value of the co2 column.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: highest and lowest.

docs.title: 2. How do we choose a curve we can trust on years it has not seen?¶
docs.text: A curve that fits the past is not yet a curve to trust about the future. A flexible enough curve can pass close to every month in the record and still be wrong about next year, because it has learned the record's accidents along with its pattern. The fair test is to hide some years from the curve and see how well it does on them. In short: hide some data from yourself, then check.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 2¶
docs.text:
Which months does each set hold?

Why: every fit and every score below uses these three sets. Each is a mask on the year column, written with the table skills of the tables week.

  1. training: True for the months up to the end of 2000.
  2. validation: True for the months from 2001 to 2010, both years included.
  3. test: True for the months from 2011 on.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: training, validation and test.

docs.text:
How badly does a straight line miss the validation years?

Why: the straight line is the simplest curve, and the one to beat. It is the age-of-the-universe line, with time across instead of distance.

  1. line: a straight line fitted to the training months: decades across (as a one-column table), co2 up.
  2. residuals: the validation months' CO2 minus what the line says for them.
  3. line_validation_rmse: the RMSE of those residuals.
  4. The figure: the line drawn over the whole record.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: line and line_validation_rmse.

docs.text:
Does a squared column help on the validation years?

Why: the record bends upward; a squared column is the simplest way to let the curve bend.

  1. mlo["decades2"]: a new column, the decades column squared.
  2. squared: the curve fitted to the training months with both decades and decades2.
  3. squared_validation_rmse: its miss on the validation months.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: squared and squared_validation_rmse.

docs.text:
Do two seasonal columns help on the validation years?

Why: the teeth are what the squared curve still misses. Two waves, one fit, should draw them.

  1. angle: each month's angle, by the formula above, from the month column.
  2. mlo["sin_month"] and mlo["cos_month"]: two new columns, the sine and the cosine of each month's angle.
  3. seasonal: the curve fitted to the training months with decades, decades2, sin_month and cos_month.
  4. seasonal_validation_rmse: its miss on the validation months.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: seasonal and seasonal_validation_rmse.

docs.text:
Which of four curves should we trust?

Why: this is the choice itself. Each candidate keeps the two seasonal columns and adds one more power of decades. The loop fits each one to the training months and scores it twice: on the training months it learned from, and on the validation months it did not.

  1. The new columns, the candidates and their names are given.
  2. Inside the loop, for each list of columns: fit to the training months, then append the training RMSE to training_rmses and the validation RMSE to validation_rmses.
  3. best: the name of the candidate with the smallest validation RMSE, found with np.argmin, as in the age-of-the-universe week.
  4. The figure: both lists of RMSE, one point per candidate.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: training_rmses, validation_rmses and best.

docs.title: 3. When will CO2 pass 450 ppm?¶
docs.text: The validation months have done their job, so now they can join the training months. The choice is made: the squared curve with seasons. Fit it again to everything before the test, 1958–2010, and then, once, see how it does on 2011 onward. That one number is the honest estimate of how well this kind of curve forecasts years it has never seen.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 7¶
docs.text:
How well does the chosen curve do on the test years?

Why: the test months are the final exam. They were never used to fit or to choose, so their RMSE is the fair measure of the curve's forecasts.

  1. before_test: True for the months up to the end of 2010.
  2. chosen: the chosen curve, fitted to those months.
  3. test_rmse: its miss on the test months.
  4. The figure: the test months and what the curve said for them.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: chosen and test_rmse.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 8¶
docs.text:
When does the yearly average pass 450 ppm?

Why: this is the week's question. The answer is a mask on the forecast table.

  1. everything: the chosen curve fitted to every month of the record.
  2. future["co2"]: what it says for each year of future.
  3. year_450: the first year whose forecast is 450 ppm or more.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: everything and year_450.

docs.title: 4. How far can we trust that answer?¶
docs.text:
2034 is the answer of one curve. Three checks show how much to trust it.

First: the test misses have a direction. The test RMSE treats a miss above the curve and a miss below it alike. Average the test residuals year by year instead, and see which way they go:

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 9¶
docs.text:
How big is the yearly wave in the chosen curve, and when is it highest?

Why: the size and timing of the wave are a check the record can answer: the close-up figure of section 1 shows the data's own highs and lows.

  1. sine_weight and cosine_weight: the numbers everything found for sin_month and cos_month. The fit keeps them in .coef_, in the order of columns, so the position of a column's name in columns is the position of its number.
  2. seasonal_part: for the twelve months, sine weight × sine of the angle plus cosine weight × cosine of the angle (month_numbers and month_angle are given).
  3. mlo_swing: the wave's highest value minus its lowest.
  4. mlo_peak and mlo_low: the month numbers where the wave is highest and lowest. np.argmax gives the position of the largest value and np.argmin the position of the smallest, as in the age-of-the-universe week; read the month number at that position from month_numbers.
  5. The figure: the wave over the twelve months.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: mlo_swing, mlo_peak and mlo_low.

docs.title: The question, answered¶
docs.text: Around 2034, by the curve the validation years chose, fitted to the whole record. Other reasonable curves put the year anywhere from 2032 to 2046, and since 2016 the record has run above the curve fitted to its first 53 years.

docs.title: The science¶
docs.text:
When will CO2 pass 450 ppm? Choose a model on years it was not fitted to: fit on the training years, choose on the validation years, and test once on years nobody looked at. A model's columns are a choice: a squared column bends the line, a sine and a cosine of the month draw the seasons, and more columns always fit the training years better but can fit new years worse. A forecast beyond the data is an extrapolation: the year CO2 passes 450 ppm moves by more than ten years with the model, and the record has already pulled away from the curve fitted to its first five decades.

  • Leakage. Any route by which information about the data you are scoring on reaches the model before you score it.
  • Polynomial degree. The degree of a polynomial is how many bends it is allowed: degree 1 is a straight line, degree 2 bends once.
  • Overfitting. A curve that memorises the data you gave it fails on the data you did not.
  • Train/test split. Hide some data from yourself, then check.
  • Validation years. Years held back to choose between models. Once they have chosen, they are no longer a fair test.
  • Test years. Years nobody looks at until the end, checked once, on the model already chosen.
  • Seasonal column. A column that rises and falls once a year, so the fitted curve can rise and fall with the seasons.
  • Extrapolation. Reading a fitted curve beyond the years it was fitted on. Nothing in the data checks it there.
  • Bias-variance. Too simple and you miss the pattern; too flexible and you memorise the noise.
  • Validation curve. Plot the miss on the training years and on the held-back years against how flexible the curve is; the flexibility worth choosing is where the held-back miss is lowest.
  • Typical miss. Square every gap between what happened and what the curve said, average the squares, and take the square root: the usual size of a miss, in the data's own units.

Why it rises. Burning coal, oil and gas, and clearing forests, release CO2. About half of what people emit stays in the air (48 percent over 2014–2023, by the Global Carbon Budget 2024); the oceans and the land take up the rest. Carbon is always moving between the air, plants, soils and the ocean; burning fossil fuels adds a flow that had no return path on human time scales.

The carbon cycle: where carbon is stored (black numbers, billions of tonnes) and how fast it moves (arrows, billions of tonnes a year). The numbers are from the 1990s; today the air holds more, and fossil fuels add more each year. The shape of the cycle is what matters here. Diagram: NASA Earth Observatory, redrawn by Kevin Saff and FischX (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons.

How unusual is today's level? Bubbles of old air trapped in the Antarctic ice sheet record CO2 long before anyone measured it. Through the ice ages of the last 800,000 years it swung from below 200 ppm in the coldest times to about 300 in the warmest, and it did not go above 300 until the industrial age:

CO2 over the last 800,000 years from ice cores, with the last thousand years enlarged; the steep black end is the age of measurements like Mauna Loa's. Figure: Femke Nijsse (CC BY-SA 3.0), via Wikimedia Commons.

Each year CO2 climbs to a high in May and falls to a low in September or October, and each high sits above the last. The yearly fall comes from plants. Most of the world's land that has a winter is in the northern half of the planet: forests and grasslands that green up together in spring and summer, taking CO2 out of the air, and lose their leaves together in autumn and winter, when decay gives it back. Mauna Loa, at 19.5° N, breathes with the north.

So a curve that follows this record needs two things: a rise that gets steeper, and a ripple that repeats every twelve months. The next section builds one piece at a time, and asks how to tell whether each piece helps.

Three sets, as for an exam. Think of studying:

  • the homework problems are what you learn from;
  • a practice exam tells you whether your way of studying works, and you may change your way of studying after seeing it;
  • the final exam is taken once, at the end. If you took it again and again, changing your answers each time, it would stop measuring what you know.

A model gets the same three sets of data, here three spans of years:

  • training months, 1958–2000: each curve learns from these;
  • validation months, 2001–2010: years held back to choose between models. Once they have chosen, they are no longer a fair test.
  • test months, 2011 onward: years nobody looks at until the end, checked once, on the model already chosen.

Why years in order, and not a random third of the months? Because a forecast is about the future. Months picked at random would sit between training months, where any smooth curve does well, and the test would say nothing about years to come. That would be leakage: any route by which information about the data you are scoring on reaches the model before you score it.

How a curve's miss is measured. As in the age-of-the-universe week: a residual is the data minus what the curve says, one per month, and the root mean squared error (RMSE) sums them up. Square every residual, average the squares, take the square root. The result is a typical miss, in ppm. Here it is always worked out on the validation months, the years the curve did not learn from.

The line misses by 7.18 ppm, and the figure shows why: the record curves upward away from it: from 2001 on, almost every month lies above the line.

A new column lets a line-fitting method draw a curve. In the age-of-the-universe homework you gave the fit a second column, the distance squared. The fit finds one number for each column it is given, so with decades and decades squared it fits

$$\text{CO2} = a \times \text{decades} + c \times \text{decades}^2 + b$$

The squared term is small near 1958 and grows fast later, which is exactly the shape of a rise that gets steeper. Nothing else changes: the same fit, the same masks, the same RMSE.

A wave repeats every twelve months, and two columns can draw one. Turn each month into an angle around a circle, one full turn a year: $\text{angle} = 2\pi \times (\text{month} - 0.5) / 12$. (A full turn is $2\pi$; the $-0.5$ puts each month at its middle.) The sine of that angle rises and falls once a year, and so does the cosine, a quarter of a year later. Drawn over twelve months:

The sine is highest in March and April and lowest in September and October; the cosine is highest in December and January and lowest in June and July. Give the fit both, and it chooses how much of each, which lets the mixed wave peak in any month and be any size. Each is a seasonal column: a column that rises and falls once a year, so the fitted curve can rise and fall with the seasons. The curve is now

$$\text{CO2} = a \times \text{decades} + c \times \text{decades}^2 + s \times \sin(\text{angle}) + k \times \cos(\text{angle}) + b$$

More columns always fit the training months better. They do not always fit new months better. The squared curve with seasons misses the validation decade by only 0.77 ppm. Why stop there? A cubed column, or a fourth power, would bend the curve more freely and fit 1958–2000 even more closely. The risk has a name, overfitting: a curve that memorises the data you gave it fails on the data you did not. The highest power in a curve is its degree: the degree of a polynomial is how many bends it is allowed: degree 1 is a straight line, degree 2 bends once.

The way to find out is to try each degree and score it on the validation months. The figure that shows the answer is a validation curve: plot the miss on the training years and on the held-back years against how flexible the curve is; the flexibility worth choosing is where the held-back miss is lowest.

The two lines tell different stories. On the training months every extra power helps, or at least does no harm: 1.92, 0.97, 0.82 and 0.82 ppm. On the validation months the squared curve wins clearly, 0.77 ppm, and the cubed and fourth-power curves are four to six times worse (4.51 and 3.31). The extra powers let the curve follow small bends in the 1958–2000 record, which buys almost nothing there (from 0.97 to 0.82 ppm), and then carry those bends forward into years where they do not belong: in the figure, the cubed and fourth-power curves fall below the data after 2001. That is overfitting, seen in the data rather than described.

The two ways to fail have names. Too simple and you miss the pattern; too flexible and you memorise the noise. The line is too simple: it misses the bend everywhere (bias). The cubed and fourth-power curves are too flexible: what they learn depends on the accidents of the years they were given (variance). The squared curve sits between them.

Inside the record the three curves that can bend lie almost on top of one another; the line, which cannot bend, runs above the data in the middle years and below it at both ends. Beyond the record they spread: the line passes 450 ppm in 2046, the others in 2034, 2034 and 2032, and by 2050 they say anything from 458 to 536 ppm. That is extrapolation: reading a fitted curve beyond the years it was fitted on. Nothing in the data checks it there. The validation decade chose a curve for the ten years after its training data. It says much less about thirty years ahead, and nothing about what people will burn.

Third: the curve's seasons, as a check of its shape. The fit chose one number for each seasonal column: a weight for the sine and a weight for the cosine. Together they give the curve's yearly wave. If the curve has learned the record, that wave should be about the size and the timing of the teeth you saw in section 1.

docs.title: When will CO2 pass 450 ppm?¶
docs.text:
EPS 88 · PyEarth. Open your own copy on DataHub: click here.

Every month since March 1958, an observatory high on Mauna Loa, a volcano in Hawaii, has measured how much carbon dioxide (CO2) is in the air. It is the longest record of its kind, and its yearly average has gone up every single year. It now stands near 430 parts per million. When will it pass 450?

To answer, you need a curve that follows the record, and a fair way to tell a curve that has learned the pattern from one that has only memorised the past. Today you fit four curves, choose between them on years they never saw, test the winner once on the most recent years, and read its forecast. Then you see how much that forecast depends on the choice. At home you repeat the method at two more stations, one in the Arctic and one at the South Pole.

Every place you write something opens with a pencil icon and the words Your turn, and is followed by a cell that already has the shape of the answer written in, with ... wherever your code goes. Replace every ..., run every cell so your answers and figures are saved in the file, then download this notebook itself — the .ipynb file — and upload it to Gradescope. Not a PDF: the marking reads your notebook, and a PDF cannot be read. In JupyterLab: File ▸ Download, or right-click the file in the left-hand panel and choose Download.

Two habits from the first minute. A cell runs when you press Shift+Enter, and the notebook remembers everything it has already run — so when something breaks and you cannot see why, Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells throws the memory away and rebuilds it from the top. That is never the wrong thing to do.

docs.title: What you'll be able to do¶
docs.text:
The science. Describe the two patterns in the CO2 record, the long rise and the yearly breath; say when the yearly average reaches 450 ppm by the curve the data choose; and explain why that date is less certain than the fit makes it look.

The code. A new column made from an old one (a square, a sine, a cosine) · fitting on training months, choosing on validation months, testing once · a loop that compares four models · np.sin, np.cos and np.pi.

Thirteen places where you write something: nine in class, four at home. Each is headed Your turn, and the cell under it has the shape of the answer written in, with ... wherever your code goes and a comment beside each one saying what goes there.

The four questions of the class:

  1. What does the CO2 record show?
  2. How do we choose a curve we can trust on years it has not seen?
  3. When will CO2 pass 450 ppm?
  4. How far can we trust that answer?

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text:
Run the next cell once. It reads NOAA's Mauna Loa file (live if the network is up, the copy stored with the course if not) and the two stations for the homework, which are stored with the course. Then it adds two columns to each table:

  • time: the middle of each month, written as a year with decimals (March 1958 is 1958.21);
  • decades: the time since 1958, counted in decades (2026 is 6.8 decades).

Counting in decades keeps the numbers small. Later you will square this column and take higher powers of it; counted in years, the fourth power of 2026's value would be about 20 million, far too large for the fit to handle well.

(The numbers quoted in this notebook come from the stored copy; if your notebook read NOAA's live file, a few may differ in their last digit.)

docs.title: 1. What does the CO2 record show?¶
docs.text:
CO2 is counted in parts per million. A reading of 430 ppm means that in every million molecules of air, 430 are carbon dioxide. That is a small share, but CO2 lets sunlight in and holds back some of the heat the ground gives off. It is one of the gases behind the greenhouse effect from the liquid-water week: the difference between the temperature a world would have with no air and the temperature it actually has.

Where the numbers come from. Charles David Keeling began measuring CO2 on Mauna Loa in March 1958. The observatory sits 3,397 m up the volcano's side, far from cities and forests, so the air it samples has mixed over a wide area; one station there tells you about much of the planet.

The Mauna Loa Observatory on the volcano's bare lava slope. Photo: Brian Vasel, NOAA (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons.

docs.text:
What does the record look like?

Why: before fitting any curve, look at the data. What you see decides which curves are worth trying.

  1. The figure. Draw the monthly CO2 against time as a line, with a label and units on each axis.
  2. highest and lowest: the largest and the smallest value of the co2 column.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: highest and lowest.

docs.title: 2. How do we choose a curve we can trust on years it has not seen?¶
docs.text: A curve that fits the past is not yet a curve to trust about the future. A flexible enough curve can pass close to every month in the record and still be wrong about next year, because it has learned the record's accidents along with its pattern. The fair test is to hide some years from the curve and see how well it does on them. In short: hide some data from yourself, then check.

docs.text:
Which months does each set hold?

Why: every fit and every score below uses these three sets. Each is a mask on the year column, written with the table skills of the tables week.

  1. training: True for the months up to the end of 2000.
  2. validation: True for the months from 2001 to 2010, both years included.
  3. test: True for the months from 2011 on.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: training, validation and test.

docs.text:

Why: the straight line is the simplest curve, and the one to beat. It is the age-of-the-universe line, with time across instead of distance.

  2. residuals: the validation months' CO2 minus what the line says for them.
  3. line_validation_rmse: the RMSE of those residuals.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: line and line_validation_rmse.

Does a squared column help on the validation years?

Why: the record bends upward; a squared column is the simplest way to let the curve bend.

  2. squared: the curve fitted to the training months with both decades and decades2.
  3. squared_validation_rmse: its miss on the validation months.

docs.text:

Why: the teeth are what the squared curve still misses. Two waves, one fit, should draw them.

  1. angle: each month's angle, by the formula above, from the month column.
  2. mlo["sin_month"] and mlo["cos_month"]: two new columns, the sine and the cosine of each month's angle.
  3. seasonal: the curve fitted to the training months with decades, decades2, sin_month and cos_month.
  4. seasonal_validation_rmse: its miss on the validation months.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: seasonal and seasonal_validation_rmse.

docs.text:

Why: this is the choice itself. Each candidate keeps the two seasonal columns and adds one more power of decades. The loop fits each one to the training months and scores it twice: on the training months it learned from, and on the validation months it did not.

  1. The new columns, the candidates and their names are given.
  2. Inside the loop, for each list of columns: fit to the training months, then append the training RMSE to training_rmses and the validation RMSE to validation_rmses.

  4. The figure: both lists of RMSE, one point per candidate.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: training_rmses, validation_rmses and best.

docs.title: 3. When will CO2 pass 450 ppm?¶
docs.text: The validation months have done their job, so now they can join the training months. The choice is made: the squared curve with seasons. Fit it again to everything before the test, 1958–2010, and then, once, see how it does on 2011 onward. That one number is the honest estimate of how well this kind of curve forecasts years it has never seen.

How well does the chosen curve do on the test years?

Why: the test months are the final exam. They were never used to fit or to choose, so their RMSE is the fair measure of the curve's forecasts.

  1. before_test: True for the months up to the end of 2010.
  2. chosen: the chosen curve, fitted to those months.
  3. test_rmse: its miss on the test months.
  4. The figure: the test months and what the curve said for them.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: chosen and test_rmse.

docs.text:
When does the yearly average pass 450 ppm?

Why: this is the week's question. The answer is a mask on the forecast table.

  1. everything: the chosen curve fitted to every month of the record.
  2. future["co2"]: what it says for each year of future.
  3. year_450: the first year whose forecast is 450 ppm or more.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: everything and year_450.

docs.title: 4. How far can we trust that answer?¶
docs.text:
2034 is the answer of one curve. Three checks show how much to trust it.

First: the test misses have a direction. The test RMSE treats a miss above the curve and a miss below it alike. Average the test residuals year by year instead, and see which way they go:

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 9¶
docs.text:
How big is the yearly wave in the chosen curve, and when is it highest?

Why: the size and timing of the wave are a check the record can answer: the close-up figure of section 1 shows the data's own highs and lows.

  1. sine_weight and cosine_weight: the numbers everything found for sin_month and cos_month. The fit keeps them in .coef_, in the order of columns, so the position of a column's name in columns is the position of its number.
  2. seasonal_part: for the twelve months, sine weight × sine of the angle plus cosine weight × cosine of the angle (month_numbers and month_angle are given).
  3. mlo_swing: the wave's highest value minus its lowest.
  4. mlo_peak and mlo_low: the month numbers where the wave is highest and lowest. np.argmax gives the position of the largest value and np.argmin the position of the smallest, as in the age-of-the-universe week; read the month number at that position from month_numbers.
  5. The figure: the wave over the twelve months.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: mlo_swing, mlo_peak and mlo_low.

docs.title: The question, answered¶
docs.text: Around 2034, by the curve the validation years chose, fitted to the whole record. Other reasonable curves put the year anywhere from 2032 to 2046, and since 2016 the record has run above the curve fitted to its first 53 years.

docs.title: The science¶
docs.text:
When will CO2 pass 450 ppm? Choose a model on years it was not fitted to: fit on the training years, choose on the validation years, and test once on years nobody looked at. A model's columns are a choice: a squared column bends the line, a sine and a cosine of the month draw the seasons, and more columns always fit the training years better but can fit new years worse. A forecast beyond the data is an extrapolation: the year CO2 passes 450 ppm moves by more than ten years with the model, and the record has already pulled away from the curve fitted to its first five decades.

  • Leakage. Any route by which information about the data you are scoring on reaches the model before you score it.
  • Polynomial degree. The degree of a polynomial is how many bends it is allowed: degree 1 is a straight line, degree 2 bends once.
  • Overfitting. A curve that memorises the data you gave it fails on the data you did not.
  • Train/test split. Hide some data from yourself, then check.
  • Validation years. Years held back to choose between models. Once they have chosen, they are no longer a fair test.
  • Test years. Years nobody looks at until the end, checked once, on the model already chosen.
  • Seasonal column. A column that rises and falls once a year, so the fitted curve can rise and fall with the seasons.
  • Extrapolation. Reading a fitted curve beyond the years it was fitted on. Nothing in the data checks it there.
  • Bias-variance. Too simple and you miss the pattern; too flexible and you memorise the noise.
  • Validation curve. Plot the miss on the training years and on the held-back years against how flexible the curve is; the flexibility worth choosing is where the held-back miss is lowest.
  • Typical miss. Square every gap between what happened and what the curve said, average the squares, and take the square root: the usual size of a miss, in the data's own units.

In the Mackenzie Mountains of northwest Canada the glacial deposits of this ice age, the Sturtian, are the Rapitan Group, and right on top of them lies a cap of dark limestone, the base of the Twitya Formation, laid down in the sea as the ice ended:

The Rapitan Group (D1 to D3: rock laid down under ice; S: layered) and the cap limestone of the Twitya Formation, Mackenzie Mountains, Northwest Territories, Canada. Figure: Hoffman and others (2017), Science Advances, Fig. 19F (CC BY-NC 4.0).

How do we know ice made these rocks? Stones carried by floating ice dropped into soft mud on the sea floor and bent its layers, something only ice does in a quiet sea:

Stones dropped from floating ice into mud, Sayunei Formation of the Rapitan Group, with a coin for scale. Photo: P. F. Hoffman, snowballearth.org.

When did the ice begin, and when did it end? The start is known: a layer of volcanic ash inside the glacial deposits of the Yukon, dated with the uranium-lead clock, is 716.5 million years old, so the ice was there by then. That ash was dated by Francis Macdonald, now a professor in this department, and his colleagues (Macdonald and others, 2010). The end is the age of the cap limestone, and that is what you will measure. The plan: learn how a rock's clock works, read it on a rock with many samples (the granite of Monterey, part 2), then read it on the cap, which has only 7 (part 3).

What the numbers in "strontium-87" mean. An atom has a small nucleus made of protons and neutrons. The number of protons decides which element it is: every rubidium atom has 37, every strontium atom 38. The number after the name is the mass number, protons plus neutrons:

Atom Protons Neutrons Mass number strontium-86 38 48 86 strontium-87 38 49 87 rubidium-87 37 50 87

Strontium-86 and strontium-87 are isotopes: the same element, with different numbers of neutrons. Isotopes of one element behave the same way in chemistry, so a crystal growing in a magma takes up strontium-86 and strontium-87 in the same proportion as the magma around it. That is why every mineral of one rock starts with the same 87Sr/86Sr.

Rubidium-87 is radioactive: in its nucleus one neutron turns into a proton and an electron flies out. The atom now has 38 protons, so it is strontium, and still 87 protons plus neutrons: rubidium-87 has become strontium-87. That is why the parent and the daughter share the number 87.

Some atoms are clocks. A parent atom, such as rubidium-87, turns by itself into a daughter atom, strontium-87. Nothing speeds it up or slows it down: no heat, no pressure. Each year the same small share of the parent atoms that are left decays, so the number left falls along a curve like this one. The half-life is the time it takes for half of the parent atoms to decay, however many there are.

The share of the parent left after each half-life. Figure: Fraknoi, Morrison and Wolff, Astronomy (OpenStax), CC BY 4.0.

How the clock runs: by halving. After one half-life, half the parent atoms are left; after two, half of that half, a quarter; after three, an eighth. After any time $t$:

$$\frac{N}{N_0} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t / T_{1/2}}$$

where $N_0$ is the number of parent atoms at the start, $N$ the number left now, and $T_{1/2}$ the half-life.

The same law, written with the decay rate. The same curve is usually written with the share of the parent that decays each year, the decay rate $\lambda$ (lambda): for rubidium-87, 1.42 in every hundred billion atoms a year, rb_decay in the setup cell.

$$N = N_0 \, e^{-\lambda t}, \qquad \lambda = \frac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}}$$

Here $e = 2.718\ldots$; np.exp(x) computes $e^x$ (the probability week), and np.log(x), the natural logarithm $\ln x$, undoes it: np.log(np.exp(x)) is x.

A slow clock. In the 83.5 million years since the Monterey rocks formed, only 0.12% of their rubidium-87 has decayed; even in the 4.5 billion years of the Earth's life, only 6.19%. So the daughter ratios of the Monterey rocks differ only in the third decimal place, and reading an age takes very careful measurements, made in laboratories like this one:

The argon lab of the Berkeley Geochronology Center, where rock ages like these are measured. Photo: Berkeley Geochronology Center.

Ages answer other questions too. Clocks like this showed that the dinosaurs died out at the same time as an asteroid struck Mexico 66 million years ago, the two ages agreeing to within 32,000 years; the team was led by Paul Renne, a professor in this department and director of the Berkeley Geochronology Center (Renne and others, 2013). The search for that impact began at a thin layer of clay in Italy:

Luis Alvarez and his son Walter Alvarez, both of Berkeley, at the thin layer that marks the dinosaurs' extinction, near Gubbio, Italy; Walter Alvarez is still a professor in this department. Photo: Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory (public domain).

Back to Snowball Earth: how do the clock's atoms become two columns of numbers?

Three atoms, two ratios. The rubidium clock involves three kinds of atom in every mineral:

Atom Its role Over time rubidium-87 (87Rb) the parent: radioactive slowly decreases, as it turns into strontium-87 strontium-87 (87Sr) the daughter some was there when the mineral formed; more is added as 87Rb decays strontium-86 (86Sr) the reference: a stable strontium atom never changes: no decay makes or destroys it

A laboratory cannot easily count atoms, but it can measure the ratio of two atoms very precisely. So everything is measured against strontium-86, the atom that never changes. Dividing by it also compares every mineral for the same amount of strontium, whatever its size. That gives the two columns of the table:

  • parent = 87Rb/86Sr: how much parent a mineral has, per atom of the reference;
  • daughter = 87Sr/86Sr: how much daughter it has now, per atom of the reference.

A mineral rich in rubidium has a large parent and, as time passes, makes the most new strontium-87, so its daughter climbs fastest.

From parent to daughter. Every parent atom that decays becomes one daughter atom, so the daughter made is the parent lost. We can measure the parent left today, $N$, but not the parent at the start; turning the decay law round, $N_0 = N e^{\lambda t}$, so

$$D^{*} = N_0 - N = N \left(e^{\lambda t} - 1\right)$$

and a mineral's daughter today, $D$, is what it started with, $D_0$, plus what was made:

$$D = D_0 + N \left(e^{\lambda t} - 1\right)$$

One rock, many minerals, one line. The minerals of a rock take in different amounts of the parent when they grow, but the same ratio of daughter. So at the start they sit on a flat line; as the parent decays, each gains daughter in proportion to its parent, and the line tilts more every year. That line is an isochron ("same time"): minerals that formed together started with the same daughter atoms; each has since gained more in proportion to its parent atoms, so together they lie on a line whose slope grows with time.

Three minerals of one rock (orange, pink, blue) start on the flat line D0. As parent atoms (red) turn into daughter atoms (green), each moves up and to the left, and the line through them steepens: isochron 1, then isochron 2. Figure: Woudloper, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

The isochron equation. Divide every term of $D = D_0 + N(e^{\lambda t} - 1)$ by the strontium-86 of the mineral: $D$ becomes the daughter ratio, $D_0$ the ratio the mineral started with, and $N$ the parent ratio:

$$\frac{^{87}\mathrm{Sr}}{^{86}\mathrm{Sr}} = \left(\frac{^{87}\mathrm{Sr}}{^{86}\mathrm{Sr}}\right)_0 + \left(e^{\lambda t} - 1\right) \frac{^{87}\mathrm{Rb}}{^{86}\mathrm{Sr}}$$

In words: daughter now = daughter at the start + parent × (e^(λt) − 1). This is a straight line, $y = \text{intercept} + \text{slope} \times x$, with $x$ = parent and $y$ = daughter. Every mineral of one rock started with the same daughter ratio (the intercept) and has aged the same time $t$ (so the same slope, $e^{\lambda t} - 1$), so they all lie on one line.

First, a rock with many samples: the Monterey Peninsula. The rocky coast from Monterey to Point Lobos is a granite-like rock that cooled from magma deep underground. Close up it is a mix of crystals of different minerals, and each mineral took in a different amount of rubidium when it grew:

The Monterey granodiorite close up: pink-white feldspar crystals (Or, Pg), grey quartz (Qtz) and dark mica and hornblende (Bi, Hb). Photo: E. Clifton, Rocks of Point Lobos (2013).

These rocks sit on a long block of crust just west of the San Andreas fault, the Salinian block. It is out of place: many geologists think it formed far to the south-east, beside the southern Sierra Nevada, and was carried north-west along the fault, about 300 km on the San Andreas alone (Ross, 1984); where exactly it came from is still debated. Its age is one of the clues.

The granite-like rocks of the Salinian block (dark), between the San Andreas fault and the coast. Map: Kistler and Champion (2001), US Geological Survey (public domain).

82.7 million years. The geologists who measured these rocks reported 83.5 ± 6.2 million years, from the same table with a fit that also weighs each measurement's error.

Why the "± 6.2" matters as much as the 83.5. The same report dates these rocks with a second, different clock (argon in one of their minerals, hornblende) and gets 80.2 ± 0.5 million years. Is that a different age, or the same age measured twice? The numbers 83.5 and 80.2 alone cannot say. With their uncertainties they can: 83.5 ± 6.2 runs from 77.3 to 89.7, and 80.2 lies inside it, so the two clocks agree; the authors say they "overlap within experimental error" (Kistler and Champion, 2001). Every comparison of two numbers from data, two ages, two rates, a forecast and what happened, needs the uncertainty of each.

The "±" decides arguments, about Snowball Earth too. Did the ice melt at the same moment all over the world? The cap above the glacial deposits has been dated in three places:

Place Age of the cap (million years) northwest Canada (Rooney and others, 2014) 662.4 ± 3.9 South Australia (Cox and others, 2018) 663.03 ± 0.76 Mongolia (Rooney and others, 2015) 659.0 ± 4.5

Without the "±", 662.4, 663.0 and 659.0 look like three different thaws, millions of years apart. With it, every pair overlaps, so one thaw at the same time everywhere fits the data, which is now the common view (Hoffman and others, 2017).

Where does a "±" come from? We cannot go back to Monterey and collect 37 new rocks a thousand times. But we can ask the rocks we have.

The bootstrap. Ask the data the same question a thousand times, using a different random slice of itself each time. Draw 37 samples from our 37, at random and with replacement: after each draw the rock goes back, so it can be drawn again. Some rocks come out twice, some not at all. Fit the line again: a slightly different line, a slightly different age. table.sample(n, replace=True, random_state=rng) makes one such draw from a table.

First, a case with a known answer. The mean of the 37 parent values has a textbook uncertainty, its standard error $\sigma / \sqrt{n}$, with $\sigma$ the standard deviation of the values. Redraw the 37 rocks 10,000 times and take the mean parent of each redraw: the spread of those means should match the formula.

The same question, answered by a formula. For a line fitted by least squares, the slope's uncertainty also has an exact formula, with no redrawing. Think of each sample as a point on the true line plus a small error, $y_i = a + b\,x_i + \varepsilon_i$ (with $x_i$ its parent, $y_i$ its daughter); its residual $e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i$, how far it sits above (+) or below (−) the fitted line $\hat{y}_i = \hat{a} + \hat{b}\,x_i$, is what we can see of that error. A hat marks a number fitted from the data. Three numbers, in three steps:

1. How noisy are the samples? The typical size of a residual, the spread:

$$s = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_i e_i^2}{n - 2}}$$

(divided by $n - 2$, not $n$, because the slope and the intercept were already fitted from the same $n$ samples).

2. How far apart are the samples along the $x$ axis? With $\bar{x}$ their mean:

$$S_{xx} = \sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2$$

3. How uncertain is the slope? Noise over spread, the slope's standard error:

$$\mathrm{SE}(\hat{b}) = \frac{s}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}$$

Picture a ruler laid through points that each wobble up or down by about $s$. If the points sit close together, a small wobble tips the ruler a lot; if they are far apart, the same wobble hardly tips it. So more noise makes the slope less certain, and samples spread farther along the line make it more certain.

The 95% interval is then $\hat{b} \pm t_{95} \times \mathrm{SE}(\hat{b})$, with $t_{95}$ from a table for $n - 2$ degrees of freedom: 2.0301 for 37 samples. With many samples $t_{95}$ is close to 2 (the familiar "± 2 standard errors"); with few, it is larger, because $s$ itself is then only a rough estimate and the interval must allow for that. The age interval is the ages of the two ends. The formula assumes the errors are independent and of about the same size along the line.

That is what we hope for when there are many points, spread along the line, scattered about it evenly. When they disagree, it is a sign to look harder at the data, as in part 3.

Which to use? The formula is exact and instant, and it is what most software reports, but it rests on its assumptions and needs a new formula for every new question. The bootstrap needs no formula: it works for any number you can compute from the data, such as an age, which is a logarithm of the slope, or the difference of two ages.

The line's other number. The bootstrap does not care which number you ask of the redrawn samples, and the formula has a version for each. The slope gave the age. The intercept, where the line meets zero parent, is the strontium ratio the magma started with, before any rubidium decayed. It is a fingerprint of where the magma came from: under California's granites, a starting ratio of 0.706 marks a fundamental boundary in the crust, and geologists traced that boundary on both sides of the San Andreas fault to measure how far the fault has moved these rocks (Kistler and Champion, 2001).

A second clock, built the same way. The cap limestone is not granite: it is a dark sediment, laid down on the sea floor. As it settles, its dead organic matter takes two rare metals out of the seawater, rhenium and osmium, and keeps them (Selby and Creaser, 2003). Rhenium has a radioactive isotope, so the sediment holds a clock that started when it was laid down. Side by side with the clock of parts 1 and 2:

Rubidium clock (Monterey) Rhenium clock (the cap limestone) parent rubidium-87: 37 protons, 50 neutrons rhenium-187: 75 protons, 112 neutrons daughter strontium-87: 38 protons, 49 neutrons osmium-187: 76 protons, 111 neutrons reference, never changes strontium-86 osmium-188 decay rate, per year 1.42 in every 100 billion (rb_decay) 1.666 in every 100 billion (re_decay) the column parent 87Rb/86Sr 187Re/188Os the column daughter 87Sr/86Sr 187Os/188Os why the samples start alike crystals take their strontium from the same magma sediment takes its osmium from the same seawater, at the same time

The isochron equation is the same line, daughter now = daughter at the start + parent × (e^(λt) − 1), and the age comes out of the slope in the same three steps, with re_decay in place of rb_decay.

The last row is the catch. Samples start with the same osmium only if they were laid down at the same time, from the same water. So Rooney and others (2014) measured 7 samples of one thin bed, less than 20 cm thick and less than 2 m above the glacial deposits. Its age is when the ice ended.

How do you date a fossil? By a rock layer next to it.

  • Newfoundland: volcanic ash about 25 m above the first fronds, 574.17 ± 0.66 million years old by a uranium clock (Matthews and others, 2021). We treat it as exact.
  • Yukon, northwest Canada: the same kinds of fossil lie in dark, organic-rich mudstone, which holds the Snowball cap's rhenium-osmium clock. Rooney and others (2020) dated one layer, J1719.

The question. The two places were then on different continents. Did these organisms appear in both at the same time? If so, they were widespread from the start.

The method: the formula, because J1719 has only 8 samples, and with so few the bootstrap's redraws are lumpy (part 3). As in Your turn 6, with $\hat{b}$ the slope, $e_i$ the residuals and $x_i$ the parents:

$$s = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_i e_i^2}{n - 2}}, \qquad S_{xx} = \sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2, \qquad \mathrm{SE}(\hat{b}) = \frac{s}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}, \qquad \hat{b} \pm t_{95}\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat{b})$$

Each end of the slope's interval becomes an age.

docs.title: How long was the Earth frozen?¶
docs.text:
EPS 88 · PyEarth. Open your own copy on DataHub: click here.

In the mountains of northwest Canada, a layer of rock left by glaciers sits on older rock and under younger rock. Geologists think it records a time when ice spread over most of the planet, a "Snowball Earth". How long did the ice last? A rock layer does not come with a date written on it, but some of its atoms are a clock.

Today you read that clock with the line fit of the last two weeks: the slope of a line through a rock's measurements is its age. Then comes the question every age must answer before anyone should believe it: how sure is it? You answer that by letting the computer redraw your own measurements thousands of times. At home you read a new clock with the same steps.

Every place you write something opens with a pencil icon and the words Your turn, and is followed by a cell that already has the shape of the answer written in, with ... wherever your code goes. Replace every ..., run every cell so your answers and figures are saved in the file, then download this notebook itself — the .ipynb file — and upload it to Gradescope. Not a PDF: the marking reads your notebook, and a PDF cannot be read. In JupyterLab: File ▸ Download, or right-click the file in the left-hand panel and choose Download.

Two habits from the first minute. A cell runs when you press Shift+Enter, and the notebook remembers everything it has already run — so when something breaks and you cannot see why, Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells throws the memory away and rebuilds it from the top. That is never the wrong thing to do.

docs.title: What you'll be able to do¶
docs.text:
The science. Explain how a rock records its own age; read an age from an isochron; say how long the Sturtian Snowball Earth lasted and how sure that number is; and say why a published age carries a "±".

The code. A line fit with LinearRegression, and an age from its slope with np.log · a new table drawn from an old one with table.sample(..., replace=True) · the bootstrap: redraw, refit, repeat · a 95% interval with np.percentile.

Thirteen places where you write something: nine in class, four at home, the last two optional. Each is headed Your turn, and the cell under it has the shape of the answer written in, with ... wherever your code goes and a comment beside each one saying what goes there.

The three questions of the class:

  1. How can a rock tell its own age?
  2. How sure is an age from 37 samples?
  3. How long was the Earth frozen?

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text:
Run the next cell once. It reads four tables stored with the course, each one a published measurement, one row per sample:

  • rocks: 37 samples of the granite-like rocks of the Monterey Peninsula, California (Kistler and Champion, US Geological Survey, 2001). The column material says whether a sample is a piece of the whole rock (33) or crystals of feldspar separated from it (4);
  • cap: the rock just above the Snowball Earth glacial deposits in northwest Canada (Rooney and others, 2014). The column collected_from says where each sample came from: one thin bed, or 6 m of rock;
  • far_side and fossil_layer: the two tables for the homework.

Every table has the same two measurement columns, parent and daughter. Each is a ratio of two kinds of atom, not a count; part 1 explains which atoms. Ages are in millions of years ago, written Ma.

docs.title: 1. How can a rock tell its own age?¶
docs.text:
The question. About 717 million years ago, glaciers spread over what is now northwest Canada, which then lay at the equator: ice reached the sea in the tropics (Macdonald and others, 2010). The Snowball Earth hypothesis (Kirschvink, 1992) says ice covered nearly the whole planet:

One reconstruction of the Earth 690 million years ago, with ice (white) over the land and the sea. Map: C. R. Scotese and others, PALEOMAP Project, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0).

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 1¶
docs.text:
Do the two laws agree, and how fast does the rubidium clock run?

Why: the two forms of the decay law must give the same share left; then the age of the Earth shows how slow this clock is.

  1. halving: the share left after time $t$ by the halving law, $(1/2)^{t / T_{1/2}}$.
  2. left: the share left by the decay-rate law, $e^{-\lambda t}$, with np.exp.
  3. decayed: the share decayed after time $t$, $1 - e^{-\lambda t}$.

In the loops t is the time $t$, in years.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: left and decayed.

docs.title: 2. How sure is an age from 37 samples?¶
docs.text:
On Monterey's 37 samples you learn the two skills the 7-sample Snowball cap will need in part 3: reading the clock, and saying how sure the reading is.

From the line to the age, step by step. Part 1 ended with the isochron equation:

$$\text{daughter now} = \text{daughter at the start} + \left(e^{\lambda t} - 1\right) \times \text{parent}$$

The line you will fit in Your turn 3 has the same shape:

$$\text{daughter} = \hat{a} + \hat{b} \times \text{parent}$$

A hat marks a number fitted from the data. Match them term by term: the intercept $\hat{a}$ is the daughter ratio at the start, and the slope $\hat{b}$ is $e^{\lambda t} - 1$. Add 1, take the natural log (ln undoes e), divide by $\lambda$:

$$\hat{b} = e^{\lambda t} - 1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad e^{\lambda t} = 1 + \hat{b} \quad\Rightarrow\quad t = \frac{\ln(1 + \hat{b})}{\lambda}$$

With the Monterey numbers you are about to get: $\hat{b}$ is 0.0011749, so $1 + \hat{b}$ is 1.0011749; its natural log is 0.0011742; divided by 1.42e-11 per year, that is 82.7 million years. In code, the three steps are one line, with b for $\hat{b}$: np.log(1 + b) / rb_decay.

  2. end_age: its age from a fitted line, with re_decay in place of rb_decay.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 9¶
docs.text:
How long was the Earth frozen?

Why: the question of the week. With 7 samples the formula is the better guide (the coloured histogram above showed why), so it gives the answer; the bootstrap is set beside it to compare.

  1. start_age: given, the start of the glaciation in millions of years ago.
  2. duration: the start minus end_age.
  3. duration_formula_range: the start minus each end of end_formula_range. Subtracting flips the order: the shortest duration comes from the latest end, so take the high end first.
  4. duration_range: for comparison, the middle 95% of the start minus each of the end_ages.
  5. The figure: a histogram of the redrawn durations; the black lines (the bootstrap) and red lines (the formula) are drawn for you.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: duration, duration_formula_range and duration_range.

docs.title: The question, answered¶
docs.text: About 58.3 million years, 95% interval 49.0 to 67.6: your answer. The cap above the Sturtian glacial deposits is 658.2 million years old by your line, 648.9 to 667.5 by the formula, so the ice that began 716.5 million years ago lasted 58.3 million years. The authors' fit, which weighs each sample by its measurement error, gives about 54 ± 4, and caps of the same ice age dated since give 56 to 58 (Rooney and others, 2020); Francis Macdonald's group finds about 56 (Tasistro-Hart and others, 2025). The bootstrap's lopsided 24.5 to 63.6 is the lesson, not the answer: 7 samples, two of which hold the line.

docs.title: The science¶
docs.text:
How long was the Earth frozen? An isochron turns isotope ratios into an age: minerals or rocks that formed together lie on one line, and its slope grows with time. Two ways to an interval: the bootstrap redraws your own samples and refits, the least-squares formula computes the standard error directly; with many well-spread points they agree, with few the formula is the better guide if its assumptions hold, and about 19 in 20 such 95% intervals hold the answer.

  • Isochron. Minerals that formed together started with the same daughter atoms; each has since gained more in proportion to its parent atoms, so together they lie on a line whose slope grows with time.
  • Half-life. The time it takes for half of the parent atoms to decay, however many there are.
  • Bootstrap. Ask the data the same question a thousand times, using a different random slice of itself each time.
  • Confidence interval. Not one number but the range your number would have wandered over, had the world rolled differently.

import numpy as np from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt # house style, set once, so every plot cell below holds only what matters plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.grid": True, "grid.alpha": 0.3, "axes.axisbelow": True}) CACHE = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AI4EPS/EPS88_PyEarth/main/data" rocks = pd.read_csv(CACHE + "/week08_monterey_rbsr.csv") # Monterey granite: one row per sample cap = pd.read_csv(CACHE + "/week08_snowball_reos.csv") # Snowball Earth: the rock above the glacial deposits far_side = pd.read_csv(CACHE + "/week08_change6_rbsr.csv") # homework: lava from the far side of the Moon fossil_layer = pd.read_csv(CACHE + "/week08_nadaleen_j1719_reos.csv") # homework: a layer from the age of the first large organisms rb_decay = 1.42e-11 # the share of rubidium-87 atoms that decay each year re_decay = 1.666e-11 # the share of rhenium-187 atoms that decay each year print(len(rocks), "Monterey samples and", len(cap), "Snowball Earth samples") 
37 Monterey samples and 18 Snowball Earth samples

In the Mackenzie Mountains of northwest Canada the glacial deposits of this ice age, the Sturtian, are the Rapitan Group, and right on top of them lies a cap of dark limestone, the base of the Twitya Formation, laid down in the sea as the ice ended:

The Rapitan Group (D1 to D3: rock laid down under ice; S: layered) and the cap limestone of the Twitya Formation, Mackenzie Mountains, Northwest Territories, Canada. Figure: Hoffman and others (2017), Science Advances, Fig. 19F (CC BY-NC 4.0).

How do we know ice made these rocks? Stones carried by floating ice dropped into soft mud on the sea floor and bent its layers, something only ice does in a quiet sea:

Stones dropped from floating ice into mud, Sayunei Formation of the Rapitan Group, with a coin for scale. Photo: P. F. Hoffman, snowballearth.org.

When did the ice begin, and when did it end? The start is known: a layer of volcanic ash inside the glacial deposits of the Yukon, dated with the uranium-lead clock, is 716.5 million years old, so the ice was there by then. That ash was dated by Francis Macdonald, now a professor in this department, and his colleagues (Macdonald and others, 2010). The end is the age of the cap limestone, and that is what you will measure. The plan: learn how a rock's clock works, read it on a rock with many samples (the granite of Monterey, part 2), then read it on the cap, which has only 7 (part 3).

What the numbers in "strontium-87" mean. An atom has a small nucleus made of protons and neutrons. The number of protons decides which element it is: every rubidium atom has 37, every strontium atom 38. The number after the name is the mass number, protons plus neutrons:

Atom Protons Neutrons Mass number strontium-86 38 48 86 strontium-87 38 49 87 rubidium-87 37 50 87

Strontium-86 and strontium-87 are isotopes: the same element, with different numbers of neutrons. Isotopes of one element behave the same way in chemistry, so a crystal growing in a magma takes up strontium-86 and strontium-87 in the same proportion as the magma around it. That is why every mineral of one rock starts with the same 87Sr/86Sr.

Rubidium-87 is radioactive: in its nucleus one neutron turns into a proton and an electron flies out. The atom now has 38 protons, so it is strontium, and still 87 protons plus neutrons: rubidium-87 has become strontium-87. That is why the parent and the daughter share the number 87.

Some atoms are clocks. A parent atom, such as rubidium-87, turns by itself into a daughter atom, strontium-87. Nothing speeds it up or slows it down: no heat, no pressure. Each year the same small share of the parent atoms that are left decays, so the number left falls along a curve like this one. The half-life is the time it takes for half of the parent atoms to decay, however many there are.

The share of the parent left after each half-life. Figure: Fraknoi, Morrison and Wolff, Astronomy (OpenStax), CC BY 4.0.

How the clock runs: by halving. After one half-life, half the parent atoms are left; after two, half of that half, a quarter; after three, an eighth. After any time $t$:

$$\frac{N}{N_0} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t / T_{1/2}}$$

where $N_0$ is the number of parent atoms at the start, $N$ the number left now, and $T_{1/2}$ the half-life.

The same law, written with the decay rate. The same curve is usually written with the share of the parent that decays each year, the decay rate $\lambda$ (lambda): for rubidium-87, 1.42 in every hundred billion atoms a year, rb_decay in the setup cell.

$$N = N_0 \, e^{-\lambda t}, \qquad \lambda = \frac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}}$$

Here $e = 2.718\ldots$; np.exp(x) computes $e^x$ (the probability week), and np.log(x), the natural logarithm $\ln x$, undoes it: np.log(np.exp(x)) is x.

In [2]: Copied! 
half_life = np.log(2) / rb_decay      # T½ = ln 2 / λ, in years
print("half-life of rubidium-87:", round(half_life / 1e9, 1), "billion years")
for t in [1 * half_life, 2 * half_life, 3 * half_life]:
    halving = (1 / 2) ** (t / half_life)
    left = np.exp(-rb_decay * t)
    print(round(t / half_life), "half-lives: (1/2)^(t/T½) =", round(halving, 4), " e^(−λt) =", round(left, 4))
for t in [83.5e6, 4.5e9]:
    decayed = 1 - np.exp(-rb_decay * t)
    print("after", t / 1e6, "million years,", round(100 * decayed, 2), "% of the rubidium-87 has decayed")

✓ Your turn 1 — the two laws agree; in 4.5 billion years 6.19% of the rubidium-87 has decayed

A slow clock. In the 83.5 million years since the Monterey rocks formed, only 0.12% of their rubidium-87 has decayed; even in the 4.5 billion years of the Earth's life, only 6.19%. So the daughter ratios of the Monterey rocks differ only in the third decimal place, and reading an age takes very careful measurements, made in laboratories like this one:

The argon lab of the Berkeley Geochronology Center, where rock ages like these are measured. Photo: Berkeley Geochronology Center.

Ages answer other questions too. Clocks like this showed that the dinosaurs died out at the same time as an asteroid struck Mexico 66 million years ago, the two ages agreeing to within 32,000 years; the team was led by Paul Renne, a professor in this department and director of the Berkeley Geochronology Center (Renne and others, 2013). The search for that impact began at a thin layer of clay in Italy:

Luis Alvarez and his son Walter Alvarez, both of Berkeley, at the thin layer that marks the dinosaurs' extinction, near Gubbio, Italy; Walter Alvarez is still a professor in this department. Photo: Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory (public domain).

Back to Snowball Earth: how do the clock's atoms become two columns of numbers?

Three atoms, two ratios. The rubidium clock involves three kinds of atom in every mineral:

Atom Its role Over time rubidium-87 (87Rb) the parent: radioactive slowly decreases, as it turns into strontium-87 strontium-87 (87Sr) the daughter some was there when the mineral formed; more is added as 87Rb decays strontium-86 (86Sr) the reference: a stable strontium atom never changes: no decay makes or destroys it

A laboratory cannot easily count atoms, but it can measure the ratio of two atoms very precisely. So everything is measured against strontium-86, the atom that never changes. Dividing by it also compares every mineral for the same amount of strontium, whatever its size. That gives the two columns of the table:

  • parent = 87Rb/86Sr: how much parent a mineral has, per atom of the reference;
  • daughter = 87Sr/86Sr: how much daughter it has now, per atom of the reference.

A mineral rich in rubidium has a large parent and, as time passes, makes the most new strontium-87, so its daughter climbs fastest.

From parent to daughter. Every parent atom that decays becomes one daughter atom, so the daughter made is the parent lost. We can measure the parent left today, $N$, but not the parent at the start; turning the decay law round, $N_0 = N e^{\lambda t}$, so

$$D^{*} = N_0 - N = N \left(e^{\lambda t} - 1\right)$$

and a mineral's daughter today, $D$, is what it started with, $D_0$, plus what was made:

$$D = D_0 + N \left(e^{\lambda t} - 1\right)$$

One rock, many minerals, one line. The minerals of a rock take in different amounts of the parent when they grow, but the same ratio of daughter. So at the start they sit on a flat line; as the parent decays, each gains daughter in proportion to its parent, and the line tilts more every year. That line is an isochron ("same time"): minerals that formed together started with the same daughter atoms; each has since gained more in proportion to its parent atoms, so together they lie on a line whose slope grows with time.

Three minerals of one rock (orange, pink, blue) start on the flat line D0. As parent atoms (red) turn into daughter atoms (green), each moves up and to the left, and the line through them steepens: isochron 1, then isochron 2. Figure: Woudloper, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

The isochron equation. Divide every term of $D = D_0 + N(e^{\lambda t} - 1)$ by the strontium-86 of the mineral: $D$ becomes the daughter ratio, $D_0$ the ratio the mineral started with, and $N$ the parent ratio:

$$\frac{^{87}\mathrm{Sr}}{^{86}\mathrm{Sr}} = \left(\frac{^{87}\mathrm{Sr}}{^{86}\mathrm{Sr}}\right)_0 + \left(e^{\lambda t} - 1\right) \frac{^{87}\mathrm{Rb}}{^{86}\mathrm{Sr}}$$

In words: daughter now = daughter at the start + parent × (e^(λt) − 1). This is a straight line, $y = \text{intercept} + \text{slope} \times x$, with $x$ = parent and $y$ = daughter. Every mineral of one rock started with the same daughter ratio (the intercept) and has aged the same time $t$ (so the same slope, $e^{\lambda t} - 1$), so they all lie on one line.

First, a rock with many samples: the Monterey Peninsula. The rocky coast from Monterey to Point Lobos is a granite-like rock that cooled from magma deep underground. Close up it is a mix of crystals of different minerals, and each mineral took in a different amount of rubidium when it grew:

The Monterey granodiorite close up: pink-white feldspar crystals (Or, Pg), grey quartz (Qtz) and dark mica and hornblende (Bi, Hb). Photo: E. Clifton, Rocks of Point Lobos (2013).

These rocks sit on a long block of crust just west of the San Andreas fault, the Salinian block. It is out of place: many geologists think it formed far to the south-east, beside the southern Sierra Nevada, and was carried north-west along the fault, about 300 km on the San Andreas alone (Ross, 1984); where exactly it came from is still debated. Its age is one of the clues.

The granite-like rocks of the Salinian block (dark), between the San Andreas fault and the coast. Map: Kistler and Champion (2001), US Geological Survey (public domain).

Monterey gives 37 samples, enough to learn the method on; the Snowball cap gives 7. The Monterey table:

rocks.head()

Check the equation on two real samples. The report says these rocks formed 83.5 million years ago with a daughter ratio of 0.70787. Take the samples with the least parent (0.26, sample SANLU9-90) and the most (3.59, SANLU1B-94), and predict their daughter ratio today:

In [5]: Copied! 
t = 83.5e6                          # years: the report's age
D0 = 0.70787                        # D0: the daughter ratio when the rocks formed (the report's value)
growth = np.exp(rb_decay * t) - 1   # e^(λt) − 1: new strontium-87 made per rubidium-87 atom
D_low = D0 + 0.26 * growth          # D = D0 + N (e^(λt) − 1), with N = 0.26: sample SANLU9-90, the least parent
D_high = D0 + 3.59 * growth         # the same, with N = 3.59: sample SANLU1B-94, the most parent
print("e^(λt) − 1 =", round(growth, 6))
print("least parent: predicted", round(D_low, 5), "measured 0.70841")
print("most parent:  predicted", round(D_high, 5), "measured 0.71203")

The sample with 14 times more parent has gained 14 times more strontium-87, and both predictions land within about 0.0002 of what was measured. That small difference is the scatter of real samples about the line.

✓ Your turn 3 — the Monterey granite is 82.7 million years old

82.7 million years. The geologists who measured these rocks reported 83.5 ± 6.2 million years, from the same table with a fit that also weighs each measurement's error.

Why the "± 6.2" matters as much as the 83.5. The same report dates these rocks with a second, different clock (argon in one of their minerals, hornblende) and gets 80.2 ± 0.5 million years. Is that a different age, or the same age measured twice? The numbers 83.5 and 80.2 alone cannot say. With their uncertainties they can: 83.5 ± 6.2 runs from 77.3 to 89.7, and 80.2 lies inside it, so the two clocks agree; the authors say they "overlap within experimental error" (Kistler and Champion, 2001). Every comparison of two numbers from data, two ages, two rates, a forecast and what happened, needs the uncertainty of each.

The "±" decides arguments, about Snowball Earth too. Did the ice melt at the same moment all over the world? The cap above the glacial deposits has been dated in three places:

Place Age of the cap (million years) northwest Canada (Rooney and others, 2014) 662.4 ± 3.9 South Australia (Cox and others, 2018) 663.03 ± 0.76 Mongolia (Rooney and others, 2015) 659.0 ± 4.5

Without the "±", 662.4, 663.0 and 659.0 look like three different thaws, millions of years apart. With it, every pair overlaps, so one thaw at the same time everywhere fits the data, which is now the common view (Hoffman and others, 2017).

Where does a "±" come from? We cannot go back to Monterey and collect 37 new rocks a thousand times. But we can ask the rocks we have.

The bootstrap. Ask the data the same question a thousand times, using a different random slice of itself each time. Draw 37 samples from our 37, at random and with replacement: after each draw the rock goes back, so it can be drawn again. Some rocks come out twice, some not at all. Fit the line again: a slightly different line, a slightly different age. table.sample(n, replace=True, random_state=rng) makes one such draw from a table.

First, a case with a known answer. The mean of the 37 parent values has a textbook uncertainty, its standard error $\sigma / \sqrt{n}$, with $\sigma$ the standard deviation of the values. Redraw the 37 rocks 10,000 times and take the mean parent of each redraw: the spread of those means should match the formula.

The same question, answered by a formula. For a line fitted by least squares, the slope's uncertainty also has an exact formula, with no redrawing. Think of each sample as a point on the true line plus a small error, $y_i = a + b\,x_i + \varepsilon_i$ (with $x_i$ its parent, $y_i$ its daughter); its residual $e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i$, how far it sits above (+) or below (−) the fitted line $\hat{y}_i = \hat{a} + \hat{b}\,x_i$, is what we can see of that error. A hat marks a number fitted from the data. Three numbers, in three steps:

1. How noisy are the samples? The typical size of a residual, the spread:

$$s = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_i e_i^2}{n - 2}}$$

(divided by $n - 2$, not $n$, because the slope and the intercept were already fitted from the same $n$ samples).

2. How far apart are the samples along the $x$ axis? With $\bar{x}$ their mean:

$$S_{xx} = \sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2$$

3. How uncertain is the slope? Noise over spread, the slope's standard error:

$$\mathrm{SE}(\hat{b}) = \frac{s}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}$$

Picture a ruler laid through points that each wobble up or down by about $s$. If the points sit close together, a small wobble tips the ruler a lot; if they are far apart, the same wobble hardly tips it. So more noise makes the slope less certain, and samples spread farther along the line make it more certain.

The 95% interval is then $\hat{b} \pm t_{95} \times \mathrm{SE}(\hat{b})$, with $t_{95}$ from a table for $n - 2$ degrees of freedom: 2.0301 for 37 samples. With many samples $t_{95}$ is close to 2 (the familiar "± 2 standard errors"); with few, it is larger, because $s$ itself is then only a rough estimate and the interval must allow for that. The age interval is the ages of the two ends. The formula assumes the errors are independent and of about the same size along the line.

The formula: 75.9 to 89.5 million years. The bootstrap: 76.9 to 89.8. Two different methods, one from a formula and one from redrawing, agree closely. That is what we hope for when there are many points, spread along the line, scattered about it evenly. When they disagree, it is a sign to look harder at the data, as in part 3.

Which to use? The formula is exact and instant, and it is what most software reports, but it rests on its assumptions and needs a new formula for every new question. The bootstrap needs no formula: it works for any number you can compute from the data, such as an age, which is a logarithm of the slope, or the difference of two ages.

The line's other number. The bootstrap does not care which number you ask of the redrawn samples, and the formula has a version for each. The slope gave the age. The intercept, where the line meets zero parent, is the strontium ratio the magma started with, before any rubidium decayed. It is a fingerprint of where the magma came from: under California's granites, a starting ratio of 0.706 marks a fundamental boundary in the crust, and geologists traced that boundary on both sides of the San Andreas fault to measure how far the fault has moved these rocks (Kistler and Champion, 2001).

A second clock, built the same way. The cap limestone is not granite: it is a dark sediment, laid down on the sea floor. As it settles, its dead organic matter takes two rare metals out of the seawater, rhenium and osmium, and keeps them (Selby and Creaser, 2003). Rhenium has a radioactive isotope, so the sediment holds a clock that started when it was laid down. Side by side with the clock of parts 1 and 2:

Rubidium clock (Monterey) Rhenium clock (the cap limestone) parent rubidium-87: 37 protons, 50 neutrons rhenium-187: 75 protons, 112 neutrons daughter strontium-87: 38 protons, 49 neutrons osmium-187: 76 protons, 111 neutrons reference, never changes strontium-86 osmium-188 decay rate, per year 1.42 in every 100 billion (rb_decay) 1.666 in every 100 billion (re_decay) the column parent 87Rb/86Sr 187Re/188Os the column daughter 87Sr/86Sr 187Os/188Os why the samples start alike crystals take their strontium from the same magma sediment takes its osmium from the same seawater, at the same time

The isochron equation is the same line, daughter now = daughter at the start + parent × (e^(λt) − 1), and the age comes out of the slope in the same three steps, with re_decay in place of rb_decay.

The last row is the catch. Samples start with the same osmium only if they were laid down at the same time, from the same water. So Rooney and others (2014) measured 7 samples of one thin bed, less than 20 cm thick and less than 2 m above the glacial deposits. Its age is when the ice ended.

The ice ended 658.2 million years ago. Here the two methods disagree: the bootstrap gives 652.9 to 692.0, lopsided toward old ages, and the formula 648.9 to 667.5, evenly about the age. The authors, fitting with each measurement's error, reported 662.4 ± 3.9. When two honest methods disagree, the data are telling you something; the figures below show what.

Why is the interval lopsided? Look again at the thin bed's 7 samples in the figure before Your turn 8: 4 sit close together in the middle, and the line is held at its two ends by just two pieces, TW1-A (lowest parent) and TW1-C (highest). Colour each redraw by which of those two it drew:

The age rests on two pieces of rock. With only 7 samples, a redraw misses an end sample often, so the bootstrap's interval is lumpy and too wide on one side: with few points, the formula is the better guide, provided its assumptions hold.

About 58 million years, with a 95% interval of 49.0 to 67.6 (the red lines). Snowball Earth was not a cold snap: the ice lasted for tens of millions of years. The bootstrap's 24.5 to 63.6 (black) is lopsided, with a long tail toward short durations: those are the redraws that missed the end samples. The authors' fit, which weighs each sample by its measurement error, gives 662.4 ± 3.9 for the end, so about 54 ± 4 million years; caps of the same glaciation dated since, in Australia and China, give 56 to 58 million years (Hoffman and others, 2017; Rooney and others, 2020).

The question. Is the far-side lava older than the youngest lava sampled on the near side, 2030 ± 4 million years (Chang'e-5; Li and others, 2021)? That age is so precise that we treat it as exact.

The method: the bootstrap, because the answer is a difference of two ages, and the bootstrap gives an interval for any number computed from the data. As in Your turn 5: redraw the rows with replacement, fit a line, turn its slope into an age; repeat 10,000 times; keep the middle 95%.

What the numbers mean. About 806 million years older, and the whole interval, 744.8 to 943.2, is far from zero: the difference is real. The far side's volcanoes erupted roughly 800 million years before the youngest lava sampled on the near side.

How do you date a fossil? By a rock layer next to it.

  • Newfoundland: volcanic ash about 25 m above the first fronds, 574.17 ± 0.66 million years old by a uranium clock (Matthews and others, 2021). We treat it as exact.
  • Yukon, northwest Canada: the same kinds of fossil lie in dark, organic-rich mudstone, which holds the Snowball cap's rhenium-osmium clock. Rooney and others (2020) dated one layer, J1719.

The question. The two places were then on different continents. Did these organisms appear in both at the same time? If so, they were widespread from the start.

The method: the formula, because J1719 has only 8 samples, and with so few the bootstrap's redraws are lumpy (part 3). As in Your turn 6, with $\hat{b}$ the slope, $e_i$ the residuals and $x_i$ the parents:

$$s = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_i e_i^2}{n - 2}}, \qquad S_{xx} = \sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2, \qquad \mathrm{SE}(\hat{b}) = \frac{s}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}, \qquad \hat{b} \pm t_{95}\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat{b})$$

Each end of the slope's interval becomes an age.

docs.title: How long was the Earth frozen?¶
docs.text:
EPS 88 · PyEarth. Open your own copy on DataHub: click here.

In the mountains of northwest Canada, a layer of rock left by glaciers sits on older rock and under younger rock. Geologists think it records a time when ice spread over most of the planet, a "Snowball Earth". How long did the ice last? A rock layer does not come with a date written on it, but some of its atoms are a clock.

Today you read that clock with the line fit of the last two weeks: the slope of a line through a rock's measurements is its age. Then comes the question every age must answer before anyone should believe it: how sure is it? You answer that by letting the computer redraw your own measurements thousands of times. At home you read a new clock with the same steps.

Every place you write something opens with a pencil icon and the words Your turn, and is followed by a cell that already has the shape of the answer written in, with ... wherever your code goes. Replace every ..., run every cell so your answers and figures are saved in the file, then download this notebook itself — the .ipynb file — and upload it to Gradescope. Not a PDF: the marking reads your notebook, and a PDF cannot be read. In JupyterLab: File ▸ Download, or right-click the file in the left-hand panel and choose Download.

Two habits from the first minute.
