docs.title: What you'll be able to do¶
docs.text:
The science. Explain how a rock records its own age; read an age from an isochron; say how long the Sturtian Snowball Earth lasted and how sure that number is; and say why a published age carries a "±".

The code. A line fit with LinearRegression, and an age from its slope with np.log · a new table drawn from an old one with table.sample(..., replace=True) · the bootstrap: redraw, refit, repeat · a 95% interval with np.percentile.

Thirteen places where you write something: nine in class, four at home, the last two optional. Each is headed Your turn, and the cell under it has the shape of the answer written in, with ... wherever your code goes and a comment beside each one saying what goes there.

The three questions of the class:

  1. How can a rock tell its own age?
  2. How sure is an age from 37 samples?
  3. How long was the Earth frozen?

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text:
Run the next cell once. It reads four tables stored with the course, each one a published measurement, one row per sample:

  • rocks: 37 samples of the granite-like rocks of the Monterey Peninsula, California (Kistler and Champion, US Geological Survey, 2001). The column material says whether a sample is a piece of the whole rock (33) or crystals of feldspar separated from it (4);
  • cap: the rock just above the Snowball Earth glacial deposits in northwest Canada (Rooney and others, 2014). The column collected_from says where each sample came from: one thin bed, or 6 m of rock;
  • far_side and fossil_layer: the two tables for the homework.

Every table has the same two measurement columns, parent and daughter. Each is a ratio of two kinds of atom, not a count; part 1 explains which atoms. Ages are in millions of years ago, written Ma.

docs.title: 1. How can a rock tell its own age?¶
docs.text:
The question. About 717 million years ago, glaciers spread over what is now northwest Canada, which then lay at the equator: ice reached the sea in the tropics (Macdonald and others, 2010). The Snowball Earth hypothesis (Kirschvink, 1992) says ice covered nearly the whole planet:

One reconstruction of the Earth 690 million years ago, with ice (white) over the land and the sea. Map: C. R. Scotese and others, PALEOMAP Project, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0).

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 1¶
docs.text:
Do the two laws agree, and how fast does the rubidium clock run?

Why: the two forms of the decay law must give the same share left; then the age of the Earth shows how slow this clock is.

  1. halving: the share left after time $t$ by the halving law, $(1/2)^{t / T_{1/2}}$.
  2. left: the share left by the decay-rate law, $e^{-\lambda t}$, with np.exp.
  3. decayed: the share decayed after time $t$, $1 - e^{-\lambda t}$.

In the loops t is the time $t$, in years.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: left and decayed.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 2¶
docs.text:
Do the Monterey rocks lie on a line?

Why: an age needs a line. Look before you fit.

  1. The figure: one dot per rock, the parent column across and the daughter column up.

Use the names in the cell, so later cells can read them.

docs.title: 2. How sure is an age from 37 samples?¶
docs.text:
On Monterey's 37 samples you learn the two skills the 7-sample Snowball cap will need in part 3: reading the clock, and saying how sure the reading is.

From the line to the age, step by step. Part 1 ended with the isochron equation:

$$\text{daughter now} = \text{daughter at the start} + \left(e^{\lambda t} - 1\right) \times \text{parent}$$

The line you will fit in Your turn 3 has the same shape:

$$\text{daughter} = \hat{a} + \hat{b} \times \text{parent}$$

A hat marks a number fitted from the data. Match them term by term: the intercept $\hat{a}$ is the daughter ratio at the start, and the slope $\hat{b}$ is $e^{\lambda t} - 1$. Add 1, take the natural log (ln undoes e), divide by $\lambda$:

$$\hat{b} = e^{\lambda t} - 1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad e^{\lambda t} = 1 + \hat{b} \quad\Rightarrow\quad t = \frac{\ln(1 + \hat{b})}{\lambda}$$

With the Monterey numbers you are about to get: $\hat{b}$ is 0.0011749, so $1 + \hat{b}$ is 1.0011749; its natural log is 0.0011742; divided by 1.42e-11 per year, that is 82.7 million years. In code, the three steps are one line, with b for $\hat{b}$: np.log(1 + b) / rb_decay.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 3¶
docs.text:
How old is the Monterey granite?

Why: the line fit of the last two weeks, with a new meaning for its slope.

  1. model: a straight line fitted to the rocks, the parent column (as a table, double brackets) to the daughter column, as in the line-fitting week.
  2. b: its slope, $\hat{b}$: model.coef_[0], as in the line-fitting week.
  3. age_ma: the age, $t = \ln(1 + \hat{b}) / \lambda$, in millions of years: np.log(1 + b) over rb_decay, then over a million.
  4. The figure: the rocks as dots and the fitted line through them, drawn with model.predict.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: b and age_ma.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 4¶
docs.text:
What does one redrawn set of rocks say?

Why: see one redraw before doing ten thousand.

  1. resample: 37 rows drawn from rocks with replacement, using the generator rng.
  2. resample_age: the age from a line fitted to resample, by the steps of Your turn 3.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: resample and resample_age.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 5¶
docs.text:
How far does the age wander over 10,000 redraws?

Why: the spread of the redrawn ages is the uncertainty of the age.

  1. The loop: start a generator from the seed 88; 10,000 times draw a resample as in Your turn 4, fit it, and append its age to boot_ages.
  2. age_range: the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of boot_ages, with np.percentile: the middle 95% of the ages lie between them.
  3. The figure: a histogram of boot_ages; the black lines at the ends of age_range are drawn for you.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: boot_ages and age_range.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 6¶
docs.text:
What does the formula say about the Monterey age?

Why: a second, independent way to the same interval, to check the bootstrap.

Each name is a symbol in the math: b is $\hat{b}$, e is $e_i$, s is $s$, Sxx is $S_{xx}$, SE_b is $\mathrm{SE}(\hat{b})$, t95 is $t_{95}$, and b_ends holds $\hat{b} \pm t_{95}\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat{b})$.

  1. b and e: the slope of model (Your turn 3), and each sample's daughter minus the line's prediction for it.
  2. s, Sxx and SE_b: steps 1, 2 and 3 above.
  3. b_ends: the two ends, $\hat{b} \pm t_{95}\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat{b})$, in one array; the given last line turns them into ages.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: SE_b and formula_range.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 7¶
docs.text:
What strontium did the Monterey magma start with, and is it surely above 0.706?

Why: the same redraws, a different number: the intercept of each redrawn line.

  1. start_sr: the intercept of model, the line fitted to all the rocks in Your turn 3: model.intercept_.
  2. start_values and start_range: 10,000 bootstrap intercepts of rocks (seed 88) and their middle 95%.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: start_sr and start_range.

docs.title: 3. How long was the Earth frozen?¶
docs.text: Back to the cap limestone above the Rapitan glacial deposits.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 8¶
docs.text:
When did the ice end?

Why: the steps of Your turns 3, 5 and 6, on the rock that dates the end of the glaciation.

  1. bed: the rows of cap whose collected_from is "thin bed".
  2. end_age: its age from a fitted line, with re_decay in place of rb_decay.
  3. end_ages and end_range: 10,000 bootstrap ages of bed (seed 88) and their middle 95%.
  4. end_formula_range: the formula's 95% interval, by the steps of Your turn 6 (b, e, s, Sxx, SE_b, b_ends), with the given t95 for 7 samples.

Each name is a symbol in the math: b is $\hat{b}$, e is $e_i$, s is $s$, Sxx is $S_{xx}$, SE_b is $\mathrm{SE}(\hat{b})$, t95 is $t_{95}$, and b_ends holds $\hat{b} \pm t_{95}\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat{b})$.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: end_age, end_range and end_formula_range.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 9¶
docs.text:
How long was the Earth frozen?

Why: the question of the week. With 7 samples the formula is the better guide (the coloured histogram above showed why), so it gives the answer; the bootstrap is set beside it to compare.

  1. start_age: given, the start of the glaciation in millions of years ago.
  2. duration: the start minus end_age.
  3. duration_formula_range: the start minus each end of end_formula_range. Subtracting flips the order: the shortest duration comes from the latest end, so take the high end first.
  4. duration_range: for comparison, the middle 95% of the start minus each of the end_ages.
  5. The figure: a histogram of the redrawn durations; the black lines (the bootstrap) and red lines (the formula) are drawn for you.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: duration, duration_formula_range and duration_range.

docs.title: The question, answered¶
docs.text: About 58.3 million years, 95% interval 49.0 to 67.6: your answer. The cap above the Sturtian glacial deposits is 658.2 million years old by your line, 648.9 to 667.5 by the formula, so the ice that began 716.5 million years ago lasted 58.3 million years. The authors' fit, which weighs each sample by its measurement error, gives about 54 ± 4, and caps of the same ice age dated since give 56 to 58 (Rooney and others, 2020); Francis Macdonald's group finds about 56 (Tasistro-Hart and others, 2025). The bootstrap's lopsided 24.5 to 63.6 is the lesson, not the answer: 7 samples, two of which hold the line.

docs.title: The science¶
docs.text:
How long was the Earth frozen? An isochron turns isotope ratios into an age: minerals or rocks that formed together lie on one line, and its slope grows with time. Two ways to an interval: the bootstrap redraws your own samples and refits, the least-squares formula computes the standard error directly; with many well-spread points they agree, with few the formula is the better guide if its assumptions hold, and about 19 in 20 such 95% intervals hold the answer.

  • Isochron. Minerals that formed together started with the same daughter atoms; each has since gained more in proportion to its parent atoms, so together they lie on a line whose slope grows with time.
  • Half-life. The time it takes for half of the parent atoms to decay, however many there are.
  • Bootstrap. Ask the data the same question a thousand times, using a different random slice of itself each time.
  • Confidence interval. Not one number but the range your number would have wandered over, had the world rolled differently.

docs.title: Homework¶

docs.title: Problem 1: Is the far side of the Moon older? (the bootstrap)¶
docs.text:
The Moon always shows us the same face. In 2024 the Chinese mission Chang'e-6 brought back the first rock from its far side: dark lava, basalt, from the South Pole–Aitken basin, a giant impact basin.

Left: the far side of the Moon, with the South Pole–Aitken basin outlined in red. Image: NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (public domain). Right: Chang'e-6 on the far side, photographed by its small rover. Photo: CNSA/Xinhua.

Far-side soil scooped by Chang'e-6, in the laboratory; the bar is 2 cm. Photo: Li and others (2024), National Science Review (CC BY 4.0).

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 10¶
docs.text:
How old is the far-side lava, and how sure is that age?

Why: Your turns 3 and 5 on a new rock.

  2. far_age: the age, with rb_decay.
  3. far_ages and far_range: 10,000 bootstrap ages (seed 88) and their middle 95%.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: far_age, far_ages and far_range.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 11¶
docs.text:
Is the far-side lava older than the near side's?

Why: an interval for a difference, as for the length of the ice age in Your turn 9: subtract the near-side age from every redrawn age.

  1. gap: far_age minus the near-side age.
  2. gap_range: the middle 95% of the far_ages minus the near-side age.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: gap and gap_range.

docs.title: Problem 2 (optional): Did large life appear at the same time on two continents? (the formula)¶
docs.text:
Optional. Your turns 12 and 13 are not graded. Do them if you have time: the same steps date many things.

After the last Snowball Earth ended, about 635 million years ago, the first organisms large enough to see appear in the rocks: soft-bodied fronds and discs, some perhaps early animals. The best-known site is Mistaken Point in Newfoundland, eastern Canada.

Left: a frond-shaped fossil at Mistaken Point, Newfoundland, with a coin for scale. Photo: Alicejmichel, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0). Right: Dickinsonia, a later Ediacaran organism. Photo: Verisimilus, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.5).

docs.text:

Two sizes for one event. Shaking travels as waves. The fastest, the P waves, push and pull the rock along their path; S waves shake it from side to side; and the slow surface waves roll along the ground behind them.

How each kind of seismic wave moves the ground: two body waves (P and S) and two surface waves (Love and Rayleigh). Figure: USGS (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons.

An explosion pushes the rock outward from one small spot, the same in every direction, so most of its shaking leaves as P waves. An earthquake is two blocks of rock slipping past each other along a fault: it sends out strong S waves, and, because the slip spreads over a large patch of fault and lasts longer, strong surface waves too.

North Korea's first test, 9 October 2006. Left: the test site (red star), earthquakes nearby (blue dots) and two seismic stations (triangles). Right: the explosion (red) and a recent earthquake nearby (blue) recorded at a station: the explosion's shaking is mostly P waves; the earthquake's largest shaking is its S waves. Figure: Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, Science & Technology Review (March 2009), via the Berkeley Seismological Laboratory blog.

So seismologists give each event two sizes. The body-wave magnitude mb is read from the first, fast P wave. The surface-wave magnitude Ms is read from the slow surface waves that follow. A small, sudden source like an explosion puts little energy into those long surface waves, so for its mb, an explosion has a small Ms. That one sentence is the physics of the whole week; the rest is how to use it well.

events[["date", "region", "depth", "mb", "Ms", "is_explosion"]].head()

Each row is one event: its date, its region, its depth below the surface in km, its two magnitudes, and is_explosion, the label: True for a nuclear explosion, False for an earthquake. The events come from three regions with test sites, from 1970 to 1996:

  • the western US: 405 events, 36 of them explosions, 35 at the Nevada Test Site and one in Colorado;
  • Central Asia: 696 events, 64 explosions, 53 at the Soviet test site near Semipalatinsk (now in Kazakhstan) and 11 at China's Lop Nur;
  • Novaya Zemlya, an Arctic island where the Soviet Union also tested: 17 events, all explosions.

Only events with both magnitudes are kept. Small explosions often have no Ms at all, so the table holds mostly large ones: only 9 of its 117 explosions have an mb below 5.4. Keep that in mind when the line meets smaller ones.

You do not need to read it — it only says whether something is off. assert round(accuracy, 3) == 0.895, "the mean of the mask always_earthquake == events['is_explosion']" assert found == 0, "the sum of always_earthquake & events['is_explosion']" print(f"✓ Your turn 1 — 'always earthquake' scores {accuracy:.3f} and finds {found} explosions")

Accuracy 0.895, and not one explosion found. Nine events in ten are earthquakes, so a rule that never flags is right nine times in ten. When one label is rare, accuracy hides the misses. A treaty needs scores that count the two kinds of mistake apart.

Four counts. Sort the events by label and by guess into four groups. A hit is an explosion the rule flagged, a miss an explosion it did not flag, and a false alarm an earthquake it flagged. The fourth group, earthquakes the rule leaves alone, is the right answer for most events. Two scores come from the counts:

  • precision = hits / (hits + false alarms): of the events you flagged, the share that were explosions;
  • recall = hits / (hits + misses): of the explosions, the share you flagged.

F1 joins them into one number, $F_1 = 2PR/(P+R)$ with $P$ the precision and $R$ the recall, which is high only when both are high.

Ten made-up events, two of them explosions, and the rule "flag every event with mb 5.7 or more":

ten_events["flagged"] = ten_events["mb"] >= 5.7
print(ten_events)
print("confusion_matrix:")

An F1 of 0.996, nearly perfect, and useless. All 117 explosions have depth 0.0, and the catalogue marks each of those depths as fixed by the analyst, not measured from the waves: the analyst set it to 0 because the event was already known to be an explosion. The column knew the answer before anyone looked. This is called leakage: a column that already holds the answer. When a score looks too good, first ask whether a column already knew the answer. (Shallow depths are hard to measure, so the catalogue fixed the depth of 343 earthquakes too, and depth cannot separate two shallow events.)

Rule two: training, validation and test. You met this in the model-selection week. Every rule from here on has something to choose: a gap, a slope, an alarm level. Anything chosen by looking at events will score well on those events, so the events that judge the choice must be kept apart:

  • the training events, used to fit and to search;
  • the validation events, used to choose between the rules found on training;
  • the test events, used once, at the end, to report how well the chosen rule does.

Logistic regression searches for the same kind of line, but in a different way, and it gives something the grid cannot: a probability for every event. It works out a value $z$ from the columns, as LinearRegression did, and bends $z$ into a probability with the S-curve

$$p = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}, \qquad z = a \times \text{mb} + b \times \text{Ms} + c$$

where $p$ is the probability that the event is an explosion, $a$, $b$, $c$ are the three numbers fit finds, and $e \approx 2.718$. For $z = -2$, $p = 0.12$; for $z = 0$, $p = 0.5$; for $z = 2$, $p = 0.88$. The events where $z = 0$, so $p = 0.5$, lie on a straight line, the decision boundary: solved for Ms it is Ms = −(a × mb + c) / b. On one side the model says explosion, on the other earthquake.

How fit scores a curve. Your grid scored a line by counting right and wrong. fit scores a curve by the probability it gives each event for the label it really has: $p$ for an explosion, $1 - p$ for an earthquake. Multiplied over all the events, that is the chance the curve gives to the labels coming out as they did; fit keeps the curve that makes it largest. Against the same curve moved one unit to the right:

six_label = six_events["is_explosion"]

for name, z in [("fitted curve", w * size + c), ("curve moved right by 1", w * (size - 1) + c)]:
    p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))                          # the S-curve
    own = six_label * p + (1 - six_label) * (1 - p)   # p for an explosion, 1 - p for an earthquake
    chance = 1
    for q in own:

Each level is one trade, one point. The ROC curve draws them all at once: the share of explosions caught (up) against the share of earthquakes falsely flagged (across), one point per level. The slope is the reason. North Korea's explosions are small: mb 4.8 to 5.3, but for 2017's 6.3. Their Ms sits 0.7 to 1.1 below their mb, as it does for the small explosions in the table (a median of 1.0 below). At mb 5.1 the fitted boundary flags an event only if its Ms is more than 1.5 below its mb; at mb 6.3, more than 0.57. The steep slope was learned from large explosions, and only 9 of the 117 were small. A test set drawn from the same places cannot show this; only a new place can. A better score on familiar events does not promise a better answer on new ones.

What monitoring agencies use. The screening line used by the treaty organisation's data centre until 2010, Ms = 1.25 mb − 2.2, has a slope between the two; with this table's magnitudes it flags 3 of the five.

The world's earthquakes of 2008 (grey) and six explosions, with the screening line (dashed). North Korea's first two tests, 2006 and 2009, sit right on the line. These magnitudes come from the treaty organisation's own network, so they differ from this table's by a few tenths. Figure: Selby et al. (2012), shown in G. Ekström's "Seismology in MTV" slides (Columbia University, 2019).

docs.title: Earthquake or nuclear explosion?¶
docs.text:
EPS 88 · PyEarth. Open your own copy on DataHub: click here.

The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty, opened for signature in 1996, bans every nuclear explosion, though it has not yet entered into force. A test can be hidden underground, out of sight, but the ground still shakes, and stations thousands of kilometres away record it. The trouble is that the Earth has thousands of earthquakes a year. To check a ban, you have to pick out the explosions among them, and you have to be right, because a false alarm accuses a country of breaking a treaty.

Today you work with 1,118 real events from the International Seismological Centre's catalogue: 117 nuclear explosions and 1,001 earthquakes in the regions around the test sites. You learn how to score a rule when explosions are rare, how to keep that score honest, how to find a line that separates the two, and where to set the alarm. At the end of class you ask the line about five explosions it has never seen, North Korea's. At home you fit the line in one part of the world and check it in another.

Every place you write something opens with a pencil icon and the words Your turn, and is followed by a cell that already has the shape of the answer written in, with ... wherever your code goes. Replace every ..., run every cell so your answers and figures are saved in the file, then download this notebook itself — the .ipynb file — and upload it to Gradescope. Not a PDF: the marking reads your notebook, and a PDF cannot be read. In JupyterLab: File ▸ Download, or right-click the file in the left-hand panel and choose Download.

Two habits from the first minute. A cell runs when you press Shift+Enter, and the notebook remembers everything it has already run — so when something breaks and you cannot see why, Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells throws the memory away and rebuilds it from the top. That is never the wrong thing to do.

docs.title: What you'll be able to do¶
docs.text:
The science. Say why an explosion and an earthquake of the same size shake the ground differently, and which seismic measurement shows it; and judge a rule that flags explosions by the two mistakes it can make.

The code. Precision, recall and F1 by hand, then with precision_score, recall_score and f1_score · train_test_split with stratify, into training, validation and test · a grid of lines scored by counting · LogisticRegression with fit and predict_proba · an alarm level chosen on validation events and tested once.

Fifteen places where you write something: eleven in class, four at home. Each is headed Your turn.

The six questions of the class:

  1. How could a seismometer tell a test from an earthquake?
  2. How do we score a rule when explosions are rare?
  3. How do we keep the score honest?
  4. Can one line through mb and Ms split them?
  5. Where should the alarm go?
  6. Does the line work somewhere new?

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text: Run the next cell once. It reads the events, stored with the course: every event in three regions with test sites, plus North Korea, for which the International Seismological Centre (ISC) Bulletin lists both magnitudes this week uses. It splits off the five North Korean explosions into their own table, korea, for the end of class, and keeps the rest in events. It also reads the coastlines for the map, and makes grid, a table of points spread over the mb–Ms plane, for the probability map at the end of class, over the same mb and Ms range, 2 to 7, as the treaty's screening plot.

docs.title: 1. How could a seismometer tell a test from an earthquake?¶
docs.text:
An underground test. A nuclear device is placed hundreds of metres underground, at the bottom of a drilled shaft or at the end of a tunnel dug into a mountain, sealed in, and fired. Usually nothing reaches the surface but the shaking (and sometimes radioactive gas that seeps out), and later, often, a crater where the rock above the blast collapses. (Firing a device inside a large underground cavity can muffle the shaking many times over, one reason small tests are hard to find.)

Left: a vertical underground test at the Nevada Test Site, the device at the bottom of a drilled hole. Diagram: US Government (public domain). Right: craters left at the Nevada Test Site where the ground collapsed into the cavities of underground tests. Photo: USGS (public domain). Both via Wikimedia Commons.

docs.title: 2. How do we score a rule when explosions are rare?¶
docs.text:
This is classification. In the regression weeks a model answered with a number. Here it answers with a label: explosion or earthquake. A guess is a column of True and False, one per event, from a rule or a model. It is scored against the label.

The laziest rule is to say "earthquake" every time. It is the baseline, the simplest rule there is, scored first: a rule that cannot beat it does no useful work.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 1¶
docs.text:
How good is "always earthquake"?

Why: a score is only useful if a rule that does no work scores badly. Find out what the usual score, accuracy, gives the laziest rule.

  1. always_earthquake: a guess of False for every event, given. It is written as a mask on a column (no event has an mb above 100) so that it is a column of True and False like every other guess this week.
  2. accuracy: the share of events where the guess equals the label: the mean of the mask always_earthquake == events["is_explosion"]. The next line prints accuracy_score beside it.
  3. found: how many explosions the rule flags: the sum of the mask always_earthquake & events["is_explosion"].

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: accuracy and found.

  2. hits, misses, false_alarms: the three counts, each as the sum of a mask. (guess_mb == False is the mask of the events not flagged.)
  3. precision_mb, recall_mb, f1_mb: the three scores from your counts, by the formulas above. The line after them prints what precision_score, recall_score and f1_score give for the same label and guess.
  4. The figure: histograms of mb for the earthquakes and the explosions, with a line at the cut.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: hits, misses, false_alarms, precision_mb, recall_mb and f1_mb.

docs.text: Rule one: no column may already know the answer. Depth looks tempting: earthquakes start kilometres down, and a test hole is a few hundred metres deep.

Why: this is what fitting does: try lines and keep the one that scores best. Here you do it by counting, with F1 as the score.

  1. The two loops: for each offset in offsets, for each slope in slopes, the guess, True where a training event's Ms is below slope × mb − offset, and its F1, appended to f1s.
  2. best_f1, best_slope, best_offset: inside the loop, when a line beats the best so far, keep its F1, slope and offset (an if, as in week 2). Ties keep the first line found.
  3. The picture of every F1, slope across and offset up, is given.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: f1s, best_f1, best_slope and best_offset.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 7¶
docs.text:
Does fit find the grid's line, and which line does best on the validation events?

Why: the grid searched by counting, fit by probability. If they agree, you know what fit did. The validation events, which none of the three lines saw, judge between them.

  1. model: LogisticRegression().fit(...) on the training events: mb and Ms, then the label.
  2. boundary_slope and boundary_offset: the boundary written as a line, like the grid's. a, b = model.coef_[0] and c = model.intercept_[0] are given: here a = 5.91, b = -3.31, c = -18.16. The boundary is where z = 0, so a × mb + b × Ms + c = 0. Move a × mb + c to the other side: b × Ms = −a × mb − c. Divide by b: Ms = (−a / b) × mb − c / b. So the slope is −a / b and the offset is c / b. And b is negative: a larger Ms makes an earthquake more likely. Dividing by a negative number turns > into <, so the side where z > 0, the explosions, is Ms < slope × mb − offset, the same form as the grid's line.
  3. f1_val_model: the model's F1 on the validation events, with model.predict(...). The F1s of the line by eye and the grid's line on the same events are given.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: boundary_slope, boundary_offset and f1_val_model.

docs.title: 5. Where should the alarm go?¶
docs.text:
predict flags an event when its probability is 0.5 or more. Nothing says 0.5 is right. A missed explosion is a secret test that got through; a false alarm accuses a state that did nothing, though an inspection team can check a flagged event by other means. The alarm level is that choice: the probability at or above which you flag an event. Lower it and you miss fewer explosions but accuse more earthquakes. It is a choice, so it is made on the validation events.

First, the probability itself, from the three numbers fit found.

  2. prob_val: the S-curve of z, 1 / (1 + e^(−z)), with np.exp.
  3. The next line prints the largest difference from model.predict_proba(...)[:, 1].

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: z and prob_val.

docs.text: The line was fitted on Nevada, Central Asia and Novaya Zemlya, 1970 to 1996. North Korea has tested since 2006 at a site none of those events came from. The ISC lists five of its explosions with both magnitudes: a test of the line at a place it never saw.

docs.title: The question, answered¶
docs.text: Mostly, with two magnitudes and an honest score. "Always earthquake" is right 0.895 of the time and finds nothing, so the scores count hits, misses and false alarms apart. A depth of 0 looks perfect only because the analyst already knew. A grid of 560 lines and logistic regression find nearly the same line through mb and Ms; the probability logistic regression adds lets the alarm be set on validation events, and on the test events, opened once, the rule catches 22 of 23 explosions with 0 false alarms. But at North Korea's small explosions the steep line misses what the plainer line catches: its slope was learned from large explosions.

docs.title: The science¶
docs.text:
Earthquake or nuclear explosion? When one label is rare, accuracy hides the misses: 'always earthquake' scores 0.895 and finds no explosion; precision, recall and F1 count the two kinds of mistake apart. Logistic regression draws a straight line through two columns and gives every event a probability; checked on events it never saw, the line through mb and Ms finds explosions that each magnitude alone misses. But its slope was learned from large explosions: at North Korea's small ones the plain line by eye does better. Where to set the alarm is a choice between missed explosions and false accusations; the ROC curve shows every choice at once, and a column that already knows the answer (a depth the analyst set to 0) is leakage, not skill.

  • Body-wave and surface-wave magnitude. Two sizes for one event: mb is read from the first, fast P wave, Ms from the slow surface waves that follow. An explosion pushes out from one small spot and makes weak surface waves for its mb; an earthquake slips along a fault and makes strong ones.
  • Baseline. Write the dumbest rule you can, first. Any model that cannot beat it is decoration.
  • Hit, miss, false alarm. A hit is an explosion you flagged, a miss an explosion you did not, a false alarm an earthquake you flagged.
  • Precision / recall. Of the ones you flagged, how many were right? Of the real ones, how many did you catch?
  • Leakage. You got 99 percent. Be suspicious. Did one of your columns already know the answer?
  • Logistic regression. The same straight line — but now it outputs a probability between 0 and 1.
  • Decision boundary. Where the model's answer flips from one label to the other — for logistic regression, always a straight line.
  • Alarm level. The probability at or above which you flag an event. Lower it and you miss fewer explosions but accuse more earthquakes.
  • ROC curve. Every alarm level at once: the share of explosions caught against the share of earthquakes falsely flagged. The closer the curve hugs the top left, the better the model.

How good is the western model in Eurasia at every alarm level at once?

Why: the ROC curve of class, in the new place, and its area computed by hand: the area is the share of (explosion, earthquake) pairs that the model puts in the right order, explosion higher.

  1. eurasia_hit_shares and eurasia_false_alarm_shares: for each level in roc_levels, the share of Eurasia's explosions flagged and the share of its earthquakes flagged.
  2. auc_by_hand: over every explosion, count the earthquakes with a lower probability; add the counts; divide by (number of explosions × number of earthquakes). The next line prints roc_auc_score beside it.
  3. The figure: the curve and the diagonal.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: eurasia_hit_shares, eurasia_false_alarm_shares and auc_by_hand.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, export_text
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, ConfusionMatrixDisplay
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# house style, set once, so every plot cell below holds only what matters
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110,
                     "axes.grid": True, "grid.alpha": 0.3, "axes.axisbelow": True})

CACHE = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AI4EPS/EPS88_PyEarth/main/data"

# One row per rock: its setting (IAB, MORB or OIB) and up to 51 chemical measurements.
# Source: Vermeesch (2006), Geochemistry, Geophysics, Geosystems 7, doi:10.1029/2005GC001092.
rocks = pd.read_csv(CACHE + "/week10_vermeesch_basalts.csv")
rocks = rocks.rename(columns={"affinity": "setting", "P2O5(wt%)": "P2O5_wt_percent"})
rocks.loc[rocks["MnO_wt_percent"] > 5, "MnO_wt_percent"] = np.nan   # one impossible value, blanked
print(len(rocks), "rocks,", rocks.shape[1] - 1, "measurements each (many blank)")
import numpy as np from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier from sklearn.svm import SVC from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, export_text from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, ConfusionMatrixDisplay import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt # house style, set once, so every plot cell below holds only what matters plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.grid": True, "grid.alpha": 0.3, "axes.axisbelow": True}) CACHE = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AI4EPS/EPS88_PyEarth/main/data" # One row per rock: its setting (IAB, MORB or OIB) and up to 51 chemical measurements. # Source: Vermeesch (2006), Geochemistry, Geophysics, Geosystems 7, doi:10.1029/2005GC001092. rocks = pd.read_csv(CACHE + "/week10_vermeesch_basalts.csv") rocks = rocks.rename(columns={"affinity": "setting", "P2O5(wt%)": "P2O5_wt_percent"}) rocks.loc[rocks["MnO_wt_percent"] > 5, "MnO_wt_percent"] = np.nan # one impossible value, blanked print(len(rocks), "rocks,", rocks.shape[1] - 1, "measurements each (many blank)")

From the outside the three look alike: dark fine-grained rock, often in rounded "pillows" where lava met cold sea water:

Pillow basalt on the sea floor. Photo: NOAA (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons.

So geologists measure what is inside. A rock analysis gives the common elements as oxides, in percent of the rock's weight (SiO2, TiO2), and the rare ones in parts per million (V, Sr).

First, lock some rocks away. The routine analysis of a rock lists nine major oxides: silica, titanium, aluminium, calcium, magnesium, manganese, potassium, sodium and phosphorus. (Iron is left out: more than half of all 756 rocks have no iron value, and the rest split it between FeO and Fe2O3 in different ways.) The next cell keeps the 640 rocks with all nine and, as in the model-selection week, splits them once: 448 training rocks to build and choose with, and 192 sealed rocks that nothing touches until the last Your turn of class. A score on rocks that helped choose the model is not a test, so from here on even our first look at the data uses the training rocks only.

In [ ]: Copied! 
oxides = ["SiO2_wt_percent", "TiO2_wt_percent", "Al2O3_wt_percent", "CaO_wt_percent", "MgO_wt_percent",
          "MnO_wt_percent", "K2O_wt_percent", "Na2O_wt_percent", "P2O5_wt_percent"]
rocks_ox = rocks.dropna(subset=oxides)   # rocks with all nine oxides measured
train, sealed = train_test_split(rocks_ox, test_size=0.3, random_state=0, stratify=rocks_ox["setting"])
print(len(train), "training rocks,", len(sealed), "sealed until the end")
oxides = ["SiO2_wt_percent", "TiO2_wt_percent", "Al2O3_wt_percent", "CaO_wt_percent", "MgO_wt_percent", "MnO_wt_percent", "K2O_wt_percent", "Na2O_wt_percent", "P2O5_wt_percent"] rocks_ox = rocks.dropna(subset=oxides) # rocks with all nine oxides measured train, sealed = train_test_split(rocks_ox, test_size=0.3, random_state=0, stratify=rocks_ox["setting"]) print(len(train), "training rocks,", len(sealed), "sealed until the end")

What is basalt made of? The next cell takes the middle (median) training rock, oxide by oxide, and draws it.

In [ ]: Copied! 
middle = train[oxides].median().sort_values()   # the median of each oxide, smallest first
plt.figure(figsize=(7, 3.5))
plt.barh(middle.index, middle)
plt.xlabel("weight percent of the rock")
plt.title("The middle training basalt")
plt.show()
print("the nine add up to", round(middle.sum()), "percent")
middle = train[oxides].median().sort_values() # the median of each oxide, smallest first plt.figure(figsize=(7, 3.5)) plt.barh(middle.index, middle) plt.xlabel("weight percent of the rock") plt.title("The middle training basalt") plt.show() print("the nine add up to", round(middle.sum()), "percent")

Half of basalt is silica. The middle rock holds 49.6 percent SiO2, then 15.6 Al2O3, 11.0 CaO, 7.5 MgO and 2.6 Na2O; most of the missing 11 percent is the iron left out above. These big five are what basalt's minerals are built from: olivine and pyroxene (magnesium, iron, silica; pyroxene also much of the calcium) and feldspar (aluminium, calcium, sodium, silica). The other four are small: 1.4 percent TiO2, 0.5 K2O, and P2O5 and MnO about 0.2 each.

Think before you run the next cell. The three homes melt the same kind of mantle, in different ways. Which oxides would you expect to differ between the homes: the big ones that build the minerals, or the small ones? The cell prints each oxide's median in each setting, then, for each oxide, the largest of the three medians divided by the smallest.

In [ ]: Copied! 
by_setting = train.groupby("setting")[oxides].median()   # one row per setting, one column per oxide
print(by_setting.T.round(2))                              # .T turns it: one row per oxide
spread = np.max(by_setting, axis=0) / np.min(by_setting, axis=0)   # largest median over smallest, down each column
print(spread.sort_values().round(1))
by_setting = train.groupby("setting")[oxides].median() # one row per setting, one column per oxide print(by_setting.T.round(2)) # .T turns it: one row per oxide spread = np.max(by_setting, axis=0) / np.min(by_setting, axis=0) # largest median over smallest, down each column print(spread.sort_values().round(1))

The big oxides barely move; three small ones do. Silica's median runs only from 46.8 to 50.1 percent across the three settings, and no big oxide's largest median is even one and a half times its smallest. Phosphorus differs 2.9 times, titanium 3.1 times, potassium 5.9 times. Why these three?

Each home melts the mantle in its own way, and the melt keeps the mark. Titanium, potassium and phosphorus fit badly into the mantle's minerals, so they prefer the melt. When only a little of the mantle melts, what there is of them gathers into a little liquid and the basalt is rich in them; when much melts, they are diluted. The table follows titanium and potassium, the two that differ most.

Home Why the mantle melts How much melts Titanium Potassium Examples Mid-ocean ridge (MORB) the plates pull apart; hot mantle rises to fill the gap and melts as the pressure on it drops a large share middle: diluted in much melt low: this mantle lost it in melts long ago Mid-Atlantic Ridge, East Pacific Rise Island arc (IAB) water from the sinking plate lowers the mantle's melting point, as salt melts ice varies low: this mantle has often melted before, and the water brings little raised: the water carries it, with strontium, out of the sinking plate; some arcs (Tonga, Izu-Bonin) still hold little Mariana, Izu-Bonin, Tonga, Aleutians Ocean island (OIB) a plume of unusually hot mantle rises, usually far from any plate edge; the thick plate above stops it rising far a small share, deep down, of a mantle richer in both elements high highest Hawaii, Samoa, the Canary Islands

Read the table against the medians you printed. The middle arc rock holds 0.9 percent TiO2 and 0.51 percent K2O; the middle ridge rock 1.42 and 0.16; the middle ocean-island rock 2.78 and 0.94. Titanium puts all three in order; potassium helps where titanium overlaps, ridge from arc at low titanium and ridge from ocean island at high. Phosphorus behaves like potassium without the arc's water (0.14, 0.14 and 0.4): raised only in the islands.

Geologists have drawn lines between the settings by hand since the 1980s, on plots of two elements such as these; the homework meets the most famous one.

The bar. Write the dumbest rule you can, first. Any model that cannot beat it is decoration. The next cell counts the training rocks in each setting (value_counts lists the commonest first) and scores the guess "always the commonest setting".

In [ ]: Copied! 
counts = train["setting"].value_counts()
print(counts)
print("guess the commonest setting every time: right", round(counts.iloc[0] / len(train), 3), "of the time")
counts = train["setting"].value_counts() print(counts) print("guess the commonest setting every time: right", round(counts.iloc[0] / len(train), 3), "of the time")

0.355, the score to beat. Last week, when explosions were rare, the share right hid the misses, and you counted them apart. Here the three settings are nearly equal in number (159, 151 and 138 training rocks), so the share right is a fair score; the confusion matrix still shows where the misses fall. The next cell draws the training rocks on the two elements the first models use.

In [ ]: Copied! 
ti_k = ["TiO2_wt_percent", "K2O_wt_percent"]   # the names of the titanium and potassium columns
plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4.5))
for setting, marker in [("IAB", "o"), ("MORB", "s"), ("OIB", "^")]:
    some = train[train["setting"] == setting]
    plt.scatter(some["TiO2_wt_percent"], some["K2O_wt_percent"], s=12, marker=marker, label=setting)
plt.xlabel("TiO2 (weight percent)")
plt.ylabel("K2O (weight percent)")
plt.title("The training rocks")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

0.862, against 0.355 for a guess. Read the matrix row by row, as last week's recall: of 159 arc rocks it predicts 135 right, of 151 ridge rocks 128, of 138 ocean-island rocks 123. Of its 62 misses, 33 are arcs and ridges mistaken for each other. Last week each event got one probability, of being an explosion; now each rock gets three, one per setting, adding up to 1:

In [ ]: Copied! 
one_rock = train.loc[[59], ti_k]   # one training rock, picked by its index label
print(one_rock)
probabilities = line_tk.predict_proba(one_rock)[0]   # one probability per setting
print("probabilities", line_tk.classes_, ":", probabilities.round(2))
print("they add up to", probabilities.sum().round(2))
print("predicted:", line_tk.predict(one_rock)[0])
one_rock = train.loc[[59], ti_k] # one training rock, picked by its index label print(one_rock) probabilities = line_tk.predict_proba(one_rock)[0] # one probability per setting print("probabilities", line_tk.classes_, ":", probabilities.round(2)) print("they add up to", probabilities.sum().round(2)) print("predicted:", line_tk.predict(one_rock)[0])

0.27, 0.71 and 0.01: the model predicts the largest, MORB (the rock is MORB). What regions did the model draw? The next cell writes a small function, draw_regions, that asks a fitted model to predict the setting at every point of a fine grid of titanium and potassium values, and colours the map by its predictions; the lines around it open and show the figure. It is used again in sections 4 and 5, for the new models.

In [ ]: Copied! 
def draw_regions(model, title):
    """Colour a TiO2-K2O map by what a fitted model predicts at each point, and draw the training rocks on it."""
    # 1. a grid of made-up rocks, every 0.05 percent of TiO2 and of K2O
    ti_grid, k_grid = [], []
    for ti in np.arange(0, 4.51, 0.05):
        for k in np.arange(0, 3.01, 0.05):
            ti_grid.append(ti)
            k_grid.append(k)
    grid = pd.DataFrame({"TiO2_wt_percent": ti_grid, "K2O_wt_percent": k_grid})
    # 2. the model's prediction for each made-up rock
    predicted = model.predict(grid)
    # 3. colour each made-up rock by its prediction, and draw the real training rocks on top
    for setting, colour, light in [("IAB", "tab:blue", "#c6dbef"), ("MORB", "tab:orange", "#fdd0a2"), ("OIB", "tab:green", "#c7e9c0")]:
        here = predicted == setting             # the made-up rocks predicted as this setting
        plt.scatter(grid["TiO2_wt_percent"][here], grid["K2O_wt_percent"][here], s=30, marker="s", color=light, lw=0)
        some = train[train["setting"] == setting]   # and the real training rocks of this setting
        plt.scatter(some["TiO2_wt_percent"], some["K2O_wt_percent"], s=12, color=colour, edgecolor="black", lw=0.3, label=setting)
    plt.xlabel("TiO2 (weight percent)")
    plt.ylabel("K2O (weight percent)")
    plt.title(title)
    plt.grid(False)                             # no grid lines over the coloured map
    plt.legend()

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4.5))
draw_regions(line_tk, "The lines on Ti and K: three regions with straight edges")
plt.show()
def draw_regions(model, title): """Colour a TiO2-K2O map by what a fitted model predicts at each point, and draw the training rocks on it.""" # 1. a grid of made-up rocks, every 0.05 percent of TiO2 and of K2O ti_grid, k_grid = [], [] for ti in np.arange(0, 4.51, 0.05): for k in np.arange(0, 3.01, 0.05): ti_grid.append(ti) k_grid.append(k) grid = pd.DataFrame({"TiO2_wt_percent": ti_grid, "K2O_wt_percent": k_grid}) # 2. the model's prediction for each made-up rock predicted = model.predict(grid) # 3. colour each made-up rock by its prediction, and draw the real training rocks on top for setting, colour, light in [("IAB", "tab:blue", "#c6dbef"), ("MORB", "tab:orange", "#fdd0a2"), ("OIB", "tab:green", "#c7e9c0")]: here = predicted == setting # the made-up rocks predicted as this setting plt.scatter(grid["TiO2_wt_percent"][here], grid["K2O_wt_percent"][here], s=30, marker="s", color=light, lw=0) some = train[train["setting"] == setting] # and the real training rocks of this setting plt.scatter(some["TiO2_wt_percent"], some["K2O_wt_percent"], s=12, color=colour, edgecolor="black", lw=0.3, label=setting) plt.xlabel("TiO2 (weight percent)") plt.ylabel("K2O (weight percent)") plt.title(title) plt.grid(False) # no grid lines over the coloured map plt.legend() plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4.5)) draw_regions(line_tk, "The lines on Ti and K: three regions with straight edges") plt.show()

Three regions with straight edges, each edge where two settings' $z$'s tie. Most rocks sit in the region of their own colour; the arc and ridge rocks at low titanium overlap, and no straight edge can part them.

More columns: all nine oxides. The next cell names the nine oxides of every training rock X and their settings y, fits the same model on X, and scores it on the training rocks beside the two-element model.

In [ ]: Copied! 
X = train[oxides]      # the nine oxides of every training rock
y = train["setting"]   # and its setting
line_nine = LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000)
line_nine.fit(X, y)
train_score_tk = line_tk.score(train[ti_k], y)
train_score_nine = line_nine.score(X, y)
print("the lines on Ti and K:     ", round(train_score_tk, 3), "of the training rocks right")
print("the lines on nine oxides:  ", round(train_score_nine, 3))
X = train[oxides] # the nine oxides of every training rock y = train["setting"] # and its setting line_nine = LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000) line_nine.fit(X, y) train_score_tk = line_tk.score(train[ti_k], y) train_score_nine = line_nine.score(X, y) print("the lines on Ti and K: ", round(train_score_tk, 3), "of the training rocks right") print("the lines on nine oxides: ", round(train_score_nine, 3))

0.922 against 0.862. Are nine oxides better? These training scores cannot say. Both are scores on the rocks the models learned from. A model with more columns has more ways to fit those very rocks, accidents and all, so a training score flatters it. What we want is how a model does on rocks it has never seen: how well it generalizes. The next section measures that.

Which fifth to hold out for validation? The next cell holds out a different random fifth of the training rocks 20 times. Each time it fits the nine-oxide lines on the other four fifths and scores them on the fifth held out.

In [ ]: Copied! 
split_scores = []
for seed in range(20):
    fit_80, held_20 = train_test_split(train, test_size=0.2, random_state=seed, stratify=train["setting"])
    model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000)
    model.fit(fit_80[oxides], fit_80["setting"])
    split_scores.append(model.score(held_20[oxides], held_20["setting"]))

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 3))
plt.scatter(range(20), split_scores)
plt.xticks(range(0, 20, 2))
plt.xlabel("random split number (random_state)")
plt.ylabel("share right on the held-out fifth")
plt.title("One model, 20 validation splits of the 448 training rocks")
plt.show()
print("lowest", round(np.min(split_scores), 3), " highest", round(np.max(split_scores), 3))
split_scores = [] for seed in range(20): fit_80, held_20 = train_test_split(train, test_size=0.2, random_state=seed, stratify=train["setting"]) model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000) model.fit(fit_80[oxides], fit_80["setting"]) split_scores.append(model.score(held_20[oxides], held_20["setting"])) plt.figure(figsize=(7, 3)) plt.scatter(range(20), split_scores) plt.xticks(range(0, 20, 2)) plt.xlabel("random split number (random_state)") plt.ylabel("share right on the held-out fifth") plt.title("One model, 20 validation splits of the 448 training rocks") plt.show() print("lowest", round(np.min(split_scores), 3), " highest", round(np.max(split_scores), 3))

The same model scores anywhere from 0.867 to 0.967, depending only on which rocks were held out. With one validation split, a difference of a few points between two models can be nothing but the luck of the split.

Cross-validation fixes this. Cut the rows into five parts; hold out each part in turn, train on the other four, and score on the one held out. Five scores, and every row tested once.

Top: all the rocks, split once into training rocks and the sealed test rocks. Middle: the training rocks cut into five parts (the figure calls them folds); in each of the five splits one part (blue) is held out and scored, and the model is fitted on the other four (green). The mean of the five scores is the model's cross-validation score, and it is what models are chosen by. Bottom: the chosen model is scored once on the test rocks. Figure: scikit-learn documentation (BSD licence).

The library does all five rounds in one line:

scores = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=5)

model is a new, unfitted model; X the columns and y the labels of the training rocks; cv=5 asks for five parts. The library cuts the parts itself, keeping each setting's share the same in every part, then fits and scores five times and returns the five scores, one per round.

In [ ]: Copied!

nine_cv = np.mean(...)                              # the mean of the five scores
nine_spread = np.std(...)                           # their standard deviation
print("five held-out scores:", np.round(nine_scores, 3))
print("mean", round(nine_cv, 3), "  spread", round(nine_spread, 3))
print("training score", round(train_score_nine, 3), "  cross-validation mean", round(nine_cv, 3))

Five scores, from 0.878 to 0.921, mean 0.902: below the training score, 0.922. That gap is what the training score hid. The spread of the five, 0.016, says how much one part's luck can move a score. Now the question the training scores could not answer.

The training score climbs from 0.609 to 1.000; the cross-validation mean peaks at 0.833 at depth 5, then falls to about 0.812. Past depth 5 the tree learns the training rocks themselves, odd ones included, rather than the pattern behind them. That is overfitting: the training score cannot see it, because it only gets better, and cross-validation can. A tree grown with no depth limit has 77 end points, 12 questions deep (counted when this notebook was built).

A tree also changes with its rocks. Grown on a bootstrap sample of the same training rocks (rows drawn at random with replacement, as in the uncertainty week), a two-question tree asks a different first question each time: TiO2 at 2.01, 1.85 or 2.13. One tree's answer depends on which rocks it happened to see.

So use many trees. Ask many slightly different trees and take a vote. Each tree learns from its own bootstrap sample and looks at only a few columns at each question, so the trees make different mistakes, and their majority vote is steadier than any one tree. Think of many geologists, each trained on a different box of rocks, voting on a new one.

Many decision trees each give a prediction; the forest's prediction is the majority vote. (The figure feeds the same data to every tree; in a random forest each tree gets its own bootstrap sample.) Figure: TseKiChun (CC BY-SA 4.0), via Wikimedia Commons.

Magnesium, aluminium and silica vary by about 2 percent from rock to rock; manganese by 0.03, phosphorus by 0.22, potassium by 0.55. In raw units the distance is decided by the big oxides, and the small ones, potassium, phosphorus and manganese among them, barely count.

Scaling fixes this: from each column subtract its mean and divide by its standard deviation,

$$x_\text{scaled} = \frac{x - \text{mean}}{\text{std}}$$

so every column has mean 0 and spread 1. StandardScaler does it in two steps, like a model: .fit(table) learns each column's mean and standard deviation, and .transform(table) applies them. A simple case: 2 and 6 have mean 4 and standard deviation 2, so they become −1 and 1.

The mean and standard deviation are learned, like the model, from the training rows only. They are then used, unchanged, on the held-out rows. Scaling the held-out rows by their own mean would let the rocks we score on shape the model we score. The next cell makes one validation split of the training rocks, 358 to fit and 90 held out, and lets a scaler learn from the 358 only.

To cross-validate the scaled SVM, those steps (learn the scaling, apply it, fit) must run again in every round, each time learning only from that round's four parts. Doing that by hand is easy to get wrong. A pipeline does it for you.

make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC()) joins a scaler and an SVM into one model, pipe:

  • pipe.fit(table, labels) does both of your fitting lines: the scaler learns the mean and standard deviation of table and scales it, then the SVM fits on the scaled rows;
  • pipe.score(other, labels) and pipe.predict(other) scale other with the stored mean and standard deviation, never other's own, then score or predict;
  • given to cross_val_score, the pipeline is fitted afresh in each round on that round's four parts, so every held-out part is scaled by what the other four learned.

The next cell checks the first two on your split: the pipeline's own scaler, pipe[0], learns the same means as yours, and its score on held_rows is your scaled_score.

The ranking holds, as far as these rocks can tell. On the sealed rocks the lines on titanium and potassium score 0.854, the lines on nine oxides 0.911, and the two flexible models 0.948 (forest) and 0.953 (SVM): the same order cross-validation found, each close to its cross-validation mean. Guessing the commonest setting gets 0.354 of the sealed rocks right.

The conclusion is not "the best model is X". Two things are clear: nine oxides beat titanium and potassium, and on nine oxides the forest and the SVM both beat last week's lines. Between the forest and the SVM the rocks cannot decide: they tied exactly on the five parts, and on the sealed rocks they differ by 1 rock of 192. Picking one by its last decimal would be reading noise. Either one, used on new rocks from this compilation, should name the setting about 19 times in 20.

The answer: from its chemistry. For rocks like these, a forest or an SVM on nine oxides predicts the setting of about 19 in 20 rocks it never saw (0.948 and 0.953). Titanium carries the most, the one oxide whose medians put all three settings in order, as section 1 showed and the forest's importance confirmed. Training scores said nothing (the forest's was 1.000); cross-validation told the models apart, and the sealed rocks confirmed what it found. The three classifiers share fit, predict and score, so all three were tried: on nine oxides the flexible ones gained a little over the lines, and on two elements little or nothing. Which method wins depends on the data, and on these rocks two methods are equally good.

Lines drawn by hand: Shervais's diagram. In 1982 the geologist John Shervais plotted titanium against vanadium. Vanadium alone barely differs between the settings (median 280, 271 and 274 ppm in the arc, ridge and island training rocks). Shervais used it as a ruler. As a melt cools and grows crystals, vanadium and titanium change together, so their ratio, Ti/V, changes less than either and keeps the mark of the melting. And an arc's melt is wet and oxidised, which lets more vanadium into it, so arc basalt holds much vanadium for its titanium. He drew two lines, at Ti/V = 20 and Ti/V = 50: arc rocks below 20, ridge rocks between, ocean islands above 50. (That last field is for the alkaline ocean-island basalts; island tholeiites, like most of Hawaii's lava, plot between 20 and 50 with the ridges.)

Titanium is reported as TiO2 in weight percent. Titanium is 47.87 of TiO2's 79.87 units of mass (their atomic masses), so 1 percent TiO2 holds 10,000 × 47.87 / 79.87 ≈ 5993 parts per million of titanium. The next cell draws the training rocks with his two lines and scores his rule.

270 of 345 right (0.783), from two lines a person drew. 24 of the island rocks fall between the lines, where Shervais put the ridges. A model can draw its own lines, and strontium is another candidate partner for titanium. Arc melts are richer in it than ridge melts: the water rising from the sinking plate carries it into the melt, as it carries potassium.

docs.title: Where was this basalt made?¶
docs.text:
EPS 88 · PyEarth. Open your own copy on DataHub: click here.

Basalt is the commonest volcanic rock on Earth: the crust under every ocean is made of it. It is made in three different places, where the mantle melts, and a geologist often holds a piece without knowing which. California's Coast Ranges, for example, hold slices of old sea floor lifted onto the continent, and whether that crust was made at a mid-ocean ridge or above a sinking plate decides what story the rocks tell. The rock cannot say where it came from. Its chemistry can.

Today you work with 756 basalts whose birthplace is known, compiled by the geologist Pieter Vermeesch (2006) from published analyses. You start with last week's logistic regression, then ask the week's real question: will a model work on rocks it has never seen? Cross-validation answers it, and with it you judge two new models, a random forest and a support vector machine. Nearly a third of the rocks are locked away at the start and opened once, at the end. At home you ask whether the winner works on rocks from somewhere else.

Every place you write something opens with a pencil icon and the words Your turn, and is followed by a cell that already has the shape of the answer written in, with ... wherever your code goes. Replace every ..., run every cell so your answers and figures are saved in the file, then download this notebook itself — the .ipynb file — and upload it to Gradescope. Not a PDF: the marking reads your notebook, and a PDF cannot be read. In JupyterLab: File ▸ Download, or right-click the file in the left-hand panel and choose Download.

Two habits from the first minute. A cell runs when you press Shift+Enter, and the notebook remembers everything it has already run — so when something breaks and you cannot see why, Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells throws the memory away and rebuilds it from the top. That is never the wrong thing to do.

docs.title: What you'll be able to do¶
docs.text:
The science. Name the three places basalt melts and why, and say which element tells them apart best.

The code. Last week's LogisticRegression and confusion_matrix, now with three settings · training, validation and test, each with one job · cross-validation with cross_val_score · DecisionTreeClassifier and RandomForestClassifier · SVC, with StandardScaler and make_pipeline · the best tree depth picked with np.argmax · every model scored once on the sealed rocks.

The five questions of the class, then the three classifiers compared:

  1. What in a basalt's chemistry records where it was made?
  2. How well does last week's model sort the rocks?
  3. Which model will work best on rocks it has not seen?
  4. Can a random forest beat last week's lines?
  5. Can a support vector machine beat them?

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text: Run the next cell once. It reads the basalts, stored with the course: one row per rock, its setting (where it was made; section 1 explains) and its chemistry. Two columns are renamed so every name follows one pattern (the file calls the setting affinity), and one impossible value is blanked (a rock recorded with 19 percent MnO; basalt holds well under 1 percent).

docs.title: 1. What in a basalt's chemistry records where it was made?¶
docs.text:
A rock with no address. California's Coast Ranges hold slices of old sea floor, scraped off a sinking plate and lifted onto the continent. Was that crust made at a mid-ocean ridge, above a sinking plate, or on an ocean island? The answer decides the history the rocks tell, and the rock itself cannot say. Its chemistry can.

Basalt has three main homes in the ocean. Basalt is made in three places, where the mantle melts: where two plates pull apart (a mid-ocean ridge), where one plate sinks under another (an island arc), and over a hot plume, usually far from any plate edge (an ocean island). (It also forms on the continents, where they rift apart or flood with lava; today's rocks come from the three ocean homes.) Geologists call the kind of place a rock was made its tectonic setting. In the data it is the column setting, with three values named after the rock: IAB (island-arc basalt), MORB (mid-ocean-ridge basalt) and OIB (ocean-island basalt).

Among its features: an island arc above a sinking plate, a shield volcano over a hot spot, and a mid-ocean ridge where two plates pull apart. Cross-section by José F. Vigil, USGS (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons.

docs.title: 2. How well does last week's model sort the rocks?¶
docs.text:
Last week's logistic regression, in last week's symbols. For each event it worked out one number, $z$, from the two magnitudes, and bent $z$ into a probability with the S-curve:

$$p = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}, \qquad z = a \times \text{mb} + b \times \text{Ms} + c$$

$p$ is the probability that the event is an explosion, and fit chose the three numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$. Where $z = 0$, $p = 0.5$: those events lie on a straight line, the decision boundary, with explosions predicted on one side and earthquakes on the other.

With three settings, three z's. For a rock with titanium Ti and potassium K (both in weight percent), the model works out one $z$ for each setting:

$$z_{\text{IAB}} = a_1 \times \text{Ti} + b_1 \times \text{K} + c_1, \quad z_{\text{MORB}} = a_2 \times \text{Ti} + b_2 \times \text{K} + c_2, \quad z_{\text{OIB}} = a_3 \times \text{Ti} + b_3 \times \text{K} + c_3$$

It turns the three into three probabilities that add up to 1, and predicts the setting with the largest. Where two settings' $z$'s are equal, a straight line runs between them, so the map is cut into three regions with straight edges. fit now chooses nine numbers instead of three.

docs.text:
How well does last week's model sort the training rocks on titanium and potassium?

Why: last week's model, scored last week's way, is where every new model starts.

  2. counts_tk: its confusion matrix, as last week: the true settings, then the model's predictions for the same rocks. Three settings make three rows (the truth) and three columns (the prediction); the given lines draw it.
  3. score_tk: the share predicted right, from the diagonal of counts_tk and len(train). The library's .score (given) does the same count; from here on we use it.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: line_tk, counts_tk and score_tk.

  1. tk_scores: the five cross-validation scores of line_tk, your lines from Your turn 1, on the training rocks' titanium and potassium, train[ti_k], and y.

docs.title: 4. Can a random forest beat last week's lines?¶
docs.text:
A random forest is a vote of many decision trees. So first, one tree.

One tree. A flowchart of yes/no questions, learned from the data instead of written by hand. It works like a geologist's flowchart. The next cell grows a tree only two questions deep on titanium and potassium and prints it. Each question is the one that leaves the rocks on its two sides least mixed.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 4¶
docs.text:
How deep should a tree be?

Why: a deeper tree always fits its training rocks better. Cross-validation says whether it also does better on rocks held out, and so chooses the depth.

  1. tree_train_scores and tree_cv_means start as empty lists (given).
  2. For each depth in depths (1 to 12):
    • tree: a DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=depth, random_state=0) fitted on train[ti_k] and y; append its score on those same rocks to tree_train_scores;
    • tree_scores: the five cross-validation scores of a new tree of the same depth on train[ti_k] and y; append their mean to tree_cv_means.
  3. Plot both lists against depths, with a legend.
  4. best_depth: the depth with the highest cross-validation mean. np.argmax(values) gives the position of the largest value, as in the model-selection week.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: tree_train_scores, tree_cv_means and best_depth.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 5¶
docs.text:
On all nine oxides, does a forest beat the lines?

Why: a new model earns its place only with a better cross-validation score than the bar, 0.902, and its training score cannot tell you whether it does.

  1. forest: a RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=0) fitted on X and y.
  2. forest_train_score: its score on the same training rocks, X and y.
  3. forest_scores: the five cross-validation scores of a new forest of the same kind, on X and y, and forest_cv, their mean.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: forest, forest_train_score and forest_cv.

docs.title: 5. Can a support vector machine beat them?¶
docs.text:
The widest gap. Of all the lines separating the two groups, take the one leaving the widest gap. Many lines can part two groups of rocks. The SVM picks the one that leaves the widest empty band between them, so a new rock has the most room to land on its own side. The rocks on the edge of the band, the support vectors, alone fix the line, which gives the method its name.

Two groups (blue, green) and the line that parts them (red) with the widest gap (yellow band); the circled points on the edge of the band are the support vectors. Figure: Larhmam (CC BY-SA 4.0), via Wikimedia Commons.

Real rocks overlap, so no band is empty: the SVM lets a few rocks sit inside the band, or even on the wrong side, in exchange for a wider gap. With three settings, SVC finds a widest gap for each pair (arc–ridge, arc–island, ridge–island), and the pairs vote. And plain SVC() may bend its edges into curves to follow the clouds of rocks; the idea, the widest gap, is the same.

A gap is a distance, and a distance adds up the differences in each column in that column's own units. The oxides' standard deviations differ a lot:

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 6¶
docs.text:
Does the SVM do better on scaled columns?

Why: an SVM measures distance, so it needs scaled columns, and the scaling must be learned from the rows it fits on, then applied, unchanged, to the rows it is scored on.

fit_rows, held_rows and scaler come from the cell above. raw_score, an SVM on the raw oxides of the same rows, is given.

  1. fit_scaled and held_scaled: the oxides of fit_rows and of held_rows, each through the same scaler's transform.
  2. svm: an SVC() fitted on fit_scaled and the setting of fit_rows.
  3. scaled_score: its score on held_scaled and the setting of held_rows.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: raw_score and scaled_score.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 7¶
docs.text:
By cross-validation, does the scaled SVM beat the lines on nine oxides?

Why: one split can be lucky. The cross-validation mean is what every model is judged by, against the bar of 0.902.

  1. svm_raw_scores: the five cross-validation scores of a plain SVC() on X and y.
  2. svm_nine: the pipeline make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC()), fitted on X and y. You will use it again at the end.
  3. svm_scores: the five cross-validation scores of svm_nine on X and y.
  4. svm_raw_cv and svm_cv: the two means.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: svm_raw_cv and svm_cv.

docs.text: Three classifiers, one interface. The lines, the forest and the SVM were each made, fitted and scored with the same three calls, fit, predict and score, so trying another model was one line. What differs is the boundary each draws. Here are their regions on titanium and potassium, side by side:

Why: cross-validation is only worth trusting if its conclusions carry over to new rocks, and the sealed rocks are the one check on that.

Every model was fitted once, on all 448 training rocks: line_tk in Your turn 1, line_nine in section 2, forest in Your turn 5 and svm_nine in Your turn 7. Now each is scored once on the sealed rocks.

The given lines print each sealed score beside its cross-validation mean.

docs.title: Three classifiers, side by side¶
docs.text:
Logistic regression (the lines) Random forest Support vector machine (SVM) How it predicts a setting one weighted sum per setting, turned into probabilities; the largest wins a vote of 200 decision trees the side of the widest gap between each pair of settings Its boundary on Ti and K straight edges boxes smooth curves Strength simple, readable weights; the bar to beat bends to the data; columns in any units; feature importance strong once its columns are scaled Weakness cannot bend overfits its training rocks (1.000); not one readable rule poor on unscaled columns Cross-validation, Ti and K 0.868 0.862 0.877 Cross-validation, nine oxides 0.902 0.931 0.931 (scaled)

Which to use: start with the lines, the bar to beat. Keep a flexible model only if its cross-validation score beats the bar. Whichever you pick, test it once.

docs.title: The science¶
docs.text:
Where was this basalt made? A basalt's chemistry records where it formed. Its big oxides (silica about 50 percent, Al2O3, CaO, MgO, Na2O) build its minerals and barely differ between settings; three small ones differ a lot: P2O5 2.9 times, TiO2 3.1 times and K2O 5.9 times from the lowest setting median to the highest. They fit badly in mantle minerals and gather in the melt, so how much the mantle melts, and whether water from a sinking plate is present, sets how much of them a basalt holds. A training score is not the model's score. Training, validation and test sets each have one job: the training rocks fit, the validation rocks compare, and the test rocks, touched by no decision, check once whether the comparison holds. A forest scores 1.000 on the rocks it learned from and less on rocks held out. Cross-validation chooses the model: five parts, each held out once, give a fair score and its spread (cross_val_score, cv=5). One validation split moved the same model's score from 0.867 to 0.967. Three classifiers, compared. Logistic regression, the random forest and the SVM share fit, predict and score, so trying another is one line. Logistic regression draws straight edges: simple and readable, the model to beat, but it cannot bend. A random forest bends to the data and takes columns in any units, but cannot be read as one rule. An SVM draws smooth curves and needs scaled columns. On nine oxides the flexible models gain a little (0.931 each against 0.902); on titanium and potassium they gain little or nothing (forest 0.862, scaled SVM 0.877, against 0.868 for the lines). The method is chosen by cross-validation, not by reputation.

  • Tectonic settings of basalt. Basalt is made in three places, where the mantle melts: where two plates pull apart (a mid-ocean ridge), where one plate sinks under another (an island arc), and over a hot plume, usually far from any plate edge (an ocean island).
  • Major oxide, trace element. A rock analysis gives the common elements as oxides, in percent of the rock's weight (SiO2, TiO2), and the rare ones in parts per million (V, Sr).
  • Feature importance. How much of a forest's decisions each column carried — the model's own account of what it used.
  • Cross-validation. Cut the rows into five parts; hold out each part in turn, train on the other four, and score on the one held out. Five scores, and every row tested once.
  • Decision tree. A flowchart of yes/no questions, learned from the data instead of written by hand.
  • Random forest. Ask many slightly different trees and take a vote.
  • SVM. Of all the lines separating the two groups, take the one leaving the widest gap.

docs.title: Rocks from somewhere else¶
docs.text: The sealed rocks came from Vermeesch's own compilation, and rocks from one volcano can sit on both sides of a split. In 2022 the geologist Luc Doucet and colleagues compiled a much larger set of basalts of known setting, from two online databases (EarthChem and GEOROC), kept to rocks in the basalt silica range (43 to 53 percent silica, sodium plus potassium oxides below 5 percent; the rocks read here run from 45 to 53). The next cell reads 2,400 of their rocks, 800 per setting, with the same nine oxides and where each came from: a place, or for every ridge rock, PetDB, a database of ridge rocks from around the world.
