docs.title: How hard will the ground shake at distance R from a magnitude M earthquake?
docs.text:
The cost was enormous, and the danger was already on the map. More than 53,000 people died in Türkiye and more than 5,900 in Syria. An inspection found 164,000 buildings destroyed or badly damaged, and the damage in Türkiye was put at US$150 billion, about 9% of its economy (all from Wikipedia, 2023 Turkey–Syria earthquakes). A seismic hazard map like the one below shows how hard the ground is likely to shake at each place: here, the peak ground acceleration that has a 10% chance of being passed in 50 years. The south-east of Türkiye, where the plate boundary (black line) runs north from Syria into Türkiye, is coloured for strong shaking. Engineers design buildings for the shaking such maps give.

Seismic hazard of Türkiye and its neighbours, from the Global Seismic Hazard Assessment Program. The legend says "%g", but its numbers, 0.2 to 9.8, are in m/s², the unit of the GSHAP data: 9.8 m/s² is 1 g, so 4.8 m/s² is about half of g. Map: USGS (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons.

Every hazard map and every shaking map rests on a ground-motion model. Stations are few, so nobody measures the shaking at every building. A ground-motion model fills the gaps: from an earthquake's magnitude, the distance to a site and the ground under it, it predicts how hard that site shakes. A hazard map runs it for every earthquake that could happen; after a real one, a shaking map uses it between the stations. California has the same problem. The USGS ShakeMap below, for the magnitude 6.0 South Napa earthquake of 2014, colours the peak acceleration everywhere, though its stations (triangles) sit only in some places. Building a model that predicts well at a place it has never measured is the job of this project.

Peak ground acceleration (% of g) in the 2014 South Napa earthquake. USGS ShakeMap (public domain).

Your data: 34,481 recordings from the Engineering Strong Motion database (ESM). Each one was made by an accelerometer like the yellow box below, fixed to the ground or a building's floor, which writes how fast the ground speeds up and slows down. Its largest value is the peak ground acceleration (PGA). 43 seismic networks run the stations in your file, and INGV, Italy's national institute of geophysics, collects their recordings into one table (ESM version 3.0, doi:10.13127/esm.3). One row is one earthquake recorded at one station: its magnitude, depth, the station's distance, the ground under it, and the PGA. After cleaning, 11,949 rows remain, from 1,405 earthquakes at 1,318 stations, 1978 to 2022; 92% are from 2010 on, as the networks grew. Most stations are in Greece (54% of the recordings), Italy (25%) and Türkiye (8%); the map leaves out 287 stations farther away, 252 of them in Taiwan.

Why ESM? It is open, it is one table that is easy to read, and it holds the 2023 Türkiye recordings the leaderboard is built on. The standard worldwide table of shallow earthquakes, NGA-West2 (Ancheta and colleagues, 2014, doi), many of them in California, is open too; but its recordings stop years before 2023.

Left: a strong-motion accelerograph in a basement. Photo: EERC (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons. Right: drawn from your training file.

Researchers have built these models for decades, and four studies set up what you will try. The figure below is the model inside the Napa ShakeMap: the observations (circles and triangles; the plot does not say what each symbol means) against distance, with the model's curves for rock and soil. It falls with distance, as your models will, and the observations scatter widely around it.

ln PGA against distance to the fault (log scale), 2014 South Napa. USGS ShakeMap (public domain).

  • Atkinson (2006) compared 21 stations in Los Angeles: one station's recordings scatter less around the model than all the stations' together, because each station's ground repeats from one earthquake to the next (doi). That is the idea behind your station corrections.
  • Kotha and colleagues (2020) fitted a model to the ESM data to update Europe's seismic hazard and risk assessment, with corrections for 1,829 stations (doi). You will score their published equation.
  • Kubo and colleagues (2020) found that a machine-learning model predicted the strongest shaking too low, because strong recordings are rare in the data; adding a conventional equation reduced it (doi). Watch what your random forest does at the largest magnitudes.
  • Okazaki and colleagues (2021) showed that a flexible model can fit the stations it was trained on and miss new ones, so how the data are split decides whether a test is fair (doi).

The largest earthquakes matter most and are the rarest in the data, so predicting them is still open. In 45 years the training file holds 256 recordings of magnitude 7 or more, from 7 earthquakes. The leaderboard's recordings since 2023 hold 212. In this project you build a model step by step, test it fairly on earthquakes it has never seen, try a freer model and a correction for each station, and enter your best on a leaderboard scored on those 2023 recordings.

The next cell keeps the records a model can use, with the same rules that made the leaderboard file: the peak ground acceleration (PGA) was measured and not flagged bad; magnitude 4 or more; depth 0 to 40 km; station within 200 km, with a known Vs30. Vs30 is the speed of shear waves in the top 30 m of ground, in m/s: low for mud, high for rock. We predict ln_pga, the natural log of the PGA in g (g = 981 cm/s², the pull of gravity). The line is too low for magnitudes 5.5 to 6.5, and far too high from 7 up. Recordings of magnitude 5.5 to 6 shook +0.46 harder than the line said (a factor of 1.6); those of magnitude 7 and up, from 7 earthquakes, shook 1.17 less in ln_pga than the line said, a factor of 3.2. A straight line in magnitude cannot bend, and the data bend over at the top.

The physics says how to bend it. Ground-motion models add columns for four effects:

  • Big earthquakes stop getting stronger as fast (saturation): a large earthquake breaks a fault tens of km long, and a station is near only part of it. A term in $M^2$ lets the rise bend.
  • Big earthquakes fade more slowly with distance, for the same reason: a column $M \ln r$ lets the distance slope change with magnitude.
  • Rock absorbs a little energy every km, on top of the spreading: a column in the distance itself, $R$.
  • Soft ground shakes harder than rock: waves slow down in mud and grow taller. A column $\ln V_{s30}$.

$$\ln \mathrm{PGA} = a + b_1 M + b_2 M^2 + c_1 \ln r + c_2 M \ln r + c_3 R + d \ln V_{s30}$$

It is still linear regression: each term is a column times a number, so LinearRegression finds the seven numbers just as it found three. In Python the new columns are Mw_squared ($M^2$), Mw_ln_distance ($M \ln r$) and ln_vs30 ($\ln V_{s30}$); $R$ is distance_km.

The fix is to trust a correction only as far as its recordings allow. Instead of the mean, divide the sum of a station's misses by its number of recordings plus k:

$$\text{correction} = \frac{\text{sum of the station's misses}}{\text{its number of recordings} + k}$$

With k = 0 this is the mean. With k = 3, a station with one recording keeps a quarter of its miss, and one with 30 recordings keeps 30/33 of its mean: the correction shrinks toward 0 most where the evidence is thinnest. The next cell shows it on the three made-up stations.

The published model (Kotha et al. 2020, doi:10.1007/s10518-020-00869-1) is an equation like yours, with more physics in its shape. It adds three terms:

$$\ln \mathrm{PGA} = e_1 + f_R + f_M + f_S$$

  • distance, $f_R$: a log-distance term whose slope changes with magnitude, and a straight term in distance, much as in your equation;
  • magnitude, $f_M$: a curve up to a hinge magnitude, then a gentler straight line above it, because the largest earthquakes stop getting stronger as fast;
  • ground, $f_S$: a curve in $\ln V_{s30}$.

Its numbers were fitted by its authors to an earlier release of this same database. The function below is given: it returns the published model's ln_pga for every row of a table with Mw, distance_km, depth_km and vs30_m_s.

In [ ]: Copied! 
def kotha_ln_pga(table, M_h=5.7):
    """Kotha et al. (2020), PGA, Vs30 version, no regional terms: ln PGA in g."""
    M = table["Mw"].values
    R = table["distance_km"].values
    depth = table["depth_km"].values
    vs30 = table["vs30_m_s"].values
    # the coefficients, as the open-source hazard software OpenQuake 3.26 prints them for PGA;
    # the paper's text puts the hinge M_h at 6.2, but these coefficients were fitted with it at 5.7
    e1 = 3.93782347219377
    b1, b2, b3 = 2.06573167101440, 0.304988012209292, 0.444773874960317
    c1, c2, c3 = -1.49787542346412, 0.281241474631338, -0.609876182476899
    g0, g1, g2 = -0.222196028066344, -0.558848724731566, -0.133014864040313
    # h: 4 km for an earthquake shallower than 10 km, 8 km to 20 km, 12 km below that
    h = np.where(depth < 10, 4.0, np.where(depth < 20, 8.0, 12.0))
    r = np.sqrt(R ** 2 + h ** 2)
    r_ref = np.sqrt(30 ** 2 + h ** 2)
    f_R = (c1 + c2 * (M - 4.5)) * np.log(r / r_ref) + c3 * (r - r_ref) / 100
    # below the hinge: a curve in M; above it: a gentler straight line
    f_M = np.where(M <= M_h, b1 * (M - M_h) + b2 * (M - M_h) ** 2, b3 * (M - M_h))
    f_S = g0 + g1 * np.log(vs30 / 800) + g2 * np.log(vs30 / 800) ** 2
    return e1 + f_R + f_M + f_S - np.log(981)   # the last term turns cm/s² into g
def kotha_ln_pga(table, M_h=5.7): """Kotha et al. (2020), PGA, Vs30 version, no regional terms: ln PGA in g.""" M = table["Mw"].values R = table["distance_km"].values depth = table["depth_km"].values vs30 = table["vs30_m_s"].values # the coefficients, as the open-source hazard software OpenQuake 3.26 prints them for PGA; # the paper's text puts the hinge M_h at 6.2, but these coefficients were fitted with it at 5.7 e1 = 3.93782347219377 b1, b2, b3 = 2.06573167101440, 0.304988012209292, 0.444773874960317 c1, c2, c3 = -1.49787542346412, 0.281241474631338, -0.609876182476899 g0, g1, g2 = -0.222196028066344, -0.558848724731566, -0.133014864040313 # h: 4 km for an earthquake shallower than 10 km, 8 km to 20 km, 12 km below that h = np.where(depth < 10, 4.0, np.where(depth < 20, 8.0, 12.0)) r = np.sqrt(R ** 2 + h ** 2) r_ref = np.sqrt(30 ** 2 + h ** 2) f_R = (c1 + c2 * (M - 4.5)) * np.log(r / r_ref) + c3 * (r - r_ref) / 100 # below the hinge: a curve in M; above it: a gentler straight line f_M = np.where(M <= M_h, b1 * (M - M_h) + b2 * (M - M_h) ** 2, b3 * (M - M_h)) f_S = g0 + g1 * np.log(vs30 / 800) + g2 * np.log(vs30 / 800) ** 2 return e1 + f_R + f_M + f_S - np.log(981) # the last term turns cm/s² into g

docs.title: How hard will the ground shake at distance R from a magnitude M earthquake?¶
docs.text:
EPS 88 · PyEarth · final project. Open your own copy on DataHub: click here.

On 6 February 2023 two earthquakes, magnitude 7.7 and 7.5, struck southern Türkiye nine hours apart. How hard did the ground shake at each station that recorded them? In this project you build a model from earthquake recordings before 2023, most of them in Europe and the Middle East, and use it to predict the shaking in 2,327 recordings made since, those two earthquakes included. You never see the answers. The leaderboard does, and it ranks everyone's entries.

This notebook is built like a weekly notebook: a few questions lead it, each section answers one, and every place you work opens with a pencil icon ✏️ and the words Your turn. The difference is how much you write. Each Your turn says why the step matters and gives a numbered plan in words; the cell under it is empty, and you write all of the code, looking back at the weekly notebook it names. A self-check cell follows. Run it: it tells you whether your numbers are right, as in every week.

The last Your turn is your leaderboard entry: it saves the file submission.csv. Run every cell so your answers and figures are saved in the file, then download this notebook itself — the .ipynb file — and upload it to Gradescope together with submission.csv. In JupyterLab: File ▸ Download, or right-click the file in the left-hand panel and choose Download. The leaderboard scores your file on answers you never see and ranks everyone's entries.

Two habits from the first minute. A cell runs when you press Shift+Enter, and the notebook remembers everything it has already run — so when something breaks and you cannot see why, Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells throws the memory away and rebuilds it from the top. That is never the wrong thing to do.

docs.title: Background¶
docs.text:
On 6 February 2023, the ground under southern Türkiye shook hard enough to bring down a hospital. (The two earthquakes are magnitude 7.7 and 7.5 in this project's data; the US Geological Survey gives 7.8 and 7.5.) In the photo, from Antakya, one wing of the Hatay hospital has collapsed and the wing beside it still stands. Whether a building stands depends on how hard the ground under it shakes, and on whether it was built for that shaking.

Hatay Training and Research Hospital, Antakya, after the earthquakes. Photo: Mustafa Kuzugüdemn (CC0), via Wikimedia Commons.

docs.title: What you'll be able to do¶
docs.text:
The science. Say how hard the ground shakes at a distance from an earthquake of a given magnitude, why the shaking stops growing as fast for the largest earthquakes, why soft ground shakes harder than rock, and why each station shakes in its own way.

The code. You write every line: a scatter plot coloured by a column, a function for the typical miss, LinearRegression on columns you make, a mean for each group, a split by time, a bootstrap over whole earthquakes, RandomForestRegressor, a correction for each station chosen on a fair test, and a submission.csv file.

The four questions of the project:

  1. How does the shaking fade with distance, and grow with magnitude?
  2. Can an equation in magnitude and distance predict the shaking?
  3. How well does the equation do on earthquakes it has never seen?
  4. Does a more flexible model, or more information, do better on new earthquakes?

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text:
Run the next two cells once. All their code is given. Three files from the ESM database (see the Background) ship with the course:

  • trackT1_esm_flatfile.csv.gz: every recording of an earthquake of about magnitude 4 or more, 1972 to 2022, your training file, downloaded on 7 November 2026 and frozen, so everyone trains on the same file;
  • trackT1_leaderboard_test.csv: the leaderboard file, every recording from 1 January 2023 on, with the inputs and the station but not the shaking;
  • trackT1_submission_template.csv: the empty submission template, one row per leaderboard recording.

docs.title: 1. How does the shaking fade with distance, and grow with magnitude?¶
docs.text: We work with the log of the PGA. PGA is quoted as a fraction of g, the pull of gravity: a PGA of 1 g pushes sideways as hard as gravity pulls down. In the training file it runs from 0.000008 g far from a small earthquake to 0.83 g beside a large one, a range of about 100,000 times. Its natural log, ln_pga, runs from -11.7 to -0.2, and a change of 1 in ln_pga is a factor of e, about 2.7, at any size. To read the plots: ln_pga of −1 is 0.37 g, −3 is 0.05 g, and −6 is 0.0025 g.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 1¶
docs.text:
What do all 11,949 recordings look like, near and far, small and large?

Why: before any model, look at the data. One earthquake showed the fading with distance; all of them together show what magnitude adds.

Look back at: the scatter plot coloured by a column, from Where do earthquakes and volcanoes happen? (04_where_and_why.ipynb).

  1. Sort train by Mw, so the rare large earthquakes are drawn last, on top of the small ones.
  2. Draw a scatter plot of ln_pga (up) against distance_km (across) for every row, with small dots (s=2), each coloured by its magnitude, Mw.
  3. Add a colour bar labelled with what the colour means.
  4. Label both axes with their units, and give the plot a title with the number of recordings.

This Your turn has no self-check: a figure you can see needs none. A good figure shows, at a glance, the cloud falling from left to right and the large earthquakes as a bright band on top. Check it yourself: the title says 11,949, and the colour bar runs from magnitude 4 to above 8.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 2¶
docs.text:
How far off is the simplest guess: the same number for every recording?

Why: this number is the bar that every model after it has to clear.

Baseline: Write the dumbest rule you can, first. Any model that cannot beat it is decoration.

Typical miss: Square every gap between what happened and what the curve said, average the squares, and take the square root: the usual size of a miss, in the data's own units.

Look back at: the typical miss, from When will CO2 pass 450 ppm? (07_co2_450_ppm.ipynb).

  1. Write a function typical_miss(errors) that takes a column of errors and returns their typical miss. You will use it for every model in this notebook.
  2. The rule: guess the average ln_pga of all the training recordings. Name it average_ln_pga.
  3. Each recording's error is its ln_pga minus that guess. Their typical miss is baseline_miss.
  4. Print the guess, the typical miss, and the factor it stands for (e to the power of the miss).

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: typical_miss, average_ln_pga, baseline_miss.

docs.title: 2. Can an equation in magnitude and distance predict the shaking?¶
docs.text:
Shaking grows with magnitude and fades with the log of distance. As waves spread out from the earthquake, their energy is shared over a larger and larger sphere, so their size falls roughly as one over the distance. In logs, a fall like that is a straight line in the log of the distance. And each step of magnitude multiplies the energy released, so ln_pga rises roughly in a straight line with magnitude. Together:

$$\ln \mathrm{PGA} = a + b\,M + c\,\ln r$$

  • $M$ is the magnitude, Mw;
  • $r$ is the distance in km, with 8 km added in the way of a right triangle, $r = \sqrt{R^2 + 8^2}$, where $R$ is distance_km. The earthquake starts several km under the ground, so even a station right above it is not at distance 0, and $\ln 0$ does not exist;
  • $a$, $b$ and $c$ are three numbers that linear regression finds.

Linear regression: Draw the best straight line. Best means the smallest root mean squared error: the line that misses its points least.

With two columns it finds the best flat surface instead of a line, in the same way.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 3¶
docs.text:
How close does a straight line in magnitude and log distance get?

Why: this is the simplest model with any physics in it. Each improvement after it has to beat it.

Look back at: LinearRegression, from How old is the universe? (06_age_of_the_universe.ipynb).

  1. Add the column ln_distance to train: $\ln r$, the log of √(distance_km² + 8²).
  2. Fit a LinearRegression of ln_pga on the two columns Mw and ln_distance, for every training recording. Name it line.
  3. Bind its numbers to the equation's symbols: a is the intercept, and b and c are the two coefficients, in the order of the columns. Print the equation with them.
  4. Add the line's prediction for every recording as the column line of train.
  5. line_miss: the typical miss of ln_pga minus that prediction. Print it beside baseline_miss.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: line, a, b, c, line_miss.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 4¶
docs.text:
Does the line miss small and large earthquakes in the same way?

Why: a good model's residuals average zero at every magnitude. If one group sits above zero, the model is too low for it, and the shape of the equation is wrong there.

Look back at: groupby, from Earth's elevation has two peaks (03_two_peaks.ipynb).

  1. Write a function mean_by_magnitude(column) that takes the name of a column of train and returns its mean in each magnitude_group.
  2. Add the column line_residual to train: ln_pga minus the line's prediction.
  3. line_by_magnitude: mean_by_magnitude of that column. Print it, rounded to 2 places.
  4. Plot it: the mean residual (up) against the magnitude group (across), as dots joined by a line, with a horizontal line at zero. Write each group's value beside its dot, with a loop over the groups and plt.text(x, y, words). Label both axes and give a title. A good figure shows at a glance which magnitudes the line misses, and by how much.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: mean_by_magnitude, line_by_magnitude.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 5¶
docs.text:
Does the six-column equation miss less, and miss every magnitude more evenly?

Why: each new column stands for a piece of physics. If the physics is right, the typical miss falls and the residuals by magnitude move toward zero.

Look back at: your Your turns 3 and 4.

  1. Add three columns to train: Mw_squared, Mw_ln_distance and ln_vs30, as named in the cell above.
  2. six_columns: a list of the six column names, Mw, Mw_squared, ln_distance, Mw_ln_distance, distance_km, ln_vs30.
  3. Fit a LinearRegression of ln_pga on them, for every training recording. Name it equation, and add its prediction as the column equation of train.
  4. equation_miss: its typical miss. Print it beside line_miss.
  5. Add the column equation_residual, and equation_by_magnitude: your mean_by_magnitude of it. Print it in a table beside line_by_magnitude, rounded to 2 places.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: six_columns, equation, equation_miss, equation_by_magnitude.

docs.title: 3. How well does the equation do on earthquakes it has never seen?¶
docs.text:
A model is judged on data it did not learn from, as in the CO2 week.

Train/test split: Hide some data from yourself, then check.

But which recordings to hide? A random choice of rows would be unfair here, because the recordings of one earthquake miss together: an earthquake that shook harder than its magnitude says shook harder at every station. The next cell shows it for the five best-recorded earthquakes.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 6¶
docs.text:
How far off is the equation on earthquakes it has never seen?

Why: this is the number that predicts how your model will do on the leaderboard. The score on fitted recordings does not.

Look back at: the split by time, from When will CO2 pass 450 ppm? (07_co2_450_ppm.ipynb).

  1. fit_part: the rows of train from before 2018. hidden_part: the rows from 2018 on (take a .copy(), because you will add columns to it). Print how many recordings and earthquakes each holds.
  2. Fit the six-column equation on fit_part only. Name it equation_before.
  3. Add its prediction for each hidden recording as the column equation of hidden_part.
  4. test_miss: the typical miss on the hidden recordings. Print it beside equation_miss.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: fit_part, hidden_part, test_miss.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 7¶
docs.text:
How much could the test score move with other earthquakes like these?

Why: two models whose scores differ by less than this are not clearly different. You will need the interval to judge every comparison from here on.

Look back at: the bootstrap, from How long was the Earth frozen? (08_how_long_frozen.ipynb), and the three earthquakes just above.

  1. Add two columns to hidden_part: squared_error, each recording's (ln_pga − the equation's prediction)², and records, 1 on every row.
  2. per_quake: one row per earthquake, the sums of those two columns, as in the simple case.
  3. Make a random generator, rng = np.random.default_rng(88), and an empty list, redrawn_misses.
  4. 1,000 times: redraw as many earthquakes as per_quake holds, with replacement (random_state=rng), and append the redraw's typical miss.
  5. test_interval: the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the 1,000 misses. Print it beside test_miss.
  6. Draw a histogram of the 1,000 misses, with vertical lines at the two ends of the interval and at test_miss, each with its number in the legend, so the figure says how wide the interval is without a printout.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: per_quake, redrawn_misses, test_interval.

docs.title: 4. Does a more flexible model, or more information, do better on new earthquakes?¶
docs.text:
There are two ways to try to beat the equation. One is a more flexible model, free to find any shape in the data. The other is more information: something about each recording that the six columns do not hold. This section tries both, on the same hidden earthquakes.

A random forest learns its shape from the data, not from an equation. You met it in the basalt week, where its trees voted for a setting.

Random forest: Ask many slightly different trees and take a vote.

For a number instead of a label, RandomForestRegressor averages its trees' answers instead of taking a vote.

How a random forest decides, in one picture:

Many decision trees each give an answer; a forest that predicts a number averages them. Each tree is grown on its own bootstrap sample. Figure: TseKiChun (CC BY-SA 4.0), via Wikimedia Commons.

It needs no made-up columns: a tree can cut distance_km anywhere, so it is given the four inputs as they are, Mw, distance_km, depth_km and vs30_m_s. But a tree can only predict values like those in its leaves, and large earthquakes are rare: 48 of the 890 earthquakes in fit_part are magnitude 6 or more.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 8¶
docs.text:
Does a random forest beat the equation on the hidden earthquakes?

Why: the forest is free to find any shape the data show. If the equation's shape is missing something, the forest should do better.

Look back at: the random forest, from Where was this basalt made? (10_where_basalt.ipynb).

  1. four_inputs: the list Mw, distance_km, depth_km, vs30_m_s.
  2. forest: a RandomForestRegressor, fitted on fit_part's four inputs and ln_pga, for example with n_estimators=100, min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=0 (min_samples_leaf=5 keeps at least five recordings in each leaf, so no tree learns one station by heart). Other settings are fine.
  3. Add its prediction for each hidden recording as the column forest of hidden_part.
  4. forest_test_miss: the typical miss on the hidden recordings, with your typical_miss. Print it beside test_miss and test_interval; it should sit far below baseline_miss.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: forest, forest_test_miss.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 9¶
docs.text:
Does each station's correction help on the hidden earthquakes?

Why: this is new information, not a new shape. If stations really shake in their own way, knowing each one's offset should cut the miss on earthquakes the model has never seen.

Look back at: groupby, from Earth's elevation has two peaks (03_two_peaks.ipynb), your Your turn 6, and the three made-up stations just above.

  1. For each recording in fit_part, its miss: ln_pga minus the prediction of equation_before (fitted on fit_part's six_columns in Your turn 6). Keep it beside the recording's station.
  2. raw_correction: each station's mean miss, keyed by the station's name. Use only fit_part: the hidden recordings are the test.
  3. For each hidden recording, the equation's prediction (the column equation of hidden_part) plus its station's correction, with 0 for a station that is not in fit_part. Keep the sum as a new column, raw_corrected, and leave equation as it is: later cells read it.
  4. raw_fair_miss: the typical miss of the hidden ln_pga minus that sum. Print it beside test_miss and test_interval, and print what share of the hidden recordings were made at a station in fit_part.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: raw_correction, raw_fair_miss.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 10¶
docs.text:
At stations with only one fitting recording, do the corrections still help?

Why: a correction from one recording is the least certain. If anywhere the corrections are learning noise, it is there.

Look back at: value_counts, from the cells above, and your Your turn 9.

  1. Count the recordings of each station in fit_part.
  2. thin: the hidden recordings whose station has exactly one recording in fit_part. Print how many there are.
  3. thin_equation_miss: the typical miss on thin of the equation alone.
  4. thin_raw_miss: the typical miss on thin of the equation plus the raw corrections, the column raw_corrected of Your turn 9. Print both.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: thin_equation_miss, thin_raw_miss.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 11¶
docs.text:
Which k should the station corrections use?

Why: k sets how far to trust a station's few recordings. Too small and the corrections learn each earthquake's luck; too large and they shrink to nothing. The hidden earthquakes decide, and the cautious rule settles a tie.

Look back at: choosing between models on held-back months, from When will CO2 pass 450 ppm? (07_co2_450_ppm.ipynb), and your Your turns 6 and 9.

  1. From the misses of Your turn 9, find each station's sum of misses and its number of recordings in fit_part.
  2. Write a function that takes k and returns each station's shrunk correction, keyed by station.
  3. Try at least three values of k (0 among them is a good idea). For each, add the corrections to the predictions in the hidden recordings' equation column, without changing that column (0 for a station not in fit_part), and find the typical miss. miss_by_k: those misses, keyed by k (a dict or a Series).
  4. chosen_k: by the cautious rule, the largest k whose miss is within 0.01 of the smallest miss. (If you use another rule, say it in a comment.) station_correction: the corrections for chosen_k, keyed by station. fair_miss_with_corrections: its miss. Print them beside raw_fair_miss and test_miss.
  5. Plot the miss (up) against k (across), with a horizontal line at test_miss. A good figure also marks your chosen_k and shades the band within 0.01 of the smallest miss (plt.axhspan), so a reader sees why the cautious rule chose it.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: miss_by_k, chosen_k, station_correction, fair_miss_with_corrections.

docs.title: The leaderboard¶
docs.text:
leaderboard holds 2,327 recordings you have never seen, from 2023 on, up to magnitude 7.7; 212 of them are magnitude 7 or more. It has the input columns of train and the station (no event_id, year or ln_pga), plus row_id, the key of each prediction. It also has three columns this notebook does not use: ec8_class (the ground class of the European building code, from A for rock), fault_type (how the fault moved, blank where unknown) and region (the station's country). They come from the raw training file's preferred_ec8_code, fm_type_code and st_nation_code, so anyone who wants one can add it to train. template has the same row_ids and an empty ln_pga column for your predictions.

  • Your entry is your own model, fitted on the training file here. Do not look up or download the hidden answers (the recorded shaking of these 2023-on recordings, from ESM or anywhere else); a forecast built from them is not your model, and it scores 0.
  • The board shows a public score on one third of the earthquakes below magnitude 7. The final score, on the other two thirds and on every recording of magnitude 7 or more, is shown after the board closes, and your rank on it is graded.
  • So choose your entry by your own fair test, not by the public score. The public third is a few earthquakes; a model picked because it moved that number is tuned to them, and the rank uses the others.
  • Up to 10 uploads that change submission.csv are scored. An upload that changes only the notebook is free.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 12¶
docs.text:
Your leaderboard entry: how hard will the ground shake in 2,327 recordings from 2023 on?

Why: this is the project's answer, scored on shaking you have not seen, and ranked against the other students. Choose by your fair test: the public score is a third of the earthquakes, and your rank is decided on the rest.

Look back at: your Your turns 5, 9 and 11.

  1. Take the model your fair test chose: the six-column equation with station corrections shrunk by your chosen_k, unless your own tests found something better (the published model is not yours to enter). Make a fresh final_model, and name its list of input columns final_columns.
  2. Fit it on every training recording: the hidden years are data too, and the newest.
  3. final_correction: each station's shrunk correction, from the final model's misses on every training recording, keyed by station.
  4. Add the same made columns (Your turns 3 and 5) to leaderboard, made the same way.
  5. submission: a copy of template, with its ln_pga column filled with your model's prediction for each leaderboard recording plus its station's correction (0 for a station not in train). Save it with submission.to_csv("submission.csv", index=False).
  6. Print its first rows, its number of rows and of blanks, and the share of leaderboard recordings that got a correction.
  7. Run the self-check, then download submission.csv and this notebook and upload both together (the steps are under "What you hand in" above) to Final project: ground motion.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: final_model, final_columns, final_correction, submission.

docs.title: The question, answered¶
docs.text: On earthquakes it has never seen, an equation in magnitude, log distance and Vs30 predicts the peak shaking within a typical factor of 2.6 (a miss of 0.96 in ln_pga, against 1.90 for always the average); a random forest does no better, but a shrunk correction for each station brings the miss down to about 0.82, a factor of 2.3. The equation's shape is the physics of how shaking grows and fades, so here, on this split by time and these four inputs, a freer algorithm added nothing; what helped was new information about the ground under each station.

docs.title: The open question¶
docs.text:
Can a model you fit beat the published model on the largest earthquakes?

Your hidden years held 18 recordings of magnitude 7 or more, from 1 earthquake, so your fair test could not answer it. The leaderboard can: it holds the 2023 Türkiye earthquakes, and after the board closes it shows each student's final score on its 212 recordings of magnitude 7 or more, beside the published model's. Station corrections will not settle it alone: only 10 of those 212 recordings (5%) were made at a station in the training file, against 74% of all the leaderboard's recordings, so on the largest earthquakes your entry is mostly the equation itself. What would help where no station has recorded before is still an open question.

The Niño 3.4 box sits in the middle of the Pacific, between Asia and the Americas.

The data. NOAA's daily sea-surface temperature analysis (OISST) blends measurements from satellites, ships, buoys and floats onto a global grid, from September 1981 on. The Climate Prediction Center averages it over the Niño 3.4 box each month and subtracts the usual temperature for that calendar month (the 1991–2020 average). The result, nino34, is an anomaly: +1 °C in December means one degree warmer than a usual December. NOAA speaks of El Niño conditions when the anomaly stays at +0.5 °C or more, and of La Niña at −0.5 °C or less.

The next cell draws every month of the file, and marks the biggest El Niños.

The anomaly swings up and down every few years, and in 2026 the monthly anomaly climbs higher than in any El Niño before it. An El Niño builds through the northern summer and peaks around December, so its strongest month can fall in either of two calendar years. To give each El Niño one number, count a year from July to the next June: an El Niño year. July 1997 to June 1998 is El Niño year 1997.

By its warmest month, 2026 is already the strongest El Niño year in the file, ahead of 2015 (+2.72 °C), 1982 and 1997, and its winter peak is probably still to come. The held-back years 2018 to 2025 had no month as warm as October 2026 either.

Why forecast it from data? Forecasting centres run two kinds of model: physical models of the ocean and air, and statistical models fitted to the past record, like the ones you will build. A study of twenty real-time forecast models found them less skilful in 2002–2011 than models had been in the 1980s and 1990s, because that decade was harder to predict (Barnston and others, 2012, doi:10.1175/BAMS-D-11-00111.1). How far ahead an El Niño can be seen, and which measurements give warning, are still open questions. Section 2 starts with the simplest forecasts.

The share left three months later depends strongly on the start month. From March only 35% of an anomaly is left by June; from July, August, September, October the slope is above 1: an anomaly in the northern summer tends to grow into the winter. One line, with 0.77 for every month, is too small in summer and too large in spring.

This is the spring predictability barrier. El Niño and La Niña are tied to the seasons: they grow from the northern summer, peak around December and fade in spring, when a new one may or may not start. A forecast that starts in spring has the least to go on. Forecasting centres see the same: a study of twenty real-time forecast models found that start times just before the middle of the year are when prediction has proven most difficult (Barnston and others, 2012, doi:10.1175/BAMS-D-11-00111.1).

One line per start month misses the test years by 0.53 °C, against 0.63 °C for one line; look at the 2015 El Niño, where one line lags behind the climb. But the test is 93 months from 8 years. Would a different 8 years agree? A bootstrap tells.

Bootstrap: Ask the data the same question a thousand times, using a different random slice of itself each time.

Here the slice is a whole year, not single months: the months of one year belong to the same El Niño or La Niña, so they miss together. And because the question is which of two models is better, use a paired bootstrap: redraw the years once, score both models on the same redraw, keep the difference, and repeat. A hard year is then hard for both, and only the difference between the models is left to vary. A redraw's typical miss is the square root of (all the squared errors its years hold ÷ all the months they hold).

docs.title: Record monthly warmth in the Pacific: is a record El Niño coming, and how far ahead can we forecast it?¶
docs.text:
EPS 88 · PyEarth · final project. Open your own copy on DataHub: click here.

In October 2026 the sea surface in the middle of the tropical Pacific was 3.25 °C warmer than usual for the month, the largest excess for any month in NOAA's satellite-era record, which starts in 1982 (the previous largest was +2.72 °C, in November 2015). A strong El Niño is under way. Is it a record? Not yet by NOAA's official measure, the Oceanic Niño Index, which averages three months: for August 2026 to October 2026 it stood at +2.46 °C, below the record +2.59 °C of November 2015 to January 2016 (the index starts in 1950). The coming winter decides. El Niño shifts rain and drought around the world, so forecasters try to see it coming months ahead. In this project you build a forecast of the Pacific's temperature three months ahead and test it on years it has never seen. The leaderboard scores your forecasts for 2018 to 2025, which your file leaves blank, and ranks everyone's entries.

This notebook is built like a weekly notebook: a few questions lead it, each section answers one, and every place you work opens with a pencil icon ✏️ and the words Your turn. The difference is how much you write. Each Your turn says why the step matters and gives a numbered plan in words; the cell under it is empty, and you write all of the code, looking back at the weekly notebook it names. A self-check cell follows. Run it: it tells you whether your numbers are right, as in every week.

The last Your turn is your leaderboard entry: it saves the file submission.csv. Run every cell so your answers and figures are saved in the file, then download this notebook itself — the .ipynb file — and upload it to Gradescope together with submission.csv. In JupyterLab: File ▸ Download, or right-click the file in the left-hand panel and choose Download. The leaderboard scores your file on answers you never see and ranks everyone's entries.

Two habits from the first minute. A cell runs when you press Shift+Enter, and the notebook remembers everything it has already run — so when something breaks and you cannot see why, Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells throws the memory away and rebuilds it from the top. That is never the wrong thing to do.

docs.title: What you'll be able to do¶
docs.text:
The science. Say what El Niño is and how it is measured, why an anomaly that appears in summer tends to grow while one in spring tends to fade, and how warm water stored along the equator can warn of an El Niño months ahead.

The code. You write every line: a groupby and a ranking, a function for the typical miss, .shift to line up each month with the month three later, a loop over forecast leads, a split by time, LinearRegression one start month at a time, a function that makes those forecasts, a paired bootstrap over whole years, and a submission.csv table.

The four questions of the project:

  1. How strong is this El Niño compared with every one since 1982?
  2. How far ahead does "the same as now" work?
  3. Does a fitted line do better, and why does the start month matter?
  4. Does the ocean's stored heat help, and in every decade?

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text:
Run the next two cells once. All their code is given. Two files ship with the course:

  • trackT15_enso_monthly.csv: one row per month from January 1982. nino34 is the sea-surface temperature anomaly in the Niño 3.4 box, in °C, from NOAA's Climate Prediction Center; wwv is the warm water volume anomaly, from NOAA's Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory (PMEL), in units of 1014 m³. Section 1 and section 4 explain each.
  • trackT15_submission_template.csv: the empty submission template, the table the leaderboard reads.

docs.title: 1. How strong is this El Niño compared with every one since 1982?¶
docs.text:
El Niño is a warming of the surface of the central and eastern tropical Pacific that lasts about a year. Normally the trade winds blow from east to west along the equator and pile warm water up in the west, near Indonesia, while cooler water rises to the surface in the east. Every few years the winds weaken, the warm water spreads east, and the sea surface there warms by a degree or more. The opposite, a cooling, is La Niña. Together they are ENSO, the El Niño–Southern Oscillation.

A slice along the equator, from Asia (left) to South America (right), normal years above and an El Niño below. The warm top layer ends at the 20 °C line, below which the water is cold. Normally the trade winds hold the warm water in the west and the 20 °C line comes close to the surface in the east; in an El Niño the winds weaken, the warm layer spreads east and the line flattens. A sketch drawn for this course, not to scale.

It matters far beyond the Pacific. NOAA's buoy laboratory calls ENSO the strongest year-to-year swing of climate on the planet: it shifts where rain and drought fall, and so affects farming, water and energy supplies and the lives of millions of people, as well as the Pacific's fisheries, such as tuna and anchovy. A warning a season ahead gives people time to prepare, which is why forecasting El Niño matters.

It is measured in boxes along the equator, and below the surface by buoys. The next cell draws the boxes on a map. The main one, Niño 3.4, runs from 5°S to 5°N and from 170°W to 120°W. The black triangles are the TAO array of moored buoys, as PMEL lists the sites in place by the end of 1994: each buoy measures the wind, the sea-surface temperature and the water temperature at ten depths below the surface. Section 4 uses what they measure below the surface.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 1¶
docs.text:
How does the peak of the 2026 El Niño rank among the El Niño years in the file?

Why: before forecasting anything, see what is being forecast, and how unusual this year is.

Look back at: groupby, from Earth's elevation has two peaks (03_two_peaks.ipynb).

  1. Add the column el_nino_year to enso: the year for July to December, and the year minus one for January to June.
  2. peak_by_year: the highest nino34 in each El Niño year. Years with no values (the held-back ones) come out blank; drop them.
  3. Print the five strongest, highest first.
  4. rank_2026: the place of El Niño year 2026 in that order, 1 for the strongest. Count how many years peaked higher, and add one. Print it.

Some El Niño years are only partly in the file, because the file starts in January 1982 and the held-back months are blank: 1981 (January 1982 to June 1982); 2017 (July 2017 to December 2017); 2025 (November 2025 to June 2026); 2026 (July 2026 to October 2026). Their peak is the highest of the months there are, so a partial year may rank lower than it really was. Keep them; 2026 is one of them.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: peak_by_year, rank_2026.

docs.title: 2. How far ahead does "the same as now" work?¶
docs.text:
A forecast made in one month for a month later is made at a lead. In this project the leaderboard asks for a lead of 3 months: in September, the anomaly in December.

Start with two baselines, forecasts that need no model at all.

Baseline: Write the dumbest rule you can, first. Any model that cannot beat it is decoration.

  • zero: the usual temperature for the month, so an anomaly of 0;
  • persistence: the same anomaly as now.

Each forecast is scored by its typical miss, in °C.

Typical miss: Square every gap between what happened and what the curve said, average the squares, and take the square root: the usual size of a miss, in the data's own units.

To compare a month with the month 3 later, line the two up in one row. .shift(-3) moves a column up by three rows, so each row holds the value from three rows below. Because the file has one row for every month, three rows below is three months later. A simple case first:

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 2¶
docs.text:
Three months ahead, how far off are "zero" and "the same as now"?

Why: these are the bars any model must clear. The leaderboard's pass line is zero.

Look back at: the typical miss, from When will CO2 pass 450 ppm? (07_co2_450_ppm.ipynb).

  1. Write a function typical_miss(errors) that takes a column of errors and returns their typical miss. You will use it for every forecast in this notebook.
  2. Add the column nino34_in_3 to enso: the anomaly three months after each row's month.
  3. Keep the rows that have both nino34 and nino34_in_3.
  4. persistence_miss: the typical miss of persistence on those rows, the anomaly three months later minus the anomaly now. zero_miss: the typical miss of forecasting 0. Print both, in °C.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: typical_miss, persistence_miss, zero_miss.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 3¶
docs.text:
At what lead does "the same as now" become worse than forecasting zero?

Why: a forecast is only worth making where it beats the usual. This tells you how far ahead the present alone can see.

Look back at: loops that fill a dictionary and a plot of two lines, from When will CO2 pass 450 ppm? (07_co2_450_ppm.ipynb), and your Your turn 2.

  1. For each lead from 1 to 12 months: the anomaly that many months later (.shift), the rows that have both values, and the typical miss of persistence and of zero on those rows.
  2. persistence_by_lead and zero_by_lead: those misses, keyed by the lead (a dict or a Series). Print them. At a lead of 3 they are your persistence_miss and zero_miss.
  3. first_lead_worse: the smallest lead at which persistence misses by more than zero. Print it.
  4. Plot both misses (up) against the lead (across) on one figure, with a vertical line at first_lead_worse, labelled axes and a legend.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: persistence_by_lead, zero_by_lead, first_lead_worse.

docs.title: 3. Does a fitted line do better, and why does the start month matter?¶
docs.text:
A line can learn from the record how much of today's anomaly is left three months later. Fit nino34_in_3 on nino34 by linear regression: the slope is the share that remains, and the intercept the drift.

Linear regression: Draw the best straight line. Best means the smallest root mean squared error: the line that misses its points least.

But a line must be scored on months it did not learn from.

Train/test split: Hide some data from yourself, then check.

Split by structure: by time, not at random. Here a random split would not just be kind, it would leak the answers: the target of June is the input of September, so a model that trained on September's row has already seen June's answer. And the leaderboard hides whole years. So fit on the months up to 2009 and test on 2010 to 2017, the last years in your file before the held-back ones.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 4¶
docs.text:
On years it has not seen, does one fitted line beat persistence?

Why: this is the fair test every later model in this notebook is judged on.

Look back at: LinearRegression, from How old is the universe? (06_age_of_the_universe.ipynb), and the split by time, from When will CO2 pass 450 ppm? (07_co2_450_ppm.ipynb).

  1. pairs: the rows of enso up to 2017 that have both nino34 and nino34_in_3.
  2. fit_part: the rows of pairs up to 2009. test_part: the rows from 2010 on. Take a .copy() of each, because you will add columns. Print how many rows each holds.
  3. Fit a LinearRegression of nino34_in_3 on nino34, on fit_part only. Name it line_fit, and print its slope and intercept.
  4. Add its forecast for each test month as the column line of test_part.
  5. line_test_miss and persistence_test_miss: the typical miss of the line and of persistence on test_part. Print both.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: pairs, fit_part, test_part, line_fit, line_test_miss, persistence_test_miss.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 5¶
docs.text:
How much of an anomaly is left three months later, for each start month?

Why: if the share differs by month, one line for every month must be wrong somewhere.

Look back at: loops, masks and LinearRegression, and your Your turn 4.

  1. For each start month from 1 to 12: the rows of fit_part in that month; fit a LinearRegression of nino34_in_3 on nino34 on those rows; keep its slope.
  2. slope_by_month: the twelve slopes, keyed by the month (a dict or a Series). Print it.
  3. weakest_month: the start month with the smallest slope. Print it.
  4. Draw the slopes as bars against the month, with a dashed line at the slope of your one line, a line at 1, the spring start months (3 to 5) shaded (plt.axvspan(2.5, 5.5, ...)), labelled axes and a legend.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: slope_by_month, weakest_month.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 6¶

Does one line per start month forecast the test years better than one line for all?

docs.text:
On redrawn test years, how often does one line per month beat one line?

Why: a gain is worth trusting only if it shows up year after year, not in one lucky year. You will reuse this function in section 4.

    • add to a copy of table each row's squared error for new_column and for old_column (the error is nino34_in_3 minus the forecast);
    • one row per year: the sums of the two squared errors and the number of months;

    • return the 1,000 differences.
  2. month_differences: your function on test_part, "per_month" against "line". On all the years at once the difference is per_month_test_miss minus line_test_miss.

docs.title: 4. Does the ocean's stored heat help, and in every decade?¶
docs.text:
El Niño's fuel is stored below the surface. The tropical sea is warm only in a top layer; below it the temperature drops sharply, at the 20 °C line of the slice in section 1. The warm water volume (wwv) is the volume of that warm layer, the water warmer than 20 °C, between 5°S and 5°N across the Pacific, from 120°E to 80°W (the dotted box on the map in section 1), as an anomaly from the usual, in units of 1014 m³. NOAA's Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory computes it every month from temperatures measured below the surface; along the equator many come from the TAO buoys (the triangles on the map), built from 1985 to 1994 to understand and predict El Niño.

What earlier research found. Using measurements from 1980–1999, years in which the buoy array was still being built, Meinen and McPhaden (2000, Journal of Climate, doi:10.1175/1520-0442(2000)013<3551:OOWWVC>2.0.CO;2) confirmed that the El Niño cycle recharges and discharges warm water along the equator: warm water piles up before an El Niño, and the El Niño drains it. They also found that larger swings in the warm water volume go with larger swings in surface temperature.

The next cell draws both records together.

docs.title: The leaderboard¶
docs.text:
The leaderboard cannot give you a file of 2018 to 2025 inputs: each month's target is another month's input, so the file would hold the answers. Instead, your entry is a forecast table. template has one row for each start month (1 to 12), each nino34 from -2.5 to +3.5 °C in steps of 0.5, and each wwv from -5.0 to +4.0 in steps of 0.5: 2,964 rows, with an empty forecast column. You fill in the anomaly three months later that your model forecasts for each row.

  • How it is read. For each of the 91 hidden start months, January 2018 to July 2025, the board takes your table's rows for that start month and reads it at that month's nino34 and wwv, along straight lines between the grid's values (a value beyond the grid is read at its edge). For a per-month line the reading is exactly your line's forecast.
  • The board shows a public score, the typical miss in °C on three of the eight years. The final score, on the other five, is shown after the board closes, and your rank on it is graded.
  • So choose your entry by your own fair tests, not by the public score. Three years are a few El Niños at most.
  • Do not look up or download the hidden answers, the published Niño 3.4 and warm water volume values for 2018 to 2025: a table built from them is not your model, and it scores 0.

How the board reads between rows: a worked example. Say your table holds, for start month 9 and a wwv on the grid, a forecast of 1.0 °C in the row with nino34 = 2.0 and 1.4 °C in the row with nino34 = 2.5. A September with nino34 = 2.2 is read on the straight line between those two rows. The next cell does the arithmetic.

docs.title: The question, answered¶
docs.text: October 2026 was the warmest month in the Niño 3.4 record since 1982, and three months ahead it could be forecast better than "the same as now" by a model that knows the season and the ocean's stored heat. On 2010 to 2017 one line per start month cut the typical miss from 0.63 to 0.53 °C, because an anomaly grows from summer and fades through spring; the warm water volume cut it to 0.50 °C, but it did not help in the 2000s.

docs.title: The open question¶
docs.text:
What does your model forecast for this winter's peak, and how far should you trust a line pushed past every El Niño it has seen?

Your model forecasts +3.9 °C for December 2026. Both of its inputs in September are beyond anything it was fitted on (the warmest month up to 2017 was +2.72 °C), so a straight line is carrying it into a region with no data. NOAA's Climate Prediction Center publishes its own forecasts every month, and January 2027 will bring the measurement. Compare the three. After the board closes, its final scores also show whose models held up on 2018 to 2025.

Curiosity climbed 848 m, from -4,521 m to -3,673 m, and the higher it stood, the lower the residual: about 7.4 Pa less for every 100 m. On a mountain there is less air above you, so it presses less: the year-to-year fall is the climb, not the planet.

Air pressure falls with height in a known way. Each metre up takes away the weight of one metre of air, and the thinner the air, the less a metre of it weighs. So the pressure falls by the same fraction with every metre:

$$p = p_0\, e^{-z/H} \qquad\text{so}\qquad \ln p = \ln p_0 - \frac{z}{H}$$

  • $p$ is the pressure and $z$ the height, elev_m;
  • $p_0$ is the pressure at height 0, which changes with the season;
  • $H$ is the scale height: the climb over which the pressure falls by a factor of e, about 2.7.

In logs, the height is one more straight-line column. So fit np.log(pressure) on the seasonal columns and elev_m: the seasonal columns give $\ln p_0$, the coefficient of elev_m is $-1/H$, and np.exp turns a prediction back into pascals.

If the new model wins on almost every redraw, the gain is not the luck of which months the year held.

docs.title: Is Mars's air thinning, or is Curiosity just climbing?¶
docs.text:
EPS 88 · PyEarth · final project. Open your own copy on DataHub: click here.

Since August 2012 the Curiosity rover has measured the air pressure on Mars every day. Year after year the readings come out lower. Is Mars losing its air? In this project you build a model of the pressure from Mars years 31 to 37 and use it to forecast 608 sols of Mars year 38, from its start to Ls 341. You never see the answers. The leaderboard does, and it ranks everyone's entries.

docs.title: Background: what is going on with Mars's air?¶
docs.text:
1. A barometer on Mars reads less every year. Curiosity is a car-sized rover. It landed in Gale crater in August 2012, and its weather station has read the air pressure every day since. In its first Mars year (from 2012) its highest reading was 925 Pa; in its seventh (to 2024) the highest was 871 Pa, 6% less. Taken at face value, Mars is losing its air fast. This project finds out whether it is.

Curiosity on the lower slopes of Mount Sharp in January 2015: a self-portrait stitched from its arm camera, with the upper part of Mount Sharp on the horizon. NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS, PIA19142.

2. Mars's air is thin, and every winter part of it freezes. The median reading is 835 Pa, 0.8% of the air pressure at sea level on Earth (101,325 Pa). That air is almost all carbon dioxide (CO2). Over the pole that is in winter it gets cold enough for CO2 to freeze out of the air as frost on the polar cap; in spring the frost turns back into gas. So the pressure over the whole planet rises and falls with the seasons: in Mars year 32 Curiosity read from 732 to 925 Pa, a swing of 21%.

Mars's north polar cap seen by the Hubble Space Telescope, from early spring (October 1996) to the start of summer (March 1997): the CO2 frost turns back into air and the cap shrinks. P. James, T. Clancy, S. Lee and NASA/STScI, via Wikimedia Commons.

3. Why it matters: Mars did lose most of its air, but slowly. Early Mars was warmer than today. NASA's MAVEN orbiter measured gas escaping from the top of Mars's air to space at 2 to 3 kg every second, mostly hydrogen and oxygen atoms split from water, not the carbon dioxide of the air. Run back over Mars's history, escape removed at least about 0.8 bar of CO2 (96 times today's air), and it is the main reason Mars became cold and dry (Jakosky and others, 2018, doi:10.1016/j.icarus.2018.05.030). Today's air weighs about 32 million billion kg (its pressure times the area of Mars, divided by gravity). Even if all 3 kg per second came out of that air, escape would remove only 36 parts in a billion of it over Curiosity's 12 years: far too little to see. So the 6% drop is something else.

4. Three things move the barometer at once, and a model pulls them apart. The season moves it, through the polar caps. The rover's height moves it: Curiosity has been driving up Mount Sharp, a mountain about 5 km high in the middle of the crater, and climbed 848 m in these years; the higher you stand, the less air is above you. And the weather moves it, above all dust storms. You cannot tell the three apart by looking at the readings. A model with one part for each can measure each one, and you can test it by forecasting a year it has never seen.

Mount Sharp from where Curiosity worked in its first weeks (September 2012), with the colours adjusted to Earth-like light. NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS, via Wikimedia Commons.

5. The data: one reading per sol from the rover's weather station, 2012 to 2024. The station is REMS (Rover Environmental Monitoring Station), built in Spain. Its wind and air-temperature sensors sit on two small booms on the rover's mast; its pressure sensor sits inside the rover's body. NASA publishes one pressure value for each sol (a Mars day, 24 hours 40 minutes) on its public weather page, and the rover's height from its map of the rover's drives. Your training file holds the 4,110 sols with a pressure from 2012-08-16 to 2024-11-11, Mars years 31 to 37. One row is one sol: the date on Earth, the season, the Mars year, the pressure, the day's lowest and highest air temperature, and the rover's height.

Gale crater, about the size of Connecticut and Rhode Island together, with Mount Sharp in its middle; the green dot inside the blue ellipse is where Curiosity landed. NASA/JPL-Caltech/ESA/DLR/FU Berlin/MSSS, PIA16058.

An engineer fits one of the REMS booms to Curiosity's mast in 2011. NASA/JPL-Caltech, via Wikimedia Commons.

6. What earlier studies found.

  • Haberle and others (2014) read REMS's first 100 sols. The sensor worked well and showed the CO2 cycle, and daily pressure swings (the "thermal tides") several times larger than other landers had seen, partly because the crater amplifies them. doi:10.1002/2013JE004488
  • Guzewich and others (2019) describe the 2018 global dust storm from Curiosity: the dust hid 97% of the Sun's ultraviolet light at the ground, the day-to-night temperature range fell by 30 K, and the pressure wave that rises and falls twice a day grew to an amplitude of 40 Pa. doi:10.1029/2018GL080839
  • Lange and others (2022) compared the pressure measured by two landers 40 years apart, Viking 1 and InSight: the CO2 cycle changed by no more than 8 Pa. They saw hints of a larger north polar cap after the 2018 storm, with no agreed cause. doi:10.1029/2022JE007190
  • de la Torre Juárez and others (2024) compared the Gale record before and after the 2018 storm and found the pressure lower than usual after it, a deficit later dust storms did not erase, and, from an orbiter, a larger north polar cap. doi:10.1029/2023JE007810

The same view of Gale crater's rim from Curiosity on 7 and 10 June 2018: in three days the global dust storm hid it. NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS, PIA22520.

7. What is still open, and what you will do. Whether the 2018 storm really changed how much air Mars holds, and why, is still argued: a dusty crater, a bigger polar cap or a sensor are all on the table. You will build the model one part at a time: show that the 6% drop is the climb, measure from the readings how fast air thins with height, forecast a Mars year the model has not seen, find the storm's mark in what the model misses, and enter a forecast for Mars year 38 on the leaderboard.

Mars from the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter in May 2018 (left) and July 2018 (right), when dust covered the whole planet. NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS, PIA22487.

docs.title: How this notebook works¶
docs.text:
This notebook is built like a weekly notebook: a few questions lead it, each section answers one, and every place you work opens with a pencil icon ✏️ and the words Your turn. The difference is how much you write. Each Your turn says why the step matters and gives a numbered plan in words; the cell under it is empty, and you write all of the code, looking back at the weekly notebook it names. A self-check cell follows. Run it: it tells you whether your numbers are right, as in every week.

The last Your turn is your leaderboard entry: it saves the file submission.csv. Run every cell so your answers and figures are saved in the file, then download this notebook itself — the .ipynb file — and upload it to Gradescope together with submission.csv. In JupyterLab: File ▸ Download, or right-click the file in the left-hand panel and choose Download. The leaderboard scores your file on answers you never see and ranks everyone's entries.

Two habits from the first minute. A cell runs when you press Shift+Enter, and the notebook remembers everything it has already run — so when something breaks and you cannot see why, Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells throws the memory away and rebuilds it from the top. That is never the wrong thing to do.

docs.title: What you'll be able to do¶
docs.text:
The science. Say why the air pressure on Mars rises and falls twice every year, why a rover that climbs a mountain measures less air, how the height over which air thins (the scale height) follows from the temperature, and what a planet-wide dust storm did to the air.

The code. You write every line: a plot with a loop over the years, a function for the typical miss, a function that makes seasonal columns, LinearRegression on the log of the pressure, a mean for each group, a split by Mars year, a choice made on a held-out year, a bootstrap over blocks of sols, a paired bootstrap of two models, and a submission.csv file.

The four questions of the project:

  1. How does the air pressure change through a Mars year, and from year to year?
  2. Can the seasons alone predict the pressure, or does the rover's climb matter?
  3. How well does the model forecast a Mars year it has never seen?
  4. Did the 2018 dust storm leave a mark, and is the forecast better without it?

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text:
Run the next two cells once. All their code is given. Three files ship with the course:

  • trackT13_mars_daily.csv: the sols from the landing, in Mars year 31, to the end of Mars year 37, your training file;
  • trackT13_mars_year38_inputs.csv: the leaderboard file, 608 sols of Mars year 38, from its start to Ls 341, with the season and the rover's height but not the pressure;
  • trackT13_submission_template.csv: the empty submission template, one row per leaderboard sol.

docs.title: 1. How does the air pressure change through a Mars year, and from year to year?¶
docs.text:
The season is counted by ls, Mars's position around the Sun, in degrees. Ls = 0 is the start of northern spring, 90 of northern summer, 180 of northern autumn and 270 of northern winter. One full circle, a Mars year, takes 668 sols; Mars year 32 began on 2013-08-01 on Earth. Curiosity sits in Gale crater, a little south of the equator.

Does the record sink from year to year? The next cell draws every reading against time, and marks the highest reading of each Mars year with its value.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 1¶
docs.text:
Does the pressure follow the same seasonal shape every Mars year?

Why: before any model, look at the data. If each year has the same shape, a model of the season should work; if the years differ, something else is changing.

Look back at: the loop that drew several curves with a legend, from When will CO2 pass 450 ppm? (07_co2_450_ppm.ipynb).

  1. Loop over the Mars years 31 to 37. For each one, take its rows of train and plot pressure (up) against ls (across), as small dots or a thin line, labelled with the year.
  2. Label both axes with their units, add a legend, and give the plot a title.

This Your turn has no self-check: a figure you can see needs none. A good figure shows seven curves you can tell apart, each rising and falling twice between Ls 0 and 360, with the years in order in the legend. Colours that run in order from the first year to the last (for example color=plt.cm.viridis((year - 31) / 6)) make it easy to see whether the later years sit lower.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 2¶
docs.text:
How far off is the simplest guess: the same pressure for every sol?

Why: every model in this notebook has to beat the number you find here.

Baseline: Write the dumbest rule you can, first. Any model that cannot beat it is decoration.

Typical miss: Square every gap between what happened and what the curve said, average the squares, and take the square root: the usual size of a miss, in the data's own units.

Look back at: the typical miss, from When will CO2 pass 450 ppm? (07_co2_450_ppm.ipynb).

  1. Write a function typical_miss(errors) that takes a column of errors and returns their typical miss. You will use it for every model in this notebook.
  2. The rule: guess the average pressure of all the training sols. Name it average_pressure.
  3. Each sol's error is its pressure minus that guess. Their typical miss is baseline_miss.
  4. Print the guess and the typical miss, in Pa.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: typical_miss, average_pressure, baseline_miss.

docs.title: 2. Can the seasons alone predict the pressure, or does the rover's climb matter?¶
docs.text:
Mars's pressure needs more than the one wave a year that CO2 on Earth needed. In the CO2 week a pair of seasonal columns did the job:

Seasonal column: A column that rises and falls once a year, so the fitted curve can rise and fall with the seasons.

One pair, the sine and the cosine of the month's angle, was enough there, because CO2 rises and falls once a year. Mars's pressure rises and falls twice, with highs of different heights, and one pair can draw only one high.

More pairs draw more shapes. A second pair goes round twice a year, a third three times. With the angle of the season in radians, $\theta$ = np.radians(ls), the pairs are

$$\sin\theta,\ \cos\theta,\quad \sin 2\theta,\ \cos 2\theta,\quad \sin 3\theta,\ \cos 3\theta,\ \dots$$

and linear regression finds how much of each to add:

$$p = a + b_1 \sin\theta + c_1 \cos\theta + b_2 \sin 2\theta + c_2 \cos 2\theta + \dots$$

Linear regression: Draw the best straight line. Best means the smallest root mean squared error: the line that misses its points least.

With many columns it finds the best mix of all of them in the same way. The next cell draws the sine of each of the first three pairs.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 3¶
docs.text:
How close do three seasonal pairs get?

Why: if the seasons were all there is, this model would follow every year.

Look back at: functions and LinearRegression, from How old is the universe? (06_age_of_the_universe.ipynb), and the seasonal columns of the CO2 week.

  1. Write a function add_season_columns(table, n_pairs). It adds to table one sine and one cosine column for each n from 1 to n_pairs, of n times the angle of ls in radians, and returns the list of the names it added. Name the columns as you like.
  2. season_columns: what your function returns for train with 3 pairs.
  3. Fit a LinearRegression of pressure on those six columns, for every training sol. Name it season_fit, and add its prediction as the column season of train.
  4. season_miss: its typical miss, in Pa. Print it beside baseline_miss.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: add_season_columns, season_columns, season_fit, season_miss.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 4¶
docs.text:
Does the seasonal model miss every Mars year in the same way?

Why: a good model's residuals average zero in every year. A steady fall from year to year means something the season columns do not hold is changing.

Look back at: groupby, from Earth's elevation has two peaks (03_two_peaks.ipynb).

  1. Add the column season_residual to train: pressure minus the seasonal prediction.
  2. season_by_year: its mean in each Mars year. Print it, rounded to 1 place.
  3. Plot it: one bar per Mars year (plt.bar), the mean residual up, with a horizontal line at zero. Label both axes and give a title. A good figure shows at a glance which years sit above zero and which below; writing each bar's value on it (plt.text) makes the trend readable without the printout.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: season_by_year.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 5¶
docs.text:
With the rover's height added, how small is the miss, and what scale height does the fit find?

Why: if the climb explains the fall from year to year, adding it should shrink the miss many times over, and the fitted $H$ should agree with the physics of the air.

Look back at: your Your turn 3, and np.log and np.exp.

  1. height_columns: your three-pair season_columns plus elev_m.
  2. Fit a LinearRegression of the natural log of pressure on them, for every training sol. Name it height_fit.
  3. Add its prediction, turned back into Pa, as the column height_model of train.
  4. height_miss: its typical miss in Pa. Print it beside season_miss.
  5. H_km: the scale height in km, from the coefficient of elev_m, which is $-1/H$ with $H$ in metres. Print it.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: height_fit, height_miss, H_km.

docs.title: 3. How well does the model forecast a Mars year it has never seen?¶
docs.text:
A model is judged on data it did not learn from.

Train/test split: Hide some data from yourself, then check.

But which sols to hide? Not sols picked at random. The weather of one sol is much like that of the sol before and after, so a model that has seen sol 2,000 and sol 2,002 has nearly seen sol 2,001, and the test would be too kind. And the leaderboard does not hide scattered sols: it hides most of a Mars year, 38 up to Ls 341, at heights the rover had not reached. So we split by structure, the way the leaderboard does, one year earlier: fit on Mars years 31 to 36, and hide Mars year 37.

A fair baseline for a new year is not the average of all sols, which ignores the season, but the same season one year earlier: for each sol of Mars year 37, the pressure Curiosity read at the same ls in Mars year 36. It is the leaderboard's pass line.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 6¶
docs.text:
How far off is "the same season last year" on a Mars year it has not seen?

Why: this is the bar a forecast of a new year must clear, and the leaderboard's pass line.

Look back at: the split by time, from When will CO2 pass 450 ppm? (07_co2_450_ppm.ipynb), and groupby.

  1. fit_part: the rows of train from Mars years 31 to 36. hidden_part: the rows of Mars year 37. Take a .copy() of each, because you will add columns. Print how many sols each holds.
  2. From fit_part, the mean pressure of Mars year 36 at each value of ls.
  3. For each hidden sol, that mean at its own ls. A few values of ls have no sol in Mars year 36; leave those sols out of the score (.dropna() drops them).
  4. last_year_miss: the typical miss of the hidden pressure minus that guess. Print it, and the mean of the errors: is the guess too high or too low?

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: fit_part, hidden_part, last_year_miss.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 7¶
docs.text:
How many seasonal pairs forecast the hidden year best?

Why: the number of pairs is a choice, and a choice is made on data the fit has not seen.

Look back at: choosing between curves on held-back years, from When will CO2 pass 450 ppm? (07_co2_450_ppm.ipynb), and your Your turns 3 and 5.

  2. miss_by_pairs: those misses, keyed by the number of pairs (a dict or a Series). Print it.
  3. chosen_pairs: the fewest pairs whose miss is within 0.01 Pa of the smallest miss. test_miss: its miss. Print both beside last_year_miss.
  4. Plot the miss (up) against the number of pairs (across), with a horizontal line at last_year_miss. A log scale on the miss axis (plt.yscale("log")) shows the small and the large misses together. A good figure also marks the chosen number of pairs, so a reader sees at once which point won and by how much it beats last year's guess.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: miss_by_pairs, chosen_pairs, test_miss.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 8¶
docs.text:
How much could the hidden-year score move with other months like these?

Why: two models whose scores differ by less than this are not clearly different. You will need it in the next section.

Look back at: the bootstrap, from How long was the Earth frozen? (08_how_long_frozen.ipynb).

  1. Fit the chosen model again on fit_part (chosen_pairs pairs and elev_m, the log of pressure). Name it chosen_fit, and add its prediction for each hidden sol, in Pa, as the column with_storm of hidden_part. (The next section explains the name.) Its typical miss, with your typical_miss, should be your test_miss.
  2. Number each hidden sol's block: its sol minus the first hidden sol, divided by 30 and rounded down (//).
  3. per_block: one row per block, with the sum of its squared errors and its number of sols.
  4. Make a random generator, rng = np.random.default_rng(88), and an empty list, redrawn_misses. 1,000 times: redraw as many blocks as per_block holds, with replacement (random_state=rng), and append the redraw's typical miss.
  5. test_interval: the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the 1,000 misses. Print it beside test_miss.
  6. Draw a histogram of the 1,000 misses, with vertical lines at the two ends of the interval and at test_miss.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: chosen_fit, per_block, redrawn_misses, test_interval.

docs.title: 4. Did the 2018 dust storm leave a mark, and is the forecast better without it?¶
docs.text: The global dust storm of the Background (step 6) began in early June 2018; the file reaches Ls 185 of Mars year 34 on 2018-05-31, sol 2068. Dust in the air soaks up sunlight and warms the air, which changes the winds and how much carbon dioxide freezes onto the polar caps. De la Torre Juárez and others (2024) found the pressure at Gale about 3 to 6 Pa lower than usual after the storm. If the storm left a mark, your model's residuals should show it, and a model fitted on a year the storm disturbed may have learned the wrong season.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 9¶
docs.text:
After the storm began, did the air press less than the model says?

Why: a mark the storm left is a residual: a few pascals below zero, starting when it began.

Look back at: your Your turns 4 and 8.

  1. Add the column residual to fit_part: pressure minus the prediction of chosen_fit (Your turn 8) for every fitting sol, in Pa.
  2. storm_residual: the mean residual over the sols of Mars year 34 from Ls 185 on, the storm and the half year after it.
  3. calm_residual: the mean residual over the sols of Mars years 32 and 33 from Ls 185 on: the same season in two years with no global storm. Print both.
  4. Plot the residual (up) against sol (across) as small dots, with a horizontal line at zero and a vertical line at the first sol of Mars year 34 from Ls 185 on. A good figure makes a dip of a few pascals visible: limit the vertical axis to about ±12 Pa (plt.ylim), and draw the mean residual of each 30-sol stretch as a line on top of the dots (a groupby, as for the blocks of Your turn 8).

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: storm_residual, calm_residual.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 10¶
docs.text:
Fitted without the storm's sols, does the model forecast the hidden year better?

Why: this is new information about the data, not a new shape: which sols show the usual air. If the storm's year taught the model the wrong season, leaving it out should cut the miss on a year without a storm.

Look back at: masks joined with & and |, and your Your turns 7 and 8.
