  2. Fit the chosen model (chosen_pairs pairs and elev_m, the log of pressure) on the rows of fit_part outside the window. Name it calm_fit.
  3. Add its prediction for each hidden sol, in Pa, as the column no_storm of hidden_part.
  4. no_storm_test_miss: its typical miss on the hidden year, with your typical_miss. Print it beside test_miss and test_interval.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: storm_sols, calm_fit, no_storm_test_miss.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 11¶
docs.text:
On the same redrawn months, how often does the model without the storm win?

Why: a gain smaller than one model's interval can still be real, if it shows up month after month. This tells you which model to enter.

Look back at: your Your turn 8.

  1. Add two columns to hidden_part: each sol's squared error for with_storm, and for no_storm.
  2. One row per block: the sums of the two columns and the number of sols.
  3. A new generator, rng = np.random.default_rng(88), and an empty list, miss_differences. 1,000 times: redraw the blocks with replacement, find each model's typical miss on the redraw, and append the miss without the storm minus the miss with it. On all the blocks at once this difference is no_storm_test_miss minus test_miss.
  4. difference_interval: the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the differences. share_better: the share of redraws where the difference is below zero. Print both.
  5. Draw a histogram of the differences, with a vertical line at zero.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: miss_differences, difference_interval, share_better.

docs.title: The leaderboard¶
docs.text:
leaderboard holds 608 sols of Mars year 38, from its start to Ls 341, with row_id, sol, ls and elev_m, and no pressure. template has the same row_ids and an empty pressure column for your forecasts. In Mars year 38 the rover climbed to -3,500 m; 78% of the leaderboard's sols are higher than any sol in the training file.

  • Your entry is your own model, fitted on the training file here; never download REMS data. Do not look up or download the hidden answers (the pressures Curiosity published for Mars year 38); a forecast built from them is not your model, and it scores 0.
  • The board shows a public score, the typical miss in Pa on one third of the leaderboard's sols, in whole blocks of 30 sols. The final score, on the other two thirds, is shown after the board closes, and your rank on it is graded.
  • So choose your entry by your own fair test, not by the public score. A third of a year is a few months; a model picked because it moved that number is tuned to them, and the rank uses the others.
  • Up to 10 uploads that change submission.csv are scored. An upload that changes only the notebook is free.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 12¶
docs.text:
Your leaderboard entry: what pressure will Curiosity read on each of the 608 sols of Mars year 38?

Why: this is the project's answer, scored on readings you have not seen, and ranked against the other students. Choose by your fair test: the public score is a third of the year, and your rank is decided on the rest.

  2. Fit it on every training sol outside the storm window, Mars year 37 included: the newest year is data too, and the nearest in height to Mars year 38. Name it final_fit.
  3. Add the same seasonal columns to leaderboard, made the same way.
  4. submission: a copy of template, with its pressure column filled with your forecast for each leaderboard sol, in Pa. Save it with submission.to_csv("submission.csv", index=False).
  5. Print its first rows, its number of rows and of blanks, and its lowest and highest forecast.
  6. Run the self-check, then download submission.csv and this notebook and upload both together (the steps are under "What you hand in" above) to Final project: Mars weather.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: final_fit, final_columns, submission.

docs.title: The question, answered¶
docs.text: Mars is not losing its air: Curiosity climbed 848 m, and with its height in the model, 4 seasonal pairs forecast a Mars year the model never saw within 3.9 Pa, against 15.9 Pa for the same season one year earlier. The fit's scale height, 11.0 km, matches the physics of the air. The 2018 dust storm left the air about 3 Pa thin for about a Mars year, and a model fitted without that year forecast the next one better, on 99.4% of paired redraws.

docs.title: The open question¶
docs.text:
What did the storm change in Mars's atmosphere, and is the small excess at the end of the record real or the model stretching beyond the heights it was trained on?

Two things in your own data point at it. The storm's deficit is a measurement; what the storm changed, more frost on a polar cap or a change in how the air moves, needs observations from orbit that this file does not have. And at the end of the training record, the second half of Mars year 37 sits +1.9 Pa above your final model, where the same half of Mars years 32, 33 and 36 sits -0.5 Pa from it. Mars year 37 is also where the rover was highest, and Mars year 38 is higher still: 78% of the leaderboard's sols are above anything the model was fitted on. After the board closes, its final scores show how well each student's model reached those heights.

What the columns hold.

  • a, e, i: the orbit. a is the average distance from the Sun in AU (the main belt lies between about 2.1 and 3.3 AU); e says how stretched the orbit is (0 is a circle); i is its tilt in degrees.
  • diameter in km, and albedo.
  • R374 to R1034: Gaia's reflectance in 16 bands, named by wavelength in nm, each divided by the reflectance at 550 nm (green). So R550 is always 1, a value above 1 means "redder than green", and a blank is a band Gaia flagged as unreliable.
  • spec_T and spec_B: the class letters of the Tholen and SMASSII (Bus) systems. Most asteroids have neither.

The next cell turns the class letters into the three kinds S, C and X of step 3 at the top. It reads the Bus letter first and the Tholen letter if Bus has none, the leaderboard's rule. A letter that names none of the three (D, T, an uncertain class with a colon) gives no kind. Tholen's dark P class counts as X here, as the leaderboard counts it. That is a choice: the newer classification of Mahlke and others (2022, step 7) puts P with C instead. In the data, 13 of the 194 X asteroids are X only through Tholen's P. Then the cell keeps the asteroids with a kind and all 14 bands from 418 to 990 nm, because every leaderboard asteroid has those.

In [ ]: Copied! 
# the letters of each kind, in each of the two systems
BUS = {"S": ["S", "Sq", "Sl", "Sa", "Sk", "Sr", "Q", "A", "K", "L", "Ld", "R", "V", "O"],
       "C": ["C", "Ch", "Cb", "Cg", "Cgh", "B"],
       "X": ["X", "Xc", "Xk", "Xe"]}
THOLEN = {"S": ["S", "A", "Q", "R", "V"],
          "C": ["C", "B", "G", "F"],
          "X": ["X", "M", "E", "P"]}


def kind_of(letter, system):
    """S, C or X for one class letter of one system, or None if it names none of them."""
    for kind, letters in system.items():
        if letter in letters:
            return kind
    return None


# Bus first; Tholen only where Bus gives no kind
kinds = []
for bus, tholen in zip(asteroids["spec_B"], asteroids["spec_T"]):
    kind = kind_of(bus, BUS)
    if kind is None:
        kind = kind_of(tholen, THOLEN)
    kinds.append(kind)
asteroids["complex"] = kinds

Does where an asteroid orbits say anything more? Earlier research found that the kinds are not mixed evenly (step 6 at the top). The belt itself has gaps, where Jupiter's pull clears asteroids out: the Kirkwood gaps. The next cell splits the belt into three zones at two of them, 2.5 and 2.82 AU, and counts the share of each kind in each zone.

Main-belt asteroids counted by their distance from the Sun a. The five dashed lines mark gaps; this notebook splits the belt at two of them, 2.5 AU (marked 3:1) and 2.82 AU (marked 5:2), into the inner (blue), middle (orange) and outer (green) belt. A random forest can use albedo and orbit together. You met it in the basalt week.

docs.title: Rock, carbon or metal: what are asteroids made of?¶
docs.text:
EPS 88 · PyEarth · final project. Open your own copy on DataHub: click here.

Nobody has visited (16) Psyche, an asteroid that may be made largely of metal, so what it is made of was read from afar: how much sunlight it reflects and what colour it is. In this project you teach a computer to read the same two things and sort asteroids into rocky, carbon-rich, and the group that holds the metal worlds. Then it sorts 368 classified asteroids whose classes you never see. The leaderboard sees them, and it ranks everyone's entries.

This notebook is built like a weekly notebook: a few questions lead it, each section answers one, and every place you work opens with a pencil icon ✏️ and the words Your turn. The difference is how much you write. Each Your turn says why the step matters and gives a numbered plan in words; the cell under it is empty, and you write all of the code, looking back at the weekly notebook it names. A self-check cell follows. Run it: it tells you whether your numbers are right, as in every week.

The last Your turn is your leaderboard entry: it saves the file submission.csv. Run every cell so your answers and figures are saved in the file, then download this notebook itself — the .ipynb file — and upload it to Gradescope together with submission.csv. In JupyterLab: File ▸ Download, or right-click the file in the left-hand panel and choose Download. The leaderboard scores your file on answers you never see and ranks everyone's entries.

Two habits from the first minute. A cell runs when you press Shift+Enter, and the notebook remembers everything it has already run — so when something breaks and you cannot see why, Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells throws the memory away and rebuilds it from the top. That is never the wrong thing to do.

docs.title: What your project is about: rock, carbon or metal?¶
docs.text: Seven steps before any code: the problem, why it matters, the data, and what is known.

docs.title: 1. A spacecraft is flying to an asteroid that may be the metal core of a planet's building block¶
docs.text:
NASA's Psyche spacecraft launched on 13 October 2023 and is due to begin exploring the asteroid (16) Psyche by August 2029. Psyche orbits the Sun between Mars and Jupiter and is about 280 km across at its widest. Scientists think it holds a lot of metal and may be part of the core of a planetesimal, one of the small bodies the planets were built from (NASA). The mission is led by Lindy Elkins-Tanton, a professor in Berkeley's Department of Earth and Planetary Science.

How Psyche might look if metal (grey-blue) and rock (brown) sit in large patches. No spacecraft has photographed it yet. Illustration: NASA/JPL-Caltech/ASU, PIA24471.

docs.title: 2. Why it matters: nobody can visit a planet's core¶
docs.text:
Earth's core lies under the whole rocky mantle, out of reach; Psyche may show us a core. NASA says Psyche is most likely the survivor of several violent hit-and-run collisions from when the Solar System formed, so it may tell us how the cores of Earth and the other rocky planets came to be. Asteroids matter for a second reason: they are leftover building blocks of the planets, and the meteorites that land on Earth come from them. Their colours have already tied several kinds of meteorite to the asteroids they came from (Reddy and others, 2015, arXiv:1502.05008).

Earth's layers, drawn to scale on the right: the core is the grey centre. Diagram: Surachit, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0).

docs.title: 3. An asteroid is read from its colour¶
docs.text:
An asteroid is a point of light, so astronomers read its make-up from the colours of that light. Each mineral absorbs some colours of sunlight more than others. The rock minerals olivine and pyroxene absorb near 1,000 nm, in the near infrared just beyond what our eyes see (Reddy and others, 2015, arXiv:1502.05008). So astronomers measure an asteroid's reflectance spectrum: the light it reflects at each wavelength, divided by the light it reflects in green (550 nm). They sort spectra into classes by shape, and group the classes into three complexes. This notebook calls each complex a kind:

  • S (stony): rises steeply toward the red and dips near 1,000 nm, the dip of olivine and pyroxene. Gaia's colours (step 5) stop at about 1,000 nm, so they see only the start of this dip, where an S spectrum begins to fall after about 800 nm;
  • C (carbon-rich): nearly flat;
  • X: rises gently with no dip. Psyche is an X, but so are asteroids that only share its colour.

Spectrum shapes of 12 of the 24 classes of the Bus–DeMeo system (2009). Across: wavelength from 0.45 to 2.45 µm (the "1" marks 1,000 nm). Up: reflectance, set to 1 at 0.55 µm. Compare S, C and X. Diagram: Wiki Remi, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

docs.title: 4. Why a model: telescopes have classified only a few asteroids¶
docs.text:
A spectrum good enough to classify an asteroid needs a large telescope and a bright asteroid, so only a few have one. Your training file holds 138,094 asteroids with a measured albedo. Gaia measured the colours of 40,642 of them, but only 1,534 have a class from telescope observations, and 861 have both a kind and a full Gaia colour spectrum. A model can learn from those few how albedo, orbit and colour go with the kind, and then name a kind for the tens of thousands that no telescope has classified.

Counted from the training file of this project. The axis is logarithmic: each step is ten times more asteroids.

docs.title: 5. The data: two space telescopes, joined on the asteroid's number¶
docs.text:
One row of the data is one asteroid, and 97% of the rows are in the main belt, between Mars and Jupiter. NASA/JPL's Small-Body Database gives each asteroid's orbit, size, albedo and class letters. Psyche, for example, orbits 2.93 AU from the Sun (1 AU is the Earth's distance), is 222 km across on average (it is not round, so its widest is longer, step 1), and has an albedo of 0.12.

The inner Solar System: the main belt is the white ring between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter. Image: Mdf, Wikimedia Commons (public domain).

  • Albedo, the share of sunlight a surface reflects (0.1 means a tenth), comes from infrared telescopes. It is measured head-on, with the Sun behind the observer, and compared with a plain white disc; a very bright surface can reflect as much as that disc or more, so a few rows of the file reach 1. NASA's WISE measured the heat glow of more than 100,000 main-belt asteroids, which gives each one's size; size and visible brightness together give the albedo (Masiero and others, 2011).
  • Colour comes from ESA's Gaia spacecraft, built to map the stars of the Milky Way, which also watches asteroids. Its third data release gives reflectance spectra of 60,518 asteroids in 16 bands from 374 to 1,034 nm, observed from 2014 to 2017: each is the asteroid's light divided by the light of stars like the Sun (Galluccio and others, 2023).
  • Classes are letters from two systems built from telescope observations: Tholen's (1984), from colours and albedo, and SMASSII (Bus and Binzel, 2002), from spectra.

Left: NASA's WISE in orbit around Earth (NASA/JPL-Caltech, PIA17254, public domain). Right: ESA's Gaia (ESA, CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO). Both artist's impressions, via Wikimedia Commons.

docs.title: 6. What earlier research found¶
docs.text:
For more than forty years astronomers have found that the kinds are not spread evenly through the belt.

  • Gradie and Tedesco (1982) sorted asteroids into colour classes and found that the share of each class changes steadily with distance from the Sun, from 1.8 to 5.2 AU. They read this as asteroids having formed near where they orbit now. doi:10.1126/science.216.4553.1405
  • Masiero and others (2011) measured the size and albedo of more than 100,000 main-belt asteroids with WISE. Albedo has two humps, dark and bright, and the average albedo changes from the inner to the outer belt. doi:10.1088/0004-637X/741/2/68
  • DeMeo and Carry (2014) mapped the belt with many smaller asteroids and found it more mixed, by size and distance, than had been known: a sign that the belt was stirred, for example as the planets moved. doi:10.1038/nature12908
  • Delbo and others (2026) trained a classifier on Gaia spectra of asteroids with known classes and named a class for every asteroid in the Gaia release. S was sorted well; X mixed with its neighbours, as Gaia's short range of wavelengths leads one to expect. doi:10.3389/fspas.2026.1774478

The share of each class against distance from the Sun, redrawn from Gradie and Tedesco (1982). S (red) peaks in the inner belt and C (blue) farther out; the grey band is the main belt. Chart: Praemonitus, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

docs.title: 7. What is still open, and what you will try¶
docs.text:
Whether an X asteroid is metal is still open. The M class (part of X) was first named for asteroids thought to be the metal cores of broken planetesimals. Psyche, the best-known M-type, was once thought to be almost all metal. New measurements of its density, its radar echo and its spectrum point instead to a mix of metal and rock: Elkins-Tanton and others (2020) estimated a density of 3,400 to 4,100 kg/m³ and 30 to 60% metal by volume, and wrote that final answers may wait until the spacecraft arrives (doi:10.1029/2019JE006296). A newer classification found that albedo separates X asteroids whose spectra look alike (Mahlke and others, 2022, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202243587).

What you will try: build a classifier that sorts S, C and X from albedo, orbit and Gaia colour; test it on asteroids it has never seen; then ask whether it can be trusted on the small asteroids that no telescope has classified.

NASA's Psyche spacecraft and its two cross-shaped solar arrays. Illustration: NASA (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons.

docs.title: What you'll be able to do¶
docs.text:
The science. Say why rocky asteroids look bright and red, carbon-rich ones dark and grey, and the metal-bearing group in between; why the rocky ones crowd the inner asteroid belt; and why colour, not orbit, is what tells the kinds apart.

The code. You write every line: a histogram for each group, a function for the macro F1 score, a rule with two cuts, RandomForestClassifier, a stratified split, a bootstrap, an SVM with scaled columns, two columns made from a colour spectrum, and a submission.csv file.

The four questions of the project:

  1. How bright are rocky, carbon-rich and metal-bearing asteroids?
  2. Can brightness and orbit sort the three kinds?
  3. How well does the classifier do on asteroids it has never seen?
  4. Does a different model, or more information, sort them better?

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text:
Run the next cells once. All their code is given. One row is one asteroid (step 5 at the top). Three files ship with the course:

  • trackT14_asteroid_catalogue.csv.gz: every numbered asteroid with a measured albedo, your training file, frozen so everyone trains on the same file. The 368 leaderboard asteroids have been taken out of it;
  • trackT14_leaderboard_inputs.csv: the leaderboard file, those 368 asteroids with their orbit, size, albedo and colour but not their class, and no name;
  • trackT14_submission_template.csv: the empty submission template, one row per leaderboard asteroid.

Use only these files. The online catalogues hold the hidden classes, and the leaderboard flags a notebook that reads them.

docs.title: 1. How bright are rocky, carbon-rich and metal-bearing asteroids?¶
docs.text: The first thing to read from an asteroid's light is how much sunlight it reflects: its albedo, the share of sunlight a surface reflects (step 5 at the top). If the three kinds are made of different stuff, they may differ in albedo. Three famous asteroids, one of each kind:

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 1¶
docs.text:
How is albedo spread within each kind?

Why: before any model, look at the data. If the three kinds sit at different albedos, albedo alone can tell them apart; where their histograms overlap, it cannot.

Look back at: histograms, from Earth's elevation has two peaks (03_two_peaks.ipynb), and the loop from Which of these worlds could have liquid water? (02_liquid_water.ipynb).

  1. Make one set of bins for all three histograms: from 0 to 0.6 in steps of 0.02.
  2. With a loop over the three kinds "S", "C" and "X", take the albedo of the rows of labelled of that kind and draw its histogram on the shared bins, half transparent (alpha=0.4), in the kind's colour from KIND_COLOURS, with a label that says the kind, how many asteroids it holds and its median albedo.
  3. Draw the median of each kind as a dashed vertical line in the same colour (plt.axvline).
  4. Label both axes, add a legend, and give the plot a title with the number of asteroids.

This Your turn has no self-check: a figure you can see needs none. A good figure lets a reader see at a glance where each kind sits: three coloured histograms, three dashed medians, and labels that add up to 861.

docs.title: Scoring a guess with three answers¶
docs.text:
The F1 score you met in the explosion week works on one kind at a time. There it asked two questions of one label, "explosion":

Precision / recall: Of the ones you flagged, how many were right? Of the real ones, how many did you catch?

F1 is the balance of the two. Here there are three kinds. We score each kind the same way, that kind against the other two, and average the three F1 scores. The average is the macro F1. The leaderboard ranks you by it.

Why the average and not the share right? The kinds are not equally common. A rule that never says X can still be right most of the time, and an average of the three F1 scores gives such a rule 0 for X. Macro F1 runs from 0 to 1, and 1 means every asteroid named correctly.

A simple case first: six made-up asteroids, their true kinds and a guess. The next cell scores one kind, S, with f1_score from the explosion week: a True for every asteroid that is S, against a True for every asteroid the guess calls S.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 2¶
docs.text:
How good is the simplest guess: the same kind for every asteroid?

Why: a classifier is worth something only if it beats the dumbest rule, so measure that rule first.

Baseline: Write the dumbest rule you can, first. Any model that cannot beat it is decoration.

Look back at: f1_score, from Earthquake or nuclear explosion? (09_explosion_or_earthquake.ipynb), and the six made-up asteroids just above.

  1. Write a function macro_f1(truth, guess) that takes the true kinds and the guessed kinds and returns the average, over "S", "C" and "X", of each kind's F1 score. You will use it for every classifier in this notebook.
  2. Print it for toy_truth and toy_guess, and beside it what f1_score gives with average="macro". The two should agree.
  3. most_common: the kind that occurs most often in labelled.
  4. baseline_f1: the macro F1 of naming most_common for every asteroid in labelled. Print both.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: macro_f1, most_common, baseline_f1.

docs.title: 2. Can brightness and orbit sort the three kinds?¶
docs.text: The histograms suggest a rule with two cuts. Below a low albedo, call it C; above a high one, call it S; in between, X. You choose the two cuts by eye from your histogram of Your turn 1.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 3¶
docs.text:
How far does albedo alone get, with two cuts?

Why: this is the simplest rule with any science in it. Every classifier after it has to beat it, or the classifier adds nothing that one number did not already say.

Look back at: np.where, from Earthquake or nuclear explosion? (09_explosion_or_earthquake.ipynb), and your histogram of Your turn 1.

  1. Choose two albedo cuts from your histogram: low_cut, below which most asteroids are C, and high_cut, above which most are S.
  2. rule_guess: for every asteroid in labelled, "C" if its albedo is below low_cut, "X" if it is from low_cut up to below high_cut, and "S" from high_cut up.
  3. rule_f1: the rule's macro F1, with your macro_f1. Print it beside baseline_f1.
  4. Try two or three other pairs of cuts and keep the pair with the highest score.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: low_cut, high_cut, rule_f1.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 4¶
docs.text:
How well does a forest on albedo and orbit sort the asteroids it learned from?

Why: the forest can combine albedo with where the asteroid orbits, which the rule cannot. If the orbit adds information, the forest should beat the rule.

Look back at: RandomForestClassifier, from Where was this basalt made? (10_where_basalt.ipynb).

  1. four_inputs: the list of the four columns albedo, a, e and i.
  2. forest: a RandomForestClassifier (for example n_estimators=100, random_state=0), fitted on those columns of every row of labelled, with complex as the answer.
  3. forest_fit_f1: the macro F1 of the forest's predictions for the same rows of labelled. Print it beside rule_f1.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: four_inputs, forest, forest_fit_f1.

docs.title: 3. How well does the classifier do on asteroids it has never seen?¶
docs.text:
A model is judged on data it did not learn from.

Train/test split: Hide some data from yourself, then check.

But which asteroids to hide? Copy how the leaderboard hid its own. Its 368 asteroids are 30% of the classified asteroids with a full colour spectrum, chosen at random so that each kind kept its share (a stratified split). Your hidden part must be made the way the leaderboard's was; this course calls that rule "split by structure". A split that is not random (all the big asteroids hidden, or one zone of the belt) would test a different question, and its score would not predict yours.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 5¶
docs.text:
How well does the forest do on asteroids it has never seen?

Why: this is the number that predicts how your model will do on the leaderboard. The score on the asteroids it learned from does not.

Look back at: train_test_split with stratify, from Where was this basalt made? (10_where_basalt.ipynb).

  1. Split labelled into fit_part (70%) and hidden_part (30%) with train_test_split, stratified by complex, with random_state=88. Take a .copy() of each, because you will add columns to them. Print the size of each, and how many of each kind the hidden part holds.
  2. Fit the same kind of forest on fit_part only. Name it forest_before.
  3. Add its kind for each hidden asteroid as the column forest of hidden_part.
  4. test_f1: the macro F1 of that column against the true kinds. Print it beside forest_fit_f1 and baseline_f1.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: fit_part, hidden_part, forest_before, test_f1.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 6¶
docs.text:
How much could the test score move with other asteroids like these?

Why: two classifiers whose scores differ by less than this are not clearly different. You will need the interval to judge every comparison from here on.

Look back at: the bootstrap, from How long was the Earth frozen? (08_how_long_frozen.ipynb), and the six made-up asteroids just above.

  1. Make a random generator, rng = np.random.default_rng(88), and an empty list, redrawn_f1.
  2. 1,000 times: redraw as many rows of hidden_part as it holds, with replacement (random_state=rng), and append the redraw's macro F1 of its forest column against its complex column.
  3. test_interval: the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the 1,000 scores. Print it beside test_f1.
  4. Draw a histogram of the 1,000 scores, with dashed vertical lines at the two ends of the interval and a solid one at test_f1. A good figure puts the numbers on it: the legend says the interval and the test score, so a reader needs no printout.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: redrawn_f1, test_interval.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 7¶
docs.text:
Which kind does the forest miss?

Why: an average can hide one kind done badly. If one kind's F1 is far below the others, that kind is where a better classifier has to gain.

Look back at: your macro_f1 of Your turn 2.

  1. f1_by_kind: a dict with keys "S", "C" and "X", each holding that kind's F1 score on the hidden asteroids (the forest column against complex). Print it. The three average to your test_f1.
  2. Draw it as a bar chart: one bar per kind in its colour, with its F1 written on the bar (plt.bar_label), a dotted line at test_f1, the y-axis from 0 to 1, axis labels and a title. The weak kind should stand out at a glance.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: f1_by_kind.

docs.title: 4. Does a different model, or more information, sort them better?¶
docs.text:
There are two ways to try to beat the forest. One is a different model that draws the boundaries between the kinds in another way. The other is more information: something about each asteroid that albedo and orbit do not hold. This section tries both, on the same hidden asteroids.

The SVM draws boundaries in a different way from a forest.

SVM: Of all the lines separating the two groups, take the one leaving the widest gap.

A forest cuts each column at a value, so its boundaries are steps; an SVM (with its default kernel) draws smooth curved ones. Because it measures distances across the columns, an albedo of 0.1 and an orbit of 2.8 AU must first be put on the same footing: StandardScaler rescales each column to an average of 0 and a spread of 1, and make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC()) joins the two, as in the basalt week.

Of all the lines that separate two groups, the SVM takes the one with the widest gap; the points on the edge of the gap, the support vectors, decide where it lies. Figure: Larhmam (CC BY-SA 4.0), via Wikimedia Commons.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 8¶
docs.text:
Does an SVM on the same four columns beat the forest on the hidden asteroids?

Why: if the forest's step-shaped boundaries are what holds it back, a model with smooth boundaries should do better with the same information.

Look back at: make_pipeline, StandardScaler and SVC, from Where was this basalt made? (10_where_basalt.ipynb).

  1. svm: a pipeline that scales the columns and then fits an SVM, fitted on fit_part's four inputs and complex (the default settings are fine; others are too).
  2. Add its kind for each hidden asteroid as the column svm of hidden_part.
  3. svm_test_f1: its macro F1 on the hidden asteroids. Print it beside test_f1 and test_interval; it should sit far above baseline_f1.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: svm, svm_test_f1.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 9¶
docs.text:
Does the forest sort the hidden asteroids better when it also knows their colour?

Why: this is new information, not a new model. If colour records what an asteroid is made of, adding it should lift the score far beyond the interval, and above all for X.

Look back at: your Your turns 5 and 7, and the spectrum just above.

  1. Add two columns to both fit_part and hidden_part: red_slope, R770 minus R462, and band_depth, R770 minus R902.
  2. six_inputs: the list of four_inputs and those two columns.
  3. colour_forest: the same kind of forest as in Your turn 5, fitted on fit_part's six inputs. Add its kind for each hidden asteroid as the column colour_forest of hidden_part.
  4. colour_test_f1: its macro F1 on the hidden asteroids, and colour_f1_by_kind: each kind's F1, as in Your turn 7. Print both beside test_f1, test_interval and f1_by_kind.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: six_inputs, colour_forest, colour_test_f1, colour_f1_by_kind.

docs.title: The leaderboard¶
docs.text:
leaderboard holds 368 classified asteroids you have never seen. It has the input columns of labelled (orbit, size, albedo and the colour bands) and row_id, the key of each answer, but no name and no class. template has the same row_ids and an empty complex column for your kinds.

  • Your entry is your own classifier, fitted on the training file here; never look up a class online. Do not look up or download the hidden answers (the published classes of the leaderboard asteroids); an entry built from them is not your model, and it scores 0.
  • The board shows a public score, the macro F1 on a random third of the 368 asteroids. The final score, on the other two thirds, is shown after the board closes, and your rank on it is graded. The board also shows a second final score on the asteroids smaller than 31.7 km.
  • So choose your entry by your own fair test, not by the public score. The public third is about 123 asteroids; a classifier picked because it moved that number is tuned to them, and the rank uses the others.
  • Up to 10 uploads that change submission.csv are scored. An upload that changes only the notebook is free.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 10¶
docs.text:
Your leaderboard entry: what kind is each of 368 hidden asteroids?

Why: this is the project's answer, scored on classes you have not seen, and ranked against the other students. Choose by your fair test: the public score is a third of the asteroids, and your rank is decided on the rest.

Look back at: your Your turns 5 and 9.

  1. Take the classifier your fair test chose: the forest with the two colour columns, unless your own tests on fit_part and hidden_part found something clearly better (all fourteen colour bands, an SVM on the colours, ...). Make a fresh final_model, and name its list of input columns final_inputs.
  2. Add any made columns (red_slope, band_depth) to labelled and to leaderboard, made the same way.
  3. Fit final_model on every row of labelled: the hidden part is data too.
  4. submission: a copy of template, with its complex column filled with your classifier's kind for each leaderboard asteroid. Save it with submission.to_csv("submission.csv", index=False).
  5. Print its first rows, its number of rows and of blanks, and how many of each kind it names.
  6. Run the self-check, then download submission.csv and this notebook and upload both together (the steps are under "What you hand in" above) to Final project: asteroids.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: final_model, final_inputs, submission.

docs.title: The question, answered¶
docs.text: Brightness and orbit sort rocky, carbon-rich and metal-bearing asteroids only part of the way: on asteroids it had never seen, a forest on albedo and orbit scored a macro F1 of 0.62, against 0.21 for always guessing S, and an SVM did no better. Two numbers read from each asteroid's colour, how red it is and whether it starts to dip after 800 nm, lifted the score to 0.88, most of all for the X group. What an asteroid is made of shows in the light it reflects, so the classifier improved when it was given that light.

docs.title: The open question¶
docs.text:
Can a classifier trained on big asteroids be trusted on the small ones that are most of the belt, and can colour ever tell metal from rock?

Every asteroid you trained on was classified because it is big and bright enough for a telescope spectrum. Most asteroids are neither. The next cell, given, runs your forest with colour from Your turn 9 on every asteroid in the training file that Gaia gave a full colour spectrum, classified or not, and draws the share of each kind it names for the small unclassified ones beside the true shares of the classified ones.

docs.title: Your own question¶
docs.text:
EPS 88 · PyEarth · final project. Open your own copy on DataHub: click here.

Bring an Earth-science question you really want to answer, find a good dataset for it, and answer it with what you have learned in this class: Python, data science and machine learning. The sections below are an outline, and the ideas under each are only suggestions to help you start. Explore freely: change the sections, try other methods, or go beyond this class if your question needs it. Just say what you did and why. Replace these instructions with your own work.

docs.title: What you hand in, and when¶
docs.text:
One Gradescope assignment, "Final project: your own question", takes everything.

  • Individual work. Start now; Gradescope takes uploads from Wed 25 Nov, and the project is due Wed 16 Dec at 23:59 Pacific time. Mon 7 Dec (RRR week) has no class, but you are welcome to come to the room in class time and work on your notebook.
  • Upload this notebook and the data files it reads (each under 50 MB). Upload as often as you like; the last upload is graded.
  • Before you upload, run Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells and check that it finishes without an error.

How it is graded (100 points), by hand:

Part Points What we look for The question 15 a clear question, why it matters, and what is already known The data 20 where it comes from, what it contains, and a first look at it The methods 30 several methods from this class, applied correctly, with a reason for each The results 20 clear figures and numbers that answer the question The discussion 10 how far to trust the answer, what did not work, and what you would do next Runs clean 5 the notebook runs from top to bottom without an error

docs.title: 1. The question¶
docs.text:
What do you want to find out, and why does it matter? What do scientists already know about it? Cite the papers or reports you used.

Ideas: start from something you are curious about, a recent event in the news, or a figure in a paper that you would like to check or extend.

docs.title: 2. The data¶
docs.text:
Where does the data come from, and what does it contain? Load it, look at it, and make a first figure.

Ideas: the data behind a research paper (often in its supplement or on Zenodo or PANGAEA), or a public archive such as the USGS earthquake catalogue, NOAA climate data or NASA Earthdata. A table you can read with pd.read_csv is the easiest place to start.

docs.title: 3. The methods¶
docs.text:
Apply methods from this class that suit your question, and say why you chose each. Where it helps, compare them with a simple answer that needs no model, and test them on data they did not learn from.

Ideas: fitting a line or a curve, classifying with logistic regression, a forest or an SVM, finding groups with clustering, a neural network, or a bootstrap to see how sure a number is. Use what fits your question; you do not need all of them.

docs.title: 4. The results¶
docs.text:
Show what you found, in figures and numbers. Give each figure labelled axes and a sentence saying what it shows.

Ideas: a map, a time series, a scatter plot of what you predicted against what happened, or a table comparing your methods.

docs.title: 5. Discussion¶
docs.text: What is your answer to the question? How far should we trust it? What did not work, and what would you try next?
